NAMES.name: height_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Full vertical height of the rectangular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor element, measured along the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The height of an antenna strap is the full vertical (poloidal) extent of the rectangular cross-section of the current-carrying strap conductor in an ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) antenna system. In ICRH antennas, the strap is the active radiating element that launches electromagnetic waves near the ion cyclotron frequency; its cross-sectional geometry governs current distribution, RF resistance, and coupling efficiency to the plasma.

For a rectangular strap cross-section, the three characteristic dimensions are height (this quantity), [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap) measured along the toroidal direction, and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) perpendicular to the strap plane. Height is measured along the vertical direction $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate. For strap conductors with annular cross-sections, the analogous radial dimensions are the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap) and [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap) of the conductor.

Typical ICRH strap heights range from a few centimeters to approximately 50 cm depending on antenna design and machine geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap, measured from the strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical boundary of the conductor.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of an antenna strap is the radial distance from the local strap conductor axis to the inner cylindrical surface of an annular strap cross-section. It applies to hollow or tubular ICRH strap conductors; straps with solid rectangular or otherwise non-annular cross-sections do not have this quantity. In a strap-local right-handed cylindrical $(r_s, \varphi_s, z_s)$ frame, $z_s$ follows the strap centerline or long current-carrying direction and $r_s$ is measured perpendicular to that axis.

The inner radius is the distance from the strap axis to the inner wall of the annulus:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \left|\mathbf{x}_\perp - \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_\perp$ is a point on the inner cylindrical boundary in a cross-section normal to the strap axis, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{axis}$ is the corresponding point on the strap centerline, and both positions are expressed in meters.

This quantity is obtained from antenna mechanical design, CAD geometry, or direct metrology of the conductor cross-section. Together with [outer_radius_of_antenna_strap](name:outer_radius_of_antenna_strap), it determines the annular conducting area, $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, and the wall thickness, $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$, which are important for cooling-channel design, RF current distribution, and impedance modeling at ion-cyclotron frequencies.

Typical ICRH tubular copper strap inner radii are about 0.005-0.03 m, depending on RF power, cooling requirements, and mechanical constraints. Larger high-power antenna conductors may use somewhat larger inner radii to reduce hydraulic resistance and thermal loading.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_antenna_strap
NAMES.short: Outer radial boundary of the annular cross-section of an ICRH antenna strap conductor, defining the larger of the two radii that bound the conductor annulus.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius of an ICRH antenna strap is the radial distance from the central axis of the strap conductor to the outer cylindrical surface of the annular cross-section. It marks the external boundary of the conductor material and, together with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_antenna_strap), fully specifies the radial extent of the annular conductor.

For an annular cross-section, the radial conductor wall thickness follows $\Delta r = r_\mathrm{out} - r_\mathrm{in}$, where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius. The nominal centerline radius reported by [radius_of_antenna_strap](name:radius_of_antenna_strap) is the mean $(r_\mathrm{out} + r_\mathrm{in})/2$.

This geometric parameter enters electromagnetic wave-coupling calculations and RF impedance modeling for ion cyclotron resonance heating systems. Together with the [width](name:width_of_antenna_strap), [height](name:height_of_antenna_strap), and [thickness](name:thickness_of_antenna_strap) of the conductor, it provides the complete geometric description needed for antenna strap simulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured radially outward from the strap conductor axis.

NAMES.name: reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: RF power returning from a lower hybrid antenna back toward the transmission line, representing the portion of forward power not coupled into the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Reflected power from a lower hybrid antenna is the component of incident RF power that fails to couple into the plasma and propagates back toward the transmission line source. Poor coupling arises from unfavorable edge plasma density gradients, suboptimal launcher–plasma distance, or antenna phasing conditions that mismatch the slow-wave accessibility window of the lower hybrid wave.

The power reflection coefficient $|\Gamma|^2$ relates reflected power $P_\text{ref}$ to forward power $P_\text{fwd}$:

$$
|\Gamma|^2 = \frac{P_\text{ref}}{P_\text{fwd}}
$$

where $P_\text{fwd}$ is the total power delivered to the antenna from the transmission line. The [launched power](name:launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) into the vacuum vessel is the difference $P_\text{fwd} - P_\text{ref}$, and the [total absorbed power](name:total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) accounts for remaining waveguide and plasma losses. The gross RF input to the antenna system is captured by the parent quantity `power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna`.

Reflected power is monitored in real time using directional couplers embedded in the transmission line feeding the lower hybrid launcher. In well-coupled regimes, $P_\text{ref}/P_\text{fwd}$ is typically below 5–10%; transients such as L–H mode transitions or edge density fluctuations can briefly increase the reflected fraction to 30–50%, triggering protection interlocks. The analogous quantity for ion cyclotron systems is [reflected power of an IC antenna](name:reflected_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna).

NAMES.name: total_absorbed_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna
NAMES.short: Net RF power deposited into the plasma by the lower hybrid antenna system, aggregated over all individual antennas.
NAMES.long:
The total absorbed power of the lower hybrid antenna system quantifies the net RF energy deposition rate from the LHCD launcher array into the confined plasma, summed over all individual antennas. It is the primary power accounting metric for lower hybrid current drive and supplemental electron heating, governing the wave energy available for driving non-inductive plasma current.

The absorbed power is defined as the volume integral of the local LH wave power deposition density over the plasma volume:

$$
P_\text{abs} = \int_V q_\text{LH}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q_\text{LH}(\mathbf{r})$ is the volumetric LH wave absorption density at position $\mathbf{r}$ within the plasma volume $V$.

This quantity is distinct from the [total launched power](name:total_launched_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna), which represents power entering the vacuum vessel and can exceed the absorbed power by any residual absorption in the edge region or scrape-off layer that does not reach the confined plasma. In practice, the absorbed power is estimated from directional-coupler measurements of the [forward power](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and [reflected power](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) on the high-power RF transmission lines, corrected for resistive dissipation in the launcher structure and waveguide network.

In current LHCD systems on medium-to-large tokamaks, total absorbed power levels range from 1-10 MW.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Nitrogen ion number density evaluated at the divertor target.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ion number density at the divertor target quantifies the local concentration of ionized nitrogen in the plasma immediately adjacent to the divertor plate surface. Nitrogen is commonly seeded as an impurity into the divertor region to enhance radiative power dissipation through atomic line emission, promoting plasma detachment and reducing peak heat loads on the target.

The ion number density $n_\mathrm{N}$ is defined as the zeroth velocity moment of the nitrogen ion velocity distribution:

$$
n_\mathrm{N} = \int f_\mathrm{N}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $f_\mathrm{N}(\mathbf{v})$ is the nitrogen ion phase-space distribution function and integration is over all velocities $\mathbf{v}$.

This quantity is inferred from optical spectroscopy of nitrogen line emission in the divertor plasma, or from Langmuir probe measurements combined with spectroscopic impurity fraction estimates. It is a key parameter for characterizing impurity seeding scenarios and controlling plasma detachment. Analogous quantities for other seeded impurity species include [neon_density_at_divertor_target](name:neon_density_at_divertor_target), [argon_density_at_divertor_target](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target), [oxygen_density_at_divertor_target](name:oxygen_density_at_divertor_target), and [xenon_density_at_divertor_target](name:xenon_density_at_divertor_target); this quantity is the nitrogen-specific component of the parent [density_at_divertor_target](name:density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when nitrogen ions are present at the divertor target.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Number density of argon ions evaluated at the H-mode pedestal top, where the steep-gradient edge transport barrier meets the flatter core profile.
NAMES.long:
The argon ion number density at the pedestal top quantifies the local concentration of argon impurity ions at the shoulder of the H-mode edge transport barrier. The pedestal top is the radial position where the steep edge-gradient region transitions to the shallower core profile, establishing the inner boundary condition for argon impurity transport into the plasma core and setting the argon inventory available for radiative power exhaust.

The local number density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the argon ion distribution function $f_{\rm Ar}$:

$$
n_{\rm Ar} = \int f_{\rm Ar}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the ion velocity. The contribution of pedestal argon to the free electron density is $n_e^{\rm Ar} = \bar{Z}_{\rm Ar} \, n_{\rm Ar}$, where $\bar{Z}_{\rm Ar}$ is the mean ionization state of argon at the pedestal.

Pedestal argon density is typically inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or spectroscopic analysis of argon line emission, supplemented by edge impurity transport modeling. Comparing this value with [argon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:argon_density_at_plasma_boundary) characterizes the argon density gradient across the pedestal, while [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) reflects core accumulation. The analogous quantity for neon seeding is [neon_density_at_pedestal](name:neon_density_at_pedestal). This quantity forms part of the broader [density_at_pedestal](name:density_at_pedestal) family describing impurity and main-ion pedestal characterization.

Typical argon pedestal densities in seeded H-mode discharges range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, several orders of magnitude below the main ion pedestal density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when argon ions populate the pedestal plasma; vanishes in the absence of argon seeding.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Boundary-averaged number density of argon ions on the plasma boundary, represented by the last closed flux surface separating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. Unless a charge state is specified separately, argon ions refers to all ionization stages combined.
NAMES.long:
Argon density at the plasma boundary is the surface-averaged number density of argon ions on the last closed flux surface, also called the separatrix. It provides a boundary-representative measure of argon impurity content, distinct from local poloidal or toroidal variations, and is the argon analog of other impurity boundary densities such as [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary) and [xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:xenon_density_at_plasma_boundary).

The boundary average over the separatrix surface is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar},b} = \left\langle n_{\mathrm{Ar}} \right\rangle_{S_\mathrm{sep}} = \frac{\int_{S_\mathrm{sep}} n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{x})\, dA}{\int_{S_\mathrm{sep}} dA}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{sep}$ is the last closed flux surface, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local total argon ion number density, and $dA$ is the surface area element. Unless an individual charge state is explicitly specified, $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ denotes the sum over all argon ionization stages.

In experiments, this quantity is inferred from argon line emission using spectroscopic measurements together with electron density, electron temperature, and collisional-radiative or impurity transport modeling. In simulations and equilibrium-edge coupling, it is often computed by averaging the modeled argon density over the separatrix, without assuming that the impurity density is constant on that surface.

Typical values are about $10^{14}-10^{16}$ m^-3 for trace argon concentrations and about $10^{16}-10^{18}$ m^-3 during deliberate radiative seeding, depending on gas injection rate, edge temperature, ionization balance, transport, and plasma size. These values are usually small compared with the total electron or main-ion density at the boundary, but can strongly affect edge radiation because argon is a high-Z impurity.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Dimensionless magnetic shear — the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius — evaluated at the H-mode pedestal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear quantifies the spatial variation of field-line helicity across nested flux surfaces, controlling the stability of MHD and drift-wave modes. Evaluated at the pedestal — the steep pressure-gradient transport barrier characteristic of H-mode confinement — it enters directly into peeling-ballooning stability criteria governing edge-localized modes and sets constraints on the maximum achievable pedestal pressure.

The pedestal magnetic shear is defined as:

$$
s = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}}
$$

where $q$ is the local safety factor and $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the separatrix. This is the scalar pedestal-locus counterpart of the radial profile [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal), and is analogous in structure to [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) evaluated on axis and [magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier) evaluated at internal barriers.

Pedestal magnetic shear is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction, combining external magnetic measurements with internal profile constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry or pressure-profile data. In conventional H-mode pedestals, $s$ spans 1–5, reflecting the rapid increase in $q$ across the narrow pedestal width; reversed-shear configurations can yield negative values near the pedestal foot.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q$ increases with increasing $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$, corresponding to outward-increasing field-line helicity toward the plasma edge.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen impurity ions evaluated at the plasma boundary (separatrix), representing the impurity concentration at the last closed flux surface separating confined plasma from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Nitrogen ion number density at the plasma boundary quantifies the concentration of nitrogen impurity ions at the separatrix — the last closed flux surface demarcating the magnetically confined plasma from the open-field-line scrape-off layer. This is the nitrogen-species instantiation of [density_at_plasma_boundary](name:density_at_plasma_boundary). Nitrogen is routinely injected into tokamaks as a controlled impurity to enhance radiative dissipation of exhaust power and reduce peak heat loads at divertor targets.

The boundary value reflects the balance between impurity sources (gas injection, ionization of recycled neutrals) and outward transport through the scrape-off layer. Its magnitude relative to the main-ion density influences the effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ and the radiated power fraction at the plasma edge. The toroidal flow of nitrogen at the same location is separately captured by [toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_nitrogen_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

The quantity is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of nitrogen line emission in the edge and divertor regions combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from fluid impurity transport simulations constrained by bolometric data. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the nitrogen injection rate and edge plasma density. Analogous separatrix densities for other impurity species include [neon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:neon_density_at_plasma_boundary), [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:oxygen_density_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive definite, as number density is a particle count per unit volume and does not change sign under any coordinate transformation.

NAMES.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the carbon impurity ion bulk flow velocity at the plasma boundary, resolved in the IMAS cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the local value at the last-closed flux surface, not a flux-surface average.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal carbon velocity at the plasma boundary is the component of the carbon impurity ion bulk flow along the toroidal direction at the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. The toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity denotes a local boundary value; the corresponding flux-surface-averaged quantity is [toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_carbon_velocity_at_plasma_boundary).

The local toroidal component is defined by projecting the carbon bulk velocity onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{C}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}} \cdot \hat{\phi} = R\Omega_{\mathrm{C}}
$$

where $v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon toroidal velocity in m.s^-1, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon ion bulk velocity in m.s^-1, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, $R$ is the major radius in m, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{C}}$ is the carbon toroidal angular rotation frequency in s^-1.

In practice, this velocity is commonly inferred from Doppler shifts of carbon spectral lines, often using charge-exchange or passive edge spectroscopy, after correcting for viewing geometry and projecting the measured line-of-sight velocity onto the toroidal direction. The plasma boundary location is usually supplied by magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, and the measured or modeled velocity is mapped to the last-closed flux surface. When only an average over the boundary flux surface is intended, the flux-surface-averaged standard name should be used instead.

Typical absolute values at the plasma boundary are of order $10^3-5 \times 10^4$ m.s^-1 in tokamak edge plasmas. Values can be close to zero in weakly rotating conditions and can approach $10^5$ m.s^-1 in plasmas with strong external torque or steep edge rotation gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the carbon ion flow is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: parallel_diamagnetic_current_density
NAMES.short: Field-aligned component of the diamagnetic current density, projected onto the local magnetic field direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel diamagnetic current density is the projection of the total [diamagnetic_current_density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) onto the local magnetic field direction at each point in the edge plasma. The diamagnetic current arises from the gyration of magnetized particles in a pressure-gradient field; in an isotropic ideal plasma, $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p)/B^2$ is purely perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$, so its parallel component vanishes in that limit. In more complete descriptions including pressure anisotropy, finite Larmor radius corrections, or the inhomogeneous magnetic geometry of the tokamak edge, a field-aligned component emerges and must be tracked separately.

The parallel projection is defined as:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{dia}$ is the diamagnetic current density vector and $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field of magnitude $B$.

In edge plasma current decompositions, this component is closely related to [parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which encodes the same physical mechanism through the explicit drift formalism. The toroidal_diamagnetic_current_density provides the complementary geometric projection of the same vector field onto the toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of the local magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$.

NAMES.name: thermal_plasma_pressure
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure of the bulk thermal plasma, equal to the sum of electron and bulk-ion thermal pressure contributions and excluding fast, suprathermal, or runaway populations.
NAMES.long:
Thermal plasma pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure associated with particle populations close to local thermodynamic equilibrium. It includes the thermal electron contribution and the contributions from bulk thermal ion species, but excludes nonthermal populations such as fast ions, suprathermal tails, and runaway electrons. It is the thermal component of the more general [plasma_pressure](name:plasma_pressure) and is closely related to [thermal_pressure](name:thermal_pressure), [total_electron_pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), and [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure).

For Maxwellian or near-Maxwellian thermal species, the pressure is defined by the species density-temperature sum:

$$
p_\mathrm{th} = n_e k_B T_e + \sum_i n_i k_B T_i
$$

where $n_e$ and $n_i$ are electron and bulk-ion number densities in m$^{-3}$, $T_e$ and $T_i$ are thermodynamic temperatures in K, $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant, and the sum is over thermal ion species. When temperatures are tabulated in eV, the equivalent SI pressure is obtained by replacing $k_B T_s$ with $e T_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge and $T_s$ is the temperature value in eV; this gives $p_\mathrm{th}$ in Pa.

In practice, thermal plasma pressure is computed from measured or modeled density and temperature for electrons and bulk ions, with quasineutrality often used to constrain the ion density composition when not all ion species are independently measured. It enters fluid and magnetohydrodynamic force balance through the pressure-gradient term and sets the thermal part of quantities such as beta, sound speed, and parallel pressure balance.

Representative edge-plasma values span a wide range because both density and temperature vary strongly across confined, near-separatrix, and scrape-off-layer regions. For densities of about $10^{18}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ and electron-plus-ion thermal temperatures of about 1-200 eV, thermal plasma pressure is typically of order 0.1-$10^4$ Pa.

NAMES.name: current_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Electric current carried by a single discrete plasma-filament element in an axisymmetric filamentary representation of the distributed plasma current.
NAMES.long:
In the filamentary model of an axisymmetric plasma, the spatially distributed plasma current is represented as an array of discrete annular current-carrying elements, each called a filament. The current of each element is its individual contribution to the net toroidal plasma current, and the ensemble of filament currents constitutes a discrete model of the plasma current density distribution across the poloidal cross-section.

The total plasma current $I_p$ is recovered by summing the contributions from all filament elements:

$$
I_p = \sum_k I_k
$$

where $I_k$ is the current of the $k$-th filament element and the sum runs over all elements in the filamentary array.

Filament currents are determined during equilibrium reconstruction or electromagnetic circuit-equation integration, treating the plasma as a collection of discrete current sources. Each filament element is fully characterized by its current together with its geometric descriptors — including area_of_plasma_filament, [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament), and [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament) — which together define the local current-density contribution. The analogous quantity for the conducting vessel structure is [toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: current_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed conductor current carried by a poloidal-field coil winding. It is the electrical current in amperes through the winding conductor, distinct from the ampere-turn product obtained by multiplying by the number of turns.
NAMES.long:
Current of a poloidal-field coil is the signed electrical current carried by the coil winding conductor. For a multi-turn winding, this quantity is the conductor current $I_\mathrm{PF}$, while the magnetomotive ampere-turn product is $N I_\mathrm{PF}$, where $N$ is the number of turns.

The vacuum poloidal-flux contribution of a coil can be written, for a field point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system where $R$ is major radius in meters and $Z$ is vertical height in meters, as

$$
\psi_\mathrm{coil}(R,Z) = M_\mathrm{coil}(R,Z) I_\mathrm{PF}
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{coil}$ is in Wb, $I_\mathrm{PF}$ is in A, and $M_\mathrm{coil}$ is the mutual inductance in Wb/A between the modeled coil winding and the flux surface label at $(R,Z)$. When $M_\mathrm{coil}$ is defined per conductor current, it includes the winding turn count and the finite coil cross-section represented by the coil model; if a per-turn Green-function response is used instead, the factor $N I_\mathrm{PF}$ appears explicitly.

In practice, poloidal-field coil currents are measured with electrical current transducers in the coil circuits and may also be estimated or constrained during equilibrium reconstruction. These currents determine the externally applied poloidal magnetic-field and flux contributions used for plasma position, boundary, and shape control, together with plasma current and currents in passive conducting structures.

Representative values are strongly device- and coil-dependent, ranging from kA-scale currents in smaller or auxiliary poloidal-field coils to several tens of kA in large shaping or vertical-field coils.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the conventional current in the winding flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: elongation_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axis of each nested magnetic flux surface, parameterizing the poloidal elongation of plasma shape as a function of the flux label.
NAMES.long:
The elongation $\kappa$ of a flux surface is a dimensionless measure of how vertically stretched the poloidal cross-section of a nested toroidal magnetic surface is relative to its horizontal extent. A value of $\kappa = 1$ denotes a circular cross-section, while $\kappa > 1$ characterizes the vertically elongated shapes used in modern tokamaks to improve MHD stability and energy confinement.

The defining relation is:

$$
\kappa = \frac{b}{a}
$$

where $b$ is the vertical semi-axis (half-height measured from the geometric center of the surface) and $a$ is the horizontal semi-axis (half-width) of the flux surface in the poloidal cross-section.

The elongation profile is derived from MHD equilibrium reconstruction by extracting the geometric shape parameters of each nested flux surface obtained from the Grad-Shafranov solution, parameterized as a function of the poloidal flux coordinate $\psi$ across the minor radius. The radial variation of $\kappa$ is captured by [radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface](name:radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface). Complementary poloidal shape descriptors include [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), which characterizes the poloidal corner geometry, and [area_of_flux_surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which gives the total enclosed cross-sectional area.

Typical values rise from $\kappa \approx 1.0$ near the magnetic axis to $\kappa \approx 1.5$–$2.0$ at the plasma boundary in shaped tokamak discharges; ITER is designed for a boundary elongation near $\kappa = 1.85$.

NAMES.name: elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the plasma boundary vertical half-height to its minor radius, quantifying the overall vertical elongation of the plasma cross-sectional shape at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The elongation $\kappa$ is a global dimensionless shape parameter characterizing the vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio of the plasma cross-section at the plasma boundary. It enters directly into MHD stability criteria, the Troyon beta limit, and confinement scaling relations, making it one of the primary descriptors of plasma shaping alongside triangularity.

The defining relation is:

$$
\kappa = \frac{b}{a}
$$

where $b$ is the vertical half-height of the plasma boundary (half the total poloidal extent between the uppermost and lowermost boundary points) and $a$ is the plasma minor radius (half the horizontal full width at the midplane).

The quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the closed poloidal boundary contour to external magnetic measurements and internal pressure or current profiles. The boundary extremal coordinates determine $b$ and $a$ directly.

A circular cross-section corresponds to $\kappa = 1$. Modern shaped tokamaks typically operate in the range $\kappa = 1.5$–$2.0$; strongly elongated configurations approach $\kappa \approx 1.8$–$2.0$. Higher elongation increases plasma volume at fixed minor radius and improves the MHD beta limit, but at the cost of reduced vertical stability requiring active position control.

When up-down asymmetry is significant, this global parameter decomposes into [upper elongation](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and [lower elongation], each measuring the half-boundary contribution. The radial variation of elongation across nested flux surfaces is captured by [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_area_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Total geometric surface area of the last closed flux surface (plasma boundary), computed by revolving the closed poloidal boundary contour through the full toroidal revolution around the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The flux surface area at the plasma boundary quantifies the full three-dimensional surface area of the last closed flux surface (LCFS) — the outermost toroidal magnetic surface that bounds the confined plasma. As a global equilibrium scalar, it is sensitive to the plasma major radius, minor radius, and poloidal shape, including elongation and triangularity, and provides a natural normalization for surface-integrated transport and heat-load analyzes.

For an axisymmetric toroidal equilibrium, the LCFS surface area follows from revolving the closed poloidal boundary contour around the torus symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
S_\mathrm{LCFS} = 2\pi \oint_\mathrm{LCFS} R \, d\ell_p
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate and $d\ell_p$ is the differential poloidal arc length along the boundary contour.

This quantity is obtained from magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium reconstruction: once the LCFS geometry is determined, the surface area follows by direct geometric integration. It appears in global power-balance studies, surface-averaged heat-load estimates, and geometric normalizations in confinement scaling. The full radial profile of flux-surface areas is [flux_surface_area](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), of which this is the outermost value; the corresponding poloidal flux label at the boundary is given by [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). Typical values range from tens of m² for compact tokamaks to several hundred m² for large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R > 0$ and the LCFS forms a single well-defined closed toroidal surface, conditions satisfied in all standard confined equilibria.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the major radius coordinate R on each nested magnetic flux surface, yielding the mean distance from the toroidal symmetry axis weighted by the inverse poloidal field strength.
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface averaged major radius $\langle R \rangle$ is the mean value of the cylindrical major radius coordinate $R$ over a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface, weighted by the local inverse poloidal magnetic field magnitude. It belongs to the family of geometric metric coefficients (sometimes denoted $gm8$ in neoclassical transport literature) that enter the flux-surface-averaged forms of transport and equilibrium equations, and is the flux-surface-averaging transformation of the parent quantity [major_radius](name:major_radius).

The defining expression is:

$$
\langle R \rangle = \frac{\oint R \, \frac{dl}{B_p}}{\oint \frac{dl}{B_p}}
$$

where $l$ is the poloidal arc length along the flux surface and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude, with integrals taken over one complete poloidal circuit. Because $B_p$ is smaller on the outboard low-field side, field lines dwell longer there, and $\langle R \rangle$ is shifted toward larger $R$ relative to a simple geometric centroid; it lies between the [inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface](name:inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface) and the [outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface](name:outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface).

This coefficient is computed directly from the magnetic geometry obtained in equilibrium reconstruction, and is closely related to [flux_surface_average_magnetic_field](name:flux_surface_average_magnetic_field) and [flux_surface_averaged_curvature](name:flux_surface_averaged_curvature), which are derived from the same surface-averaging procedure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: height_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament element, measured parallel to the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
In the filamentary model of plasma current distribution used for equilibrium reconstruction, the plasma current is represented by a set of discrete elements, each assigned a cross-sectional geometry. When the cross-section is modeled as a rectangle, the height defines the full vertical extent of that rectangle measured along the $Z$ axis of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical coordinate.

For a rectangular filament element with height $h$ and horizontal width $w$, the rectangular cross-sectional area is $A = h \times w$, which is consistent with area_of_plasma_filament. The height is specified alongside [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament) to fully characterize the rectangular geometry; for annular cross-sections, the radial bounds are instead described by [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament) and [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament).

The height is a fixed geometric input parameter assigned when constructing the filamentary current model, with its value chosen to resolve the spatial scale of interest in the current distribution. Typical values range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters depending on the resolution requirements of the equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical extent of the filament cross-section is measured in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a plasma current-carrying filament element, marking the boundary between the hollow central region and the conducting annular zone.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius $r_\mathrm{inner}$ specifies the radial position of the inner wall of an annular plasma filament cross-section, defining the boundary between the hollow (non-current-carrying) core and the conducting annular region. In filamentary models of distributed plasma current, individual elements may be assigned annular geometries bounded at the outer wall by [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament) $r_\mathrm{outer}$, with current flowing only in the region $r_\mathrm{inner} \leq r \leq r_\mathrm{outer}$.

The conducting cross-sectional area of the annular element is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2 \right)
$$

where $A$ is the geometric cross-sectional area corresponding to area_of_plasma_filament. A valid annular geometry requires $0 \leq r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$; setting $r_\mathrm{inner} = 0$ recovers a solid circular cross-section with no hollow core.

This parameter is a geometric input to the filamentary discretization of the plasma current distribution and is always specified alongside [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament). For rectangular filament cross-sections the analogous spatial parameters are [height_of_plasma_filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament) and [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inner boundary of the annular cross-section is measured outward from the local geometric center of the filament element.

NAMES.name: internal_inductance
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of plasma current profile peaking, defined as the volume-integrated squared poloidal magnetic field normalized by the square of the total plasma current and the reference major radius.
NAMES.long:
The internal inductance $l_i$ is a dimensionless global equilibrium parameter that characterizes the shape of the plasma current density profile. A broadly distributed current results in a lower $l_i$ (near 0.5 for a circular cross-section with uniform current), while a strongly peaked profile raises it toward 2. This quantity enters vertical stability analysis and the plasma–coil circuit equations relating the resistive loop voltage to the time-evolving current distribution.

The $l_{i,3}$ definition relates $l_i$ to the volume integral of the squared poloidal magnetic field:

$$
l_{i,3} = \frac{2}{R_0 \mu_0^2 I_p^2} \int B_p^2 \, dV
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius of the geometric axis, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_p$ is the total plasma current, $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude, and the integral is taken over the plasma volume.

The internal inductance is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements, or estimated from the resistive diffusion evolution of the current profile during ramp-up and flat-top phases. In H-mode flat-top conditions, $l_i$ lies in the range 0.7–1.2; sawtooth-free operation and current ramp-up can drive values toward 2. The [total plasma inductance] $L_p$ combines $l_i$ with the external inductance contribution to give the total inductive impedance of the plasma circuit.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any current-carrying plasma, since $l_{i,3}$ is proportional to $\int B_p^2 \, dV$, which is intrinsically non-negative.

NAMES.name: lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Ratio of the lower boundary half-height to the plasma minor radius, describing the vertical elongation of the plasma cross-section below the geometric axis.
NAMES.long:
The lower elongation $\kappa_{\rm lower}$ is a dimensionless shape parameter quantifying the vertical extent of the lower half of the plasma boundary cross-section relative to the plasma minor radius, complementing [upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) for up-down asymmetric plasma shaping.

The defining relation is:

$$
\kappa_{\rm lower} = \frac{Z_{\rm axis} - Z_{\rm lower}}{a}
$$

where $Z_{\rm axis}$ is the vertical coordinate of the plasma geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z_{\rm lower}$ is the vertical coordinate of the lowermost point of the boundary contour, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius.

When $\kappa_{\rm lower}$ differs from [upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary), the plasma has up-down asymmetric shaping, which is characteristic of single-null divertor configurations with the X-point in the lower divertor. The global [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) captures the overall vertical half-height ratio for symmetric boundaries, but $\kappa_{\rm lower}$ and its upper counterpart together fully characterize asymmetric boundary shapes relevant to MHD stability and confinement modeling. Typical values range from 1.0 in near-circular lower halves to approximately 2.0 in strongly shaped H-mode plasmas. The quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the boundary contour in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane using external magnetic measurements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lowermost point of the plasma boundary contour lies below the geometric axis, i.e., $Z_{\rm lower} < Z_{\rm axis}$.

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shape parameter quantifying the deviation of the lower inner quadrant of the plasma cross-section from a reference ellipse, as part of the higher-order Luce boundary parameterization.
NAMES.long:
The lower inner squareness $\zeta_{LI}$ characterizes how much the plasma boundary in the lower inner quadrant — below the equatorial plane and on the high-field inboard side — departs from the reference ellipse defined by the plasma elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$. It is a higher-order geometric shape descriptor that refines the plasma boundary representation beyond what elongation and triangularity alone can capture.

In the Luce boundary-shape framework, the plasma cross-section is divided into four quadrants, each assigned an independent squareness coefficient $\zeta$ to represent up-down and inner-outer asymmetries. A value of zero indicates that the boundary in the lower inner quadrant coincides exactly with the local reference ellipse; positive values indicate the boundary extends beyond the ellipse (producing a squarer, more rectangular profile in that quadrant), while negative values indicate the boundary lies inward of the ellipse (a more rounded profile).

This coefficient is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the reconstructed plasma boundary contour — derived primarily from magnetic diagnostics and boundary position measurements — to the higher-order shape parameterization. It is the lower-half counterpart of [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and together with [lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), provides the complete quadrant-resolved squareness description of the plasma boundary, complementing the [inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) aggregate.

Typical values in diverted tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-0.4$ to $0.4$, with the sign and magnitude sensitive to X-point position, divertor geometry, and poloidal field coil configuration.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower inner quadrant of the plasma boundary extends outward beyond the reference ellipse, producing a squarer cross-section profile in that region.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce squareness coefficient for the lower outer quadrant of each flux surface, measuring the deviation of that corner from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{lo}$ is the quadrant-specific Luce (2013) shape parameter describing how the lower outboard corner of a poloidal flux-surface cross-section departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width $a$, and elongation $\kappa$. As one of four independent corner squareness coefficients, it captures asymmetries — both up-down and in-out — that a single symmetric squareness value cannot resolve.

In the Luce parametric form, the lower outer quadrant shape is governed by:

$$
Z(\theta) = Z_0 + a\,\kappa\sin\!\bigl(\theta + \zeta_{lo}\sin 2\theta\bigr)
$$

where $\theta \in (-\pi/2,\,0)$ parameterizes the lower outer quadrant, $Z_0$ is the geometric center height of the flux surface, $a$ is the horizontal minor half-width, and $\kappa$ is the local [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). Setting $\zeta_{lo} = 0$ recovers a pure ellipse in that quadrant.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the Luce parametric contour to each nested flux surface computed from magnetics and internal measurements. At the outermost closed flux surface the value reduces to [lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary). The upper-outer analog is [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), the lower inner counterpart is [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), and the up-down symmetric outer combination is [outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower outer corner of the flux-surface cross-section bulges outward beyond the reference ellipse, increasing the cross-sectional area of the lower outer quadrant relative to the elliptic baseline.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Shape parameter for the lower outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary measuring its deviation from an inscribed ellipse, following the Luce (2013) four-corner squareness decomposition.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{lo}$ is one of four corner-specific shape parameters in the Luce (2013) plasma boundary parameterization, describing how much the lower outer quadrant of the plasma cross-section boundary deviates from an inscribed ellipse with the same elongation and triangularity. The lower outer quadrant spans the outboard lower region of the cross-section, characterized by increasing major radius $R$ and decreasing height $Z$ from the geometric midplane.

In the Luce framework the boundary near each corner is locally fitted by a superellipse whose exponent $n_{lo}$ controls the corner curvature:

$$
\zeta_{lo} = 1 - \frac{2}{n_{lo}}
$$

where $n_{lo} = 2$ corresponds to a pure ellipse ($\zeta_{lo} = 0$), $n_{lo} > 2$ produces more rectangular corners ($\zeta_{lo} > 0$), and $n_{lo} < 2$ produces more rounded corners ($\zeta_{lo} < 0$). The squareness parameters capture fourth-order boundary shaping effects that are independent of elongation and triangularity.

The squareness parameters are obtained from equilibrium reconstructions by fitting the reconstructed last-closed flux surface or separatrix boundary contour. They are particularly relevant for diverted configurations where divertor geometry shapes the lower boundary region.

Typical values of $\zeta_{lo}$ in tokamak plasmas range from approximately $-0.3$ to $+0.3$. Together with [lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary), it completes the four-corner boundary shape decomposition; the parent quantity [outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) describes outer-quadrant squareness without the upper/lower distinction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower outer quadrant of the boundary protrudes further outward than the ellipse inscribed at the same elongation and triangularity.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shaping parameter measuring the inward horizontal displacement of the lower vertical extremum of a nested toroidal flux surface, normalized by the flux-surface minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity of a flux surface quantifies how far the lower part of the poloidal cross-section is shifted inward relative to the magnetic axis. It separates up-down asymmetric shaping from the corresponding upper triangularity; for an up-down symmetric surface the upper and lower triangularities are equal, and an unsplit triangularity is commonly represented by that common value or by an average of the two.

In the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the lower triangularity is defined by

$$
\delta_\mathrm{lower} = \frac{R_\mathrm{axis} - R_\mathrm{lower}}{a}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis, $R_\mathrm{lower}$ is the major radius of the point on the flux surface with the lowest vertical position $Z$, and $a = (R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is the minor radius of the same flux surface determined from its outermost and innermost midplane intersections.

It is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction or analytic flux-surface description by locating the magnetic axis, tracing the chosen closed flux contour, finding its lower vertical extremum, and normalizing the horizontal displacement by the contour minor radius. Positive values correspond to the lower extremum lying at smaller major radius than the magnetic axis, while negative values indicate an outward-shifted lower extremum.

Typical values range from about -0.4 to 0.8. Conventional positive-triangularity tokamak plasmas often have values around 0.2-0.6 near the outer flux surfaces, nearly circular surfaces have values close to 0, and negative-triangularity configurations have values below 0.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Lower triangularity is a dimensionless shape parameter for the lower half of the plasma boundary in the IMAS cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is the inward displacement of the boundary point at minimum Z relative to the geometric center, normalized by half the maximum-minus-minimum R extent.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity $\delta_{\rm lower}$ quantifies triangular shaping of the lower half of the plasma boundary in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It compares the major radius of the lower boundary extremum with the geometric center constructed from the inboard and outboard radial extrema of the same boundary.

The geometric definition uses the boundary minor-radius normalization:

$$
\delta_{\rm lower} = \frac{R_0 - R_{\rm low}}{a}, \qquad R_0 = \frac{R_{\rm out}+R_{\rm in}}{2}, \qquad a = \frac{R_{\rm out}-R_{\rm in}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\rm low}$ is the major radius in meters at the minimum-$Z$ point of the boundary, $R_{\rm in}$ and $R_{\rm out}$ are the minimum and maximum boundary major radii in meters, $R_0$ is the geometric-center major radius in meters, and $a$ is the [minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary) in meters. This construction makes inward lower shaping, $R_{\rm low}<R_0$, positive and outward lower shaping negative.

It is computed from an equilibrium boundary contour by locating the inboard, outboard, and lower vertical extrema and applying the geometric construction above. The lower value can differ from [upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) in vertically asymmetric, single-null, or double-null configurations, while [minor_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:minor_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary) denotes a related but distinct boundary-shape measure.

Typical values are order-unity dimensionless numbers: nearly circular or weakly shaped lower boundaries are close to 0, positive-triangularity tokamak plasmas commonly lie around 0.2-0.6, and reverse-triangularity lower shaping is negative.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the active limiter point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It gives the radial distance from the machine symmetry axis to the material contact point that sets the outermost closed flux surface in a limited plasma.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of the active limiter point is the $R$ coordinate of the limiter contact point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The active limiter point is the material point at which a limited plasma boundary contacts the surrounding structure; this coordinate identifies its radial location only.

For an active limiter point with Cartesian coordinates $(x_a, y_a, z_a)$ in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame whose $\hat{z}$ direction is vertical, the corresponding major radius is

$$
R_a = \sqrt{x_a^2 + y_a^2}
$$

where $x_a$ and $y_a$ are measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $R_a$ is the major-radius coordinate of the active limiter point.

In equilibrium interpretation, this value is determined from the limiter geometry and the reconstructed last-closed flux surface for a limited configuration. It is distinct from the major radius of a general plasma-boundary point, from the major radius of the closest wall point, and from the wall gap, which describes a separation distance rather than the contact coordinate.

Typical values range from about 0.2-8 m across present and planned tokamaks, depending on machine size and whether the active contact is on an inboard, outboard, upper, or lower limiter surface.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius R coordinate of the first-wall point that is geometrically closest to the plasma boundary or magnetic separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate $R$ of the closest wall point locates, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the position on the first wall at minimum Euclidean distance from the plasma boundary or magnetic separatrix. This proximity measure characterizes the tightest clearance between the confined plasma and the surrounding vessel structure, directly relevant to heat-load assessment, disruption halo-current modeling, and plasma-shape control.

The closest wall point $(R_{cw}, Z_{cw})$ is the element of the first-wall contour $\mathcal{W}$ in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section that minimizes the distance to the plasma boundary contour $\partial\Omega$:

$$
(R_{cw}, Z_{cw}) = \underset{(R_w,\,Z_w)\,\in\,\mathcal{W}}{\arg\min}\; d\bigl((R_w, Z_w),\,\partial\Omega\bigr)
$$

where $d$ is the Euclidean distance in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane. The reported quantity is the $R$ component of this minimizing wall point.

The closest wall point is identified during equilibrium reconstruction by comparing the reconstructed plasma boundary contour against the stored first-wall geometry. In limited plasmas, [major_radius_of_active_limiter_point](name:major_radius_of_active_limiter_point) often coincides with this quantity, since the active limiter contact point is by definition the nearest wall element. For diverted plasmas, the closest approach is frequently near the divertor target as characterized by [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point). The radial position of the geometric center is given by [major_radius_of_geometric_axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis), providing a central reference against which wall clearances can be contextualized.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the closest wall point lies at a radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis measured in the $+\hat{R}$ direction.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the plasma current center, defined as the current-density-weighted centroid of the toroidal current distribution in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The current center is the centroid of the tokamak plasma toroidal current density distribution projected onto the poloidal plane. Its major-radius coordinate $R_\mathrm{cc}$ quantifies the effective radial location from which the net plasma current appears to flow, and is a compact global descriptor of the equilibrium current profile.

The defining relation is the current-density-weighted average of the major radius $R$ over the poloidal cross-section $A$:

$$
R_\mathrm{cc} = \frac{\displaystyle\int_A j_\phi \, R \, dA}{\displaystyle\int_A j_\phi \, dA}
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the current density and $R$ is measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In practice $R_\mathrm{cc}$ is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic measurements; it is closely related to, but generally distinct from, the [major radius of the magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis), which is the locus of zero poloidal field. During sawteeth, off-axis current drive, or disruption precursors, $R_\mathrm{cc}$ can depart measurably from the magnetic axis position. The companion flux-surface average of $j_\phi$ is captured by [flux_surface_averaged_current_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_\mathrm{cc}$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, consistent with $R > 0$ for all physically realized plasma positions.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, the degenerate innermost point about which all closed magnetic flux surfaces are nested and at which the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic axis is the singular point in the plasma poloidal cross-section at which the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes, $\nabla\psi = 0$, forming the innermost degenerate flux surface about which all closed nested surfaces are organized. Its major-radius coordinate $R_\mathrm{axis}$ measures the distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to this point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is measured outward from the machine symmetry axis.

The magnetic axis satisfies

$$
\left.\nabla\psi(R, Z)\right|_{(R_\mathrm{axis},\, Z_\mathrm{axis})} = 0
$$

where $\psi(R, Z)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ is the corresponding vertical coordinate. The outward displacement $R_\mathrm{axis} - R_\mathrm{geo}$, where $R_\mathrm{geo}$ is the [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis), constitutes the Shafranov shift, which increases with plasma pressure and current.

The axis position is determined by equilibrium reconstruction, which locates the extremum of the poloidal flux function on the $(R, Z)$ poloidal plane. It serves as the inner normalization reference for radial flux coordinates and is a key input to plasma position control. It differs from [major_radius_of_current_center](name:major_radius_of_current_center) when the current profile is poloidally asymmetric. Typical values range from 1.6–3.0 m for medium-sized tokamaks to approximately 6.2 m for ITER-class devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_\mathrm{axis}$ is directed outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the reference point that defines the gap between the plasma boundary and a nominated wall or limiter element.
NAMES.long:
The plasma boundary gap reference point is a nominated geometric location used to measure the gap — the separation between the last closed flux surface or separatrix and a specific wall or limiter element at that poloidal position. The major radius $R$ of this reference point is its radial coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ denotes horizontal distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.

In equilibrium reconstruction and real-time position control, an array of gap reference points distributed around the poloidal cross-section defines the plasma shape constraints. The major radius $R$ locates each reference point radially; paired with the corresponding vertical $Z$ coordinate, it fully specifies the reference point in the poloidal plane. This coordinate follows the same pattern as [major_radius_of_x_point](name:major_radius_of_x_point), [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point), and [major_radius_of_active_limiter_point](name:major_radius_of_active_limiter_point), which locate other equilibrium boundary features. It is the $R$-component of the full position described by [radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point](name:radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

Typical values span the inner-wall to outer-wall major radius of the device, roughly 0.5–10 m depending on machine size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point is located at a positive radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, which is satisfied by all physical plasma-boundary gap reference points.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_primary_x_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate R of the primary X-point, the dominant poloidal-field null point defining the separatrix vertex in a diverted tokamak equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The primary X-point is the principal null of the poloidal magnetic field on the plasma-bounding separatrix, where the poloidal flux gradient $\nabla\psi = 0$ and the separatrix forms its characteristic figure-eight topology. In single-null divertor configurations this is the sole X-point; in double-null configurations it designates the geometrically dominant or actively controlled null.

The major radius $R$ of the primary X-point locates this null in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the distance measured outward from the machine toroidal symmetry axis. It directly sets the radial entrance of the divertor throat and constrains the magnetic geometry of the scrape-off layer. The companion major_radius_of_secondary_x_point locates the secondary null in double-null configurations, while [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) gives the radial coordinate of the related divertor tile intersection. The generic form [major_radius_of_x_point](name:major_radius_of_x_point) allows indexing over multiple X-points when the primary/secondary distinction is not required.

This coordinate is extracted from equilibrium reconstruction by identifying the saddle point of the solved poloidal flux function $\psi(R, Z)$. Typical values scale with device major radius, ranging from approximately 0.5–2.0 m in present-day tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured radially outward from the toroidal symmetry axis, yielding $R \geq 0$ by definition of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the intersection of the secondary separatrix with the divertor target plate in a double-null or snowflake divertor configuration.
NAMES.long:
The secondary strike point is the location on the divertor target plate where the secondary separatrix contacts the material surface. Its major-radius coordinate $R$ locates this point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height.

In double-null configurations, two separatrices bound separate divertor legs; the secondary separatrix intersects the target at a distinct radial location from the primary. Equilibrium reconstruction traces the boundary defined by the poloidal flux value $\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{sep,2}}$ at the secondary X-point until the field line intersects the divertor plate geometry, yielding this coordinate. Compare with [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) for the analogous primary separatrix intersection, and major_radius_of_secondary_x_point for the corresponding upstream X-point. The full secondary separatrix outline in the poloidal plane is characterized by [major_radius_of_secondary_separatrix](name:major_radius_of_secondary_separatrix).

Accurate knowledge of this coordinate is essential for divertor heat load management, since the strike point position determines both the wetted area and the power flux density reaching the target material. Typical values span roughly 0.3–3 m, depending on tokamak size and divertor geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike point radius is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+R$ direction.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate R of an X-point, the poloidal-field null forming a separatrix vertex, in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
An X-point is a hyperbolic null of the poloidal magnetic field in a toroidally axisymmetric equilibrium, located at a saddle point of the poloidal magnetic flux away from the magnetic axis. The quantity $R_X$ is the major-radius coordinate of that null in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This is the generic, unqualified X-point radius; when a multi-null equilibrium distinguishes nulls by role, use [major_radius_of_primary_x_point](name:major_radius_of_primary_x_point) or [major_radius_of_secondary_x_point](name:major_radius_of_x_point).

The X-point condition is expressed through the relation between poloidal magnetic flux and poloidal magnetic field:

$$
\mathbf{B}_p(R_X, Z_X) = \frac{1}{2\pi R_X}\nabla\psi(R_X, Z_X) \times \hat{\phi} = \mathbf{0}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in webers, $R_X$ and $Z_X$ are the X-point coordinates in meters, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system. Since $R_X>0$ for a physical toroidal equilibrium, the null condition is equivalent to $\nabla\psi(R_X,Z_X)=\mathbf{0}$; the critical point has saddle character rather than the extremum character of the magnetic axis.

In practice, $R_X$ is obtained by locating saddle points of the reconstructed poloidal-flux function or, equivalently, nulls of the reconstructed poloidal magnetic field in the meridional $(R,Z)$ cross-section of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system. Magnetic measurements and direct geometric constraints on the X-point position can be used to constrain the reconstruction. The separatrix passing through the X-point is geometrically related to divertor strike-point coordinates such as [major_outer_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_outer_radius_of_strike_point), [major_inner_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_inner_radius_of_strike_point), and [major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point).

Typical values are device-geometry dependent rather than universal: $R_X$ is a meter-scale coordinate comparable to the machine major radius, from sub-meter positions in compact devices to several meters in large tokamaks. The value is set by the separatrix geometry, plasma shape, and divertor configuration rather than by the X-point definition alone.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Maximum value of the total magnetic field magnitude on a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface. It is a non-negative scalar that characterizes the strongest field encountered on that surface.
NAMES.long:
Maximum magnetic field magnitude is the largest value of $|\mathbf{B}|$ over a single nested toroidal magnetic flux surface. It is paired with [minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and, together with that minimum, characterizes the magnetic-field variation experienced by guiding-center orbits on the surface.

For a surface labeled by poloidal flux $\psi$, the quantity is defined by

$$
B_{\max}(\psi) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $S(\psi)$ is the magnetic flux surface with label $\psi$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector, and both $|\mathbf{B}|$ and $B_{\max}$ are measured in T.

In equilibrium analysis it is computed by evaluating the full magnetic field magnitude on each flux surface and taking the surface maximum, usually with interpolation between reconstructed equilibrium points. In axisymmetric tokamaks the maximum often occurs toward the inboard, higher-field side because the toroidal field usually increases there, but this location is not part of the definition and can be affected by shaping and poloidal-field contributions.

For trapped-passing physics, $B_{\max}$ gives the largest field strength a particle must access to circulate around the surface. For a particle with kinetic energy $E$ and magnetic moment $\mu$, full access to the surface requires $\mu B_{\max} < E$; equality gives the trapped-passing boundary, while $\mu B_{\max} > E$ implies reflection before the particle reaches the highest-field region.

Typical values are about 1-8 T in many present tokamak plasmas and can exceed 10 T in compact high-field devices; low-field or spherical tokamak plasmas can be below 1 T. The value depends mainly on external toroidal field strength, plasma geometry, and the poloidal-field contribution.

NAMES.name: minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Smallest value of total magnetic field magnitude on each nested toroidal flux surface, used in determining the magnetic trapping condition for charged particles in bounce motion.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic field magnitude $B_\mathrm{min}(\psi)$ is the smallest value of $|\mathbf{B}|$ over all points on the flux surface labeled by poloidal flux $\psi$. In tokamaks with a dominant toroidal field satisfying $B_\phi \propto 1/R$, the minimum occurs near the outboard (low-field-side) midplane, where the major radius $R$ reaches its largest value on the flux surface.

The ratio $B_\mathrm{min}/B_\mathrm{max}$ governs magnetic trapping of charged particles bouncing along field lines. A particle with normalized parallel velocity $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ is magnetically trapped when

$$
\xi^2 < 1 - \frac{B_\mathrm{min}}{B_\mathrm{max}}
$$

where $v_\parallel$ is the velocity component along the magnetic field and $v$ is the total particle speed. The resulting trapped particle fraction enters neoclassical transport coefficients, bootstrap current models, and bounce-averaged kinetic equations.

$B_\mathrm{min}$ is obtained from MHD equilibrium reconstruction by minimizing the total field strength $|\mathbf{B}(\psi, \theta)|$ over the poloidal angle $\theta$ on each flux surface. Together with [maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and [flux_surface_average_magnetic_field](name:flux_surface_average_magnetic_field), it fully characterizes the field-strength variation on a flux surface that is relevant for classifying particle orbits.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Half the difference between the maximum and minimum major radii of the plasma boundary contour, giving the characteristic radial half-width of the outermost closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The minor radius $a$ of the plasma boundary is a fundamental geometric length quantifying the radial half-extent of the outermost closed flux surface. Together with the [major radius of the plasma boundary](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary), it sets the first-order cross-sectional size and determines the plasma aspect ratio.

The minor radius is defined from the extremal major radii of the boundary outline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
a = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum values of the major radius $R$ along the closed poloidal boundary contour.

The minor radius is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements — flux loops and poloidal field probes — supplemented by internal constraints from motional Stark effect polarimetry or pressure-profile data. It also serves directly as a position-control reference in plasma shape control.

Values range from 0.2–0.3 m in small tokamaks to ~2 m in large high-current devices. The inverse aspect ratio $\epsilon = a / R_0$ (where $R_0$ is the major radius on axis) underpins dimensionless confinement scalings, and derived shape descriptors such as [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and the [poloidal boundary perimeter](name:length_of_plasma_boundary) are both normalized by $a$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\max} > R_{\min}$ along the boundary contour in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Normalized poloidal flux coordinate evaluated on the flux surface where the safety factor reaches its global minimum within the confined plasma. It gives the radial flux-surface location of the minimum-q surface on the 0-to-1 poloidal-flux scale.
NAMES.long:
Normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor is the value of the normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_N$ on the flux surface where the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) $q$ is globally smallest inside the last-closed flux surface. It locates the minimum-$q$ surface relative to the magnetic axis and plasma boundary, independent of the dimensional scale of [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux).

The quantity is defined by minimizing the safety factor as a function of normalized poloidal flux coordinate and applying the axis-to-boundary normalization of poloidal magnetic flux:

$$
\psi_{N,q_{\min}} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \le \psi_N \le 1} q(\psi_N), \qquad
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}{\psi_\mathrm{b} - \psi_\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $\psi_{N,q_{\min}}$ is the coordinate of the minimum-safety-factor surface, $q(\psi_N)$ is the safety factor on a closed flux surface, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux of that surface, $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ is the value at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_\mathrm{b}$ is the value at the plasma boundary. The minimization is over closed flux surfaces in the confined plasma; if several surfaces share the same minimum value, the arg-min is mathematically non-unique.

In practice this coordinate is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the safety-factor radial behavior on nested closed flux surfaces, identifying the global minimum, and converting the corresponding surface to $\psi_N$. The corresponding dimensional flux on the same surface is [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor); a toroidal-flux-radius analog is [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor).

Typical values lie in the interval 0-1. Values near 0 indicate that the minimum safety factor is on or very close to the magnetic axis, while values around 0.2-0.6 are common for reversed-shear or otherwise non-monotonic equilibria with an off-axis minimum; values approaching 1 indicate a minimum near the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label defined as the square root of the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a flux surface normalized to its value at the last closed flux surface, spanning 0 at the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ is a dimensionless radial label identifying nested magnetic flux surfaces in an axisymmetric toroidal equilibrium. It equals zero at the magnetic axis and unity at the last closed flux surface (LCFS), providing a monotonically increasing coordinate that spans the entire confined plasma region.

The defining relation is:

$$
\rho_{\rm tor,norm} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\rm tor}}{\Phi_{\rm tor,b}}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed within a given flux surface and $\Phi_{\rm tor,b}$ is the toroidal flux at the plasma boundary.

The coordinate is obtained from magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium reconstruction by integrating the toroidal magnetic field over poloidal cross-sections of increasing enclosed area. Because it is rooted in toroidal rather than poloidal flux, it is the natural abscissa for radial transport calculations and differs from the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) except in special limiting geometries. Specific physics events are located by their value of this coordinate; for example, [the minimum-safety-factor surface](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) corresponds to a well-defined $\rho_{\rm tor,norm}$ that shifts with plasma current profile.
