The coordinate spans $[0, 1]$ for all confined flux surfaces. In H-mode discharges the steep-gradient pedestal region typically spans $\rho_{\rm tor,norm} \approx 0.85$–$0.95$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ enclosed by the flux surface is directed in the same toroidal sense as the flux at the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Major radius at the outboard (low-field side) equatorial intersection of each nested magnetic flux surface, characterizing the outboard radial geometry of the plasma equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The outer major radius of a flux surface is the $R$ coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame at which that flux surface intersects the equatorial plane on the outboard (low-field side) — the larger-$R$ crossing at $Z = Z_\text{axis}$, where $Z_\text{axis}$ is the vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis.

The defining relation selects the outboard root:

$$
R_\text{out}(\psi) = R\big|_{Z = Z_\text{axis},\; R > R_\text{axis}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal flux label and $R_\text{axis}$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis. The profile $R_\text{out}(\psi)$ increases monotonically from $R_\text{axis}$ at the magnetic axis to the outboard plasma boundary.

Together with [inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface](name:inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface), this quantity determines the midplane minor half-width $a = (R_\text{out} - R_\text{in})/2$ and the Shafranov shift $\Delta = (R_\text{out} + R_\text{in})/2 - R_\text{axis}$. The [flux_surface_averaged_major_radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius) gives the poloidally-weighted mean over the full flux surface. This profile is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by tracking the outboard equatorial crossing of each closed flux contour.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outboard crossing lies at $R > 0$ measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament element, marking the external radial boundary of the hollow-disk geometry.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the external boundary of an annular cross-section when a plasma current filament element is represented as a hollow cylinder. Together with [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament), it fully characterizes the annular geometry, which contrasts with the rectangular cross-section model parametrized by [height_of_plasma_filament](name:height_of_plasma_filament) and [width_of_plasma_filament](name:width_of_plasma_filament).

For an annular cross-section, the cross-sectional area relates to both radii by:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is this outer radius, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner radius, and $A$ is the area_of_plasma_filament.

The outer radius is specified as input geometry when constructing discrete filamentary representations of plasma current distributions used in equilibrium reconstruction and mutual-inductance computations. The constraint $r_\mathrm{outer} > r_\mathrm{inner} \geq 0$ must be satisfied to define a valid non-degenerate annular region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the cross-section center to the outer boundary, satisfying $r_\mathrm{outer} > r_\mathrm{inner} \geq 0$.

NAMES.name: parallel_current_density
NAMES.short: Signed scalar projection of the total plasma current density onto the local magnetic-field direction. For the total current it includes inductive Ohmic, neoclassical bootstrap, and externally driven non-inductive contributions; positive values indicate current flowing along the field.
NAMES.long:
The parallel current density $j_\parallel$ is the field-aligned scalar component of the plasma [current_density](name:current_density). In its total-current meaning it is closely related to [parallel_total_current_density](name:parallel_total_current_density) and combines inductive Ohmic current, neoclassical bootstrap current, and externally driven non-inductive current contributions.

The local field-aligned projection is defined by:

$$
j_\parallel = \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $j_\parallel$ is the parallel current density in A.m^-2, $\mathbf{J}$ is the total current-density vector in A.m^-2, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic-field vector in T, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the magnetic field.

This local projection should be distinguished from flux-surface-averaged parallel current-density conventions such as $\langle \mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle/B_0$, where $B_0$ is a reference magnetic-field magnitude in T. Mechanism-specific quantities such as [parallel_current_density_due_to_bootstrap](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_bootstrap) may use such an averaged normalization and represent only one contribution, rather than the total local field-aligned current density.

In equilibrium analysis, $j_\parallel$ is inferred from the reconstructed current-density and magnetic-field distributions constrained by magnetic measurements and plasma profiles. In transport and magnetohydrodynamic modeling, it is commonly computed by summing the relevant current components and projecting the result along the local magnetic field; it strongly affects the safety-factor and magnetic-shear profiles.

Representative tokamak values are highly machine- and scenario-dependent. Total core values are often of order 10^5-10^7 A.m^-2, while edge, weak-current, or current-reversal regions can be much closer to 0 A.m^-2 and may have either sign.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net current-density vector has a component in the direction of the local magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: plasma_resistance
NAMES.short: Effective non-negative electrical resistance of the plasma column, defined as the volume-integrated ohmic dissipation power divided by the square of the total plasma current. It represents the resistive part of the plasma circuit response, distinct from inductive voltage associated with changing current or magnetic stored energy.
NAMES.long:
Plasma resistance is the effective scalar resistance associated with collisional ohmic dissipation in the conducting plasma column. It is a non-negative quantity for positive ohmic dissipation and characterizes how strongly the plasma converts current-driven electrical work into heat, separately from inductive effects described by total_plasma_inductance.

The effective resistance is defined from the ohmic power dissipated in the plasma:

$$
R_\mathrm{plasma} = \frac{\int_{V_p} \mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{J}\,dV}{I_p^2} = \frac{P_\Omega}{I_p^2}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{plasma}$ is in ohm, $V_p$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $P_\Omega$ is the volume-integrated ohmic heating power in W, and $I_p$ is the total plasma current in A. When a circuit representation is used, this corresponds to the resistive voltage component divided by $I_p$ for nonzero current; it should not be identified with the total loop voltage unless inductive and other non-resistive voltage contributions have been removed.

In equilibrium and transport analysis, plasma resistance is computed from reconstructed current density together with an electrical resistivity or parallel conductivity model, or inferred from the resistive component of the plasma voltage balance. Its time integral is related to resistive magnetic-flux consumption, represented by [poloidal_accumulated_resistive_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_accumulated_resistive_magnetic_flux), while the inductive part of the voltage balance is associated with changes in current and magnetic energy through total_plasma_inductance.

Typical values in tokamak plasmas are about 0.01-10 microohm, decreasing strongly as electron temperature rises and increasing with effective ion charge and collisionality. Cold startup, ramp-down, or low-temperature edge-dominated conditions can have substantially larger effective resistance than hot flattop conditions.

NAMES.name: polarization_angle_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Motional Stark effect polarization angle evaluated at a discrete spatial location designated as a measurement constraint in tokamak equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The polarization angle at a constraint position is the angle of linear polarization of Stark-split Balmer-alpha emission from fast neutral beam ions traversing the plasma, evaluated at a discrete spatial site where this measurement serves as an input constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The motional Stark effect (MSE) diagnostic exploits the Lorentz electric field experienced by injected beam neutrals to align the polarization plane of the emitted light in a direction encoding the local magnetic-field pitch angle.

The MSE polarization angle $\gamma$ is related to the local magnetic field components by:

$$
\tan(\gamma) = \frac{B_Z}{A_1 B_R + A_2 B_\phi}
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical field component, $B_R$ is the radial field component, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal field component, and $A_1$, $A_2$ are dimensionless geometric weighting factors determined by the beam trajectory and sightline orientation.

During equilibrium reconstruction, the measured value at each constraint position is compared against the corresponding reconstructed [polarization_angle](name:polarization_angle_at_constraint_position) to form residuals that enter the least-squares cost functional. The [motional_stark_radiance](name:motional_stark_radiance) provides complementary spectral intensity data from the same beam-emission event. MSE polarization angles in conventional-aspect-ratio tokamak configurations span a few degrees to roughly 20 degrees, varying with local field pitch, beam geometry, and viewing-sightline angle.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Average poloidal magnetic flux produced by circuits external to the plasma (central solenoid, poloidal-field coils, in-vessel coils, passive structures, and eddy currents), with the average taken over the plasma poloidal cross-section weighted by the local toroidal current density. The plasma self-flux is excluded.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux generated by all conductors external to the plasma, averaged over the plasma cross-section using the local toroidal current density as the weighting function. External sources comprise the central solenoid, poloidal-field coils, in-vessel coils, passive conducting structures, and induced eddy currents; the flux produced by the plasma current itself is not included. The qualifier refers to the poloidal magnetic flux being current-weighted by the toroidal current density, not to a poloidal-current weighting.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the average over a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system is defined as the toroidal-current-density-weighted integral of the external flux divided by the total plasma current:

$$
\langle \psi_\mathrm{ext} \rangle = \frac{\int_{\Omega_p} \psi_\mathrm{ext}(R,Z)\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dR\, dZ}{I_p}
$$

where $\Omega_p$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section in the $(R,Z)$ plane, $R$ is the major radius in meters, $Z$ is the vertical height in meters, $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ is the external poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal current-density component in A m$^{-2}$, and $I_p = \int_{\Omega_p} j_\phi\, dR\, dZ$ is the signed total plasma current in A. The quantity is meaningful only when $I_p$ is nonzero.

In practice it is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the poloidal flux contribution of all external circuits across the plasma cross-section and combining it with the reconstructed toroidal current-density distribution. It characterizes how externally produced flux links the current-carrying plasma region and is used in flux-consumption and loop-voltage analyzes; its time derivative is the externally driven contribution to the loop voltage seen by the plasma current channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the external-circuit vertical magnetic field threading the horizontal flux disks that define $\psi_\mathrm{ext}$ points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the value of the equilibrium flux function at the innermost closed-flux-surface point where its gradient vanishes. It provides the inner reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis, $\psi_0$, is the value of the equilibrium poloidal-flux function at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the nested closed-flux-surface family where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes. It is an extremal reference value for radial flux labeling; the absolute offset of $\psi$ is gage dependent, so physically meaningful radial labels use flux differences such as $\psi - \psi_0$.

The dimensionless normalized poloidal flux coordinate anchored at the axis is commonly defined by:

$$
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_0}{\psi_b - \psi_0}
$$

where $\psi_N$ is dimensionless, $\psi$ is the local poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $\psi_0$ is the magnetic-axis value in Wb, and $\psi_b$ is the plasma-boundary value in Wb from [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). With this normalization, $\psi_N = 0$ at the magnetic axis and $\psi_N = 1$ at the plasma boundary, matching [normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).

Equilibrium reconstruction obtains $\psi_0$ by locating the extremum of the reconstructed poloidal-flux map inside the last closed flux surface. The same axis reference is used when interpreting flux values at internal features such as an [internal transport barrier](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_internal_transport_barrier), a [secondary separatrix](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_secondary_separatrix), or a pedestal position expressed by [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_pedestal).

Because an additive gage can be chosen for $\psi$, a universal absolute range for $\psi_0$ is not physically meaningful; many equilibria set the axis value to 0 Wb. The physically relevant separation $|\psi_b - \psi_0|$ is often 0.1-10 Wb in small and medium tokamaks and 10-100 Wb in large high-current plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\psi$ increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux on the closed flux surface where the safety factor profile attains its minimum value. It is a dimensional flux given in webers that labels that surface, not the dimensionless normalized flux coordinate of the same surface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor is the value of the poloidal magnetic flux on the closed flux surface where the safety factor profile reaches its minimum. It provides an absolute, dimensional flux label (in webers) for that surface, as opposed to the dimensionless normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the same surface.

The quantity is defined by selecting the flux surface that minimizes the safety factor and reading off its poloidal flux:

$$
\psi_{q_{\min}} = \psi(\chi_\ast), \qquad \chi_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\chi \in \mathcal{D}} q(\chi)
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $q$ is the dimensionless safety factor, $\chi$ is any monotonic label ordering the nested closed flux surfaces of the domain $\mathcal{D}$, and $\chi_\ast$ labels a surface on which $q = q_\mathrm{min}$. The argmin form makes no assumption that the minimum is an interior extremum: it may occur at the magnetic axis, at an interior surface, or near the plasma boundary. The poloidal flux itself is the magnetic flux through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis, $\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'$, and is defined only up to an arbitrary additive gage constant; only flux differences (for example relative to the magnetic axis or boundary) are physically meaningful.

In practice the quantity is obtained from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating $q$ over the nested closed flux surfaces, identifying the surface that attains $q_\mathrm{min}$, and interpolating the corresponding $\psi$ value. The same surface can be expressed in dimensionless form by [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) via a normalization such as $\psi_N = (\psi - \psi_\mathrm{axis})/(\psi_\mathrm{boundary} - \psi_\mathrm{axis})$, where $\psi_\mathrm{axis}$ and $\psi_\mathrm{boundary}$ are the magnetic-axis and boundary fluxes; this removes the gage ambiguity inherent in the dimensional value.

Typical magnitudes scale with device size, plasma current, toroidal field, and the gage chosen for $\psi$, so absolute values are reported as flux differences from the magnetic axis. Monotonic-shear equilibria place the minimum at or near the magnetic axis, while reversed-shear configurations move it to mid-radius or farther out.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux through the enclosed horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis is oriented along $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the value of the axisymmetric equilibrium flux function on the last closed flux surface. It is paired with the magnetic-axis flux to define normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary, denoted $\psi_b$, is the value of the equilibrium poloidal-flux function on the last closed flux surface (LCFS), the outermost closed magnetic surface enclosing confined plasma. In diverted configurations the LCFS passes through an X-point; in limited configurations it contacts the limiter. This boundary value is the outer endpoint paired with [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) for flux-coordinate normalization.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal magnetic flux at a boundary point can be written as the flux of the vertical magnetic-field component through a horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system:

$$
\psi_b = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R', Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in tesla, $R_b$ and $Z_b$ are the coordinates of a point on the LCFS, and $R'$ is the integration radius. In an exact axisymmetric equilibrium, $\psi$ is constant on the LCFS, so any point on that surface gives the same boundary value; the resulting $\psi_b$ is in webers.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by determining the poloidal-flux function and locating its outermost closed contour. Together with the axis value $\psi_0$, it defines the [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) through the endpoint relation $\psi_N=(\psi-\psi_0)/(\psi_b-\psi_0)$, so that the magnetic axis maps to 0 and the plasma boundary maps to 1.

Typical absolute magnitudes are 0.1-5 Wb in small to medium tokamaks and several to tens of Wb in large, high-current devices, depending mainly on plasma current, toroidal magnetic field, and plasma size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the horizontal integration disk is directed in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Radial component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the magnetic-flux-density-equivalent magnetization of an iron core segment. It equals the permeability of free space times the textbook radial magnetization component, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.
NAMES.long:
Radial magnetization of an iron core segment is the radial component of the segment magnetization vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. The documented quantity is the magnetic-flux-density-equivalent component, equal to the permeability of free space times the textbook magnetization component, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.

The conversion from the textbook material magnetization to this iron-core quantity is

$$
M_R = \mu_0\,\mathbf{M}\cdot\hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{M}$ is the material magnetization vector in A/m, $\hat{R}$ is the outward radial unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m/A is the permeability of free space.

In equilibrium analysis, this quantity is inferred from magnetic measurements together with a ferromagnetic model of the iron core. The segment model treats the magnetization as uniform within each iron segment, while the fitted value can depend on nonlinear permeability, hysteresis, remanent magnetization, demagnetization effects, and the approach to magnetic saturation.

Typical values range from near 0 T in weakly magnetized or demagnetized regions to about 1.5-2.2 T in magnitude near saturation in soft iron. The radial component may be much smaller than the total magnetization if the material is magnetized mainly in another direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetization vector has a component in the $+\hat{R}$ direction, outward from the toroidal symmetry axis, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Radial (R) component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field in the IMAS cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, representing toroidally non-uniform perturbations from error fields, resonant magnetic perturbations, and finite coil effects.
NAMES.long:
The radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field $B_R^{\rm na}$ is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the vacuum magnetic-field perturbation that breaks toroidal symmetry, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Physical sources include geometric imperfections in coil placement (error fields), current-lead feeds, and deliberately applied non-axisymmetric coil currents such as resonant magnetic perturbations (RMPs) used for ELM suppression and error-field correction.

The field is defined by subtracting the toroidally averaged axisymmetric radial component from the full three-dimensional vacuum radial field:

$$
B_R^{\rm na}(R, \phi, Z) = B_R(R, \phi, Z) - \langle B_R \rangle_\phi(R, Z)
$$

where $\langle B_R \rangle_\phi$ denotes the average over toroidal angle $\phi$ at fixed $(R, Z)$.

This component is computed from three-dimensional vacuum field calculations using Biot-Savart integration over all non-axisymmetric coil elements, and evaluated on spatial field maps or at control surface points for error-field identification and feedback-correction algorithms. Together with [vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) and [toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), it provides the complete cylindrical decomposition of the non-axisymmetric vacuum field; [non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field_at_control_surface](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field_at_control_surface) gives the corresponding surface-normal projection. Typical perturbation amplitudes for RMP and error-field applications range from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$ T in medium- to large-scale tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, away from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: reference_major_radius
NAMES.short: Fixed major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system at which the vacuum toroidal magnetic field is specified. It is a non-negative geometric radius; the sign of the toroidal field is carried by the associated field value, not by the radius.
NAMES.long:
Reference major radius $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system at which the [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field) value $B_0$ is defined. It is a geometric distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and is therefore non-negative; it does not carry the sign of the magnetic field.

For an axisymmetric vacuum toroidal field in a current-free region, the toroidal field scales inversely with major radius:

$$
B_\phi^\mathrm{vac}(R) = B_0\,\frac{R_0}{R}
$$

where $B_\phi^\mathrm{vac}(R)$ is the toroidal vacuum magnetic-field component in tesla at major radius $R$ in meters, $B_0$ is the signed toroidal vacuum magnetic field in tesla at $R_0$, and $R_0$ is the reference major radius in meters. The factor $R_0/R$ is positive; the field direction is determined by the sign of $B_0$.

In practice, $R_0$ is specified from the device geometry or equilibrium reference setup rather than measured by an independent diagnostic. It identifies where $B_0$ is quoted, and quantities that use the same vacuum-field reference, including flux-radius definitions such as [toroidal flux radius of the magnetic axis](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis), should use a consistent $B_0$ and $R_0$ pair.

Representative tokamak values are about 0.3-7 m, ranging from compact or spherical devices to large conventional devices; the appropriate value is facility and configuration dependent.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95
NAMES.short: Safety factor evaluated on the closed flux surface where normalized poloidal magnetic flux is 0.95, commonly called q95.
NAMES.long:
Safety factor at normalized poloidal magnetic flux equal to 0.95, commonly denoted $q_{95}$, is the value of the safety factor on the closed flux surface whose flux coordinate $\psi_N$ is 0.95. It measures how many toroidal turns a magnetic field line makes per poloidal turn near the plasma edge, while remaining inside the separatrix where X-point geometry can make the boundary value more sensitive. It is an edge-near complement to [safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95) and [safety_factor_at_pedestal](name:safety_factor_at_pedestal).

Using the safety-factor function as a function of normalized poloidal magnetic flux, the defining relation is

$$
q_{95} = q(\psi_N = 0.95) = \left.\frac{d\Phi_\mathrm{tor}}{d\psi}\right|_{\psi_N=0.95}
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{tor}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and $\psi_N$ is normalized poloidal magnetic flux, equal to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the boundary of closed flux surfaces. The derivative is dimensionless because both fluxes are measured in webers.

In practice, $q_{95}$ is obtained from an axisymmetric magnetic equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic diagnostics and, when available, pressure and current-distribution information. The reconstruction determines the relevant closed flux surface and the flux functions; $q(\psi_N)$ is then evaluated or interpolated at $\psi_N=0.95$.

Typical tokamak values are about 2-8; H-mode and baseline scenarios often lie around 3-6, while low-current or high-safety-factor scenarios can exceed 8. Values close to low-order rational numbers, especially near 2 or 3, are important for global kink, tearing, and edge-stability limits.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, moving outward across neighboring closed flux surfaces at $\psi_N=0.95$, the signed toroidal magnetic flux changes in the same sense as the signed poloidal magnetic flux.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Total geometric surface area of a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface, computed by revolving the poloidal boundary contour through the full $2\pi$ toroidal angle around the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The surface area of a magnetic flux surface is the total area of the two-dimensional toroidal shell swept out when a closed poloidal flux contour is revolved through the full toroidal angle. It characterizes the geometric extent of each nested flux surface and enters flux-surface-averaged transport equations as a weighting factor relating cross-field particle and energy fluxes to radial gradients along the flux coordinate.

For an axisymmetric magnetic equilibrium, the surface area of the flux surface at poloidal flux label $\psi$ is:

$$
S(\psi) = 2\pi \oint_{\psi} R \, d\ell_p
$$

where $R$ is the major radius (distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame) and $d\ell_p$ is the arc-length element along the closed poloidal contour at constant $\psi$.

The surface area profile is obtained from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction, which determines the flux-surface geometry across the plasma cross-section as a function of the flux label. This quantity is geometrically distinct from the [cross-sectional area of a flux surface], which is the poloidal area enclosed by the contour rather than the revolving-surface area. The full radial profile of this quantity shares the same physical concept as [area_of_flux_surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), and its value at the outermost closed flux surface equals [flux_surface_area_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_area_at_plasma_boundary).

Surface area increases monotonically from near zero at the magnetic axis to a maximum at the plasma boundary, reaching tens of square meters in medium-sized tokamaks and several hundred square meters in large high-field devices.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Full thickness of a rectangular plasma filament cross-section, measured along the in-plane direction normal to the filament's central segment. It is the transverse side length of the rectangle, complementing the tangential length measured along the segment.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a plasma filament is the full transverse extent of a rectangular (thick-line) filament cross-section, measured in the local plane of the element along the direction normal to the filament's central segment. The central segment lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and the local tangential-normal basis is defined within that plane: the tangential direction follows the central segment while the normal direction is the in-plane perpendicular. It is a full side length, not a half-width.

For a rectangular filament cross-section, the cross-sectional area is the product of the two full local side lengths:

$$
A_\mathrm{fil} = L_\mathrm{tan}\, t
$$

where $A_\mathrm{fil}$ is the filament cross-sectional area in $\mathrm{m}^2$, $L_\mathrm{tan}$ is the [tangential length](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament) in $\mathrm{m}$, and $t$ is the thickness in $\mathrm{m}$. When the local tangential and normal directions align with the cylindrical axes, the thickness coincides with either the [width](name:width_of_plasma_filament) (radial $R$-direction extent) or the [height](name:height_of_plasma_filament) (vertical $Z$-direction extent) of the same rectangular cross-section.

In equilibrium filament descriptions, the thickness is set by the chosen local geometric representation of a discrete current-carrying plasma element. For a thick-line element it is specified directly as the rectangle side perpendicular to the central segment.

The value is a non-negative geometric length governed by the spatial resolution and local size of the filament representation. No universal device-independent numerical range applies; it should be interpreted relative to the associated tangential length and to neighboring filament spacing.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle phi coordinate of points on the control surface used for non-axisymmetric magnetic field analysis, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi$ identifies the azimuthal position of sample points on the control surface within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. The control surface is a geometric reference surface employed in studies of non-axisymmetric magnetic field distributions — for example, to evaluate boundary conditions or to perform surface integrals of perturbed field components in three-dimensional equilibrium analysis. Each point on the surface is fully specified by its $(R, \phi, Z)$ triplet; this quantity carries the $\phi$ component of that triplet, related to Cartesian coordinates by $x = R\cos\phi$ and $y = R\sin\phi$.

Values span $[0, 2\pi)$ rad for a full toroidal circuit, though a particular control surface may cover only a restricted toroidal arc. The analogous coordinate for diagnostic settings is [toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position](name:toroidal_angle_of_measurement_position), and the same coordinate applied to EC launcher geometry appears as [toroidal_angle_of_launching_position](name:toroidal_angle_of_launching_position).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases in the counter-clockwise direction viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Boundary toroidal flux radius rho_tor = sqrt(Phi_tor/(pi B0)) is the non-negative square-root radius associated with the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the plasma boundary. It provides an effective minor-radius scale for the outermost closed magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal flux radius at the plasma boundary is the radial flux label obtained from the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the selected boundary flux surface. It gives a non-negative effective minor-radius scale for the outermost closed magnetic flux surface or separatrix, rather than a purely geometric distance.

The boundary value is defined by normalizing the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux to the reference toroidal magnetic field:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is the [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic field used for the flux-radius normalization, and the flux and field are taken consistently so that the ratio is non-negative.

This quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the toroidal flux enclosed by the boundary flux surface and applying the flux-radius normalization. It sets the outer radial scale for coordinates such as the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). For a large-aspect-ratio circular plasma with nearly uniform toroidal field it is close to the geometric minor radius, while finite aspect ratio, shaping, and toroidal-field variation make it an effective flux radius rather than an exact geometric radius.

Typical values are about 0.2-1 m in small tokamaks, 0.5-2 m in medium and large tokamaks, and can exceed 2 m in reactor-scale equilibria.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a given flux surface, increasing monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis and used as a natural radial flux-surface label in equilibrium analysis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi_{tor}$ is the total flux of the toroidal magnetic field threading the poloidal cross-section enclosed by a closed magnetic flux surface. In an axisymmetric equilibrium, $\Phi_{tor}$ increases monotonically from zero at the magnetic axis to its maximum at the plasma boundary, making it one of the two fundamental flux-surface labels alongside the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

The defining integral over the poloidal cross-sectional area $S_{\rm pol}$ bounded by the flux surface is:

$$
\Phi_{tor} = \int_{S_{\rm pol}} B_\phi \, dA
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic field component in T and $dA$ is the area element of the poloidal half-plane in m². The safety factor relates the two canonical flux coordinates through $q = d\Phi_{tor}/d\psi$, linking the toroidal flux to the flux-surface geometry characterized by [flux_surface_area](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface).

In equilibrium reconstruction, $\Phi_{tor}$ profiles are computed from the Grad–Shafranov solution and tabulated as a function of normalized radial coordinates across nested flux surfaces. Typical boundary values span a few to tens of Wb in current tokamaks, with larger values for higher-field machines. The [toroidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux_at_inside_flux_surface](name:toroidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux_at_inside_flux_surface) isolates the portion of this flux arising from plasma diamagnetism.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Total toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the plasma boundary, including externally produced toroidal field and the contribution associated with plasma poloidal currents.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the net flux of toroidal magnetic field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the last-closed flux surface. It is the boundary value used to normalize toroidal-flux radial coordinates and is complementary to [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which refers to flux through a horizontal disk rather than through a poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the boundary toroidal flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \int_{A_b} B_\phi(R,Z)\, dR\, dZ = \int_{A_b} \frac{F(\psi(R,Z))}{R}\, dR\, dZ
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux in Wb, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component in T, $F=R B_\phi$ is the poloidal-current function in T m, $\psi$ is the equilibrium poloidal magnetic-flux label, $R$ and $Z$ are in m, and $A_b$ is the boundary-enclosed poloidal area in m^2 at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$.

The value is computed from an axisymmetric equilibrium by integrating the reconstructed toroidal magnetic field over the region inside the plasma boundary. The reconstructed field generally contains the externally imposed vacuum toroidal-field contribution and the plasma-current contribution represented through $F(\psi)$; the quantity is therefore an integral flux associated with the boundary, not a local boundary condition.

Typical absolute magnitudes scale approximately as $\langle B_\phi\rangle A_b$: compact or medium tokamaks are often in the 0.1-10 Wb range, while large high-field plasmas can be 10-100 Wb or more depending on toroidal field strength and boundary area.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net toroidal magnetic field threading the plasma-boundary cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field, defined as its projection along the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the IMAS cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic field that varies with toroidal angle and is not part of the axisymmetric equilibrium field. It is a local component of the perturbation field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, not a projection onto a material or control-surface normal.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ satisfying $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$, the non-axisymmetric magnetic field is decomposed as:

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}(R, \phi, Z) = B_R(R, \phi, Z)\,\hat{R} + B_\phi(R, \phi, Z)\,\hat{\phi} + B_Z(R, \phi, Z)\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component described here, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$, $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are measured in T, $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in m, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in rad increasing counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in m.

The quantity is computed from vacuum magnetic-field models for non-axisymmetric perturbation coils, error-field sources, and passive conducting structures, or inferred by combining magnetic measurements with a field model and removing the toroidally averaged axisymmetric contribution. On a control surface, $B_\phi$ is still the tangent toroidal component; the surface-normal non-axisymmetric field is the separate projection $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} \cdot \hat{n}$ and generally differs from $B_\phi$.

Representative magnitudes are device- and location-dependent because the vacuum perturbation depends on coil currents, source geometry, and distance from the conductors. In tokamak perturbation studies, $|B_\phi|$ is commonly in the range $10^{-6}-10^{-2}$ T and is often quoted as $|B_\phi|/B_0$, where $B_0$ is the magnitude of the reference axisymmetric toroidal magnetic field in T; perturbative cases usually have $|B_\phi|/B_0 \ll 1$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the non-axisymmetric magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_current
NAMES.short: Net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma, equal to the integral of the toroidal current density over the poloidal plasma cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal plasma current $I_p$ is the net electric current flowing in the toroidal $\hat{\phi}$ direction, integrated over the full poloidal cross-section of the plasma column. It is a primary global parameter governing poloidal magnetic field generation, MHD equilibrium, plasma confinement, and stability thresholds including the Kruskal-Shafranov $q = 1$ condition.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
I_p = \iint_{\mathcal{S}} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the current density, $dA$ is the area element, and $\mathcal{S}$ is the poloidal cross-section of the plasma.

$I_p$ is measured by Rogowski coils encircling the torus, or inferred from flux-loop and magnetic-pickup-coil arrays as a primary constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The closely related [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) explicitly labels this as the total aggregated current. It should be distinguished from [current_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil), which drives the external vacuum toroidal field, and from [current_of_plasma_filament](name:current_of_plasma_filament), which represents current in discrete plasma filament elements.

Typical values range from a few hundred kA in small research tokamaks to approximately 15 MA in ITER-class reactors, scaling roughly with the product of toroidal field strength and minor radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the vacuum magnetic field evaluated at the reference major radius, produced solely by the external coil system in the absence of any plasma currents.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum toroidal magnetic field $B_0$ is the $\hat{\phi}$-projection of the [vacuum_magnetic_field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field) evaluated at a fixed [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius) $R_0$. It captures the toroidal field contribution from the external coil system — primarily the toroidal field coils — with no plasma-current contribution included.

For an ideal current-free axisymmetric configuration the vacuum toroidal field follows a $1/R$ profile:

$$
B_\phi^{\rm vac}(R) = \frac{R_0 B_0}{R}
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius and $B_0 \equiv B_\phi^{\rm vac}(R_0)$. The product $R_0 B_0$ is invariant across radial position and serves as the primary magnetic normalization parameter used throughout equilibrium reconstruction, stability analysis, and flux-coordinate definitions.

The value of $B_0$ is inferred from the electrical current in the toroidal field coil system via a calibrated coil-current-to-field relationship, or confirmed by in-vessel magnetic probes under vacuum conditions. It enters the definition of the normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor} = \sqrt{\Phi_{\rm tor}/(\pi B_0)}$, linking it directly to [toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_magnetic_axis), and normalizes current densities used across core and edge plasma analysis. It also differs from the [flux_surface_average_magnetic_field](name:flux_surface_average_magnetic_field) in that the latter includes plasma diamagnetic and paramagnetic modifications. Typical values at the reference radius range from 1 T in small devices to 5–6 T in large high-field machines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Ratio of the vertical distance from the plasma cross-section geometric axis to the topmost boundary point to the minor radius, capturing vertical elongation of the upper half of the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The upper elongation $\kappa_u$ is a dimensionless shape parameter quantifying how far the upper half of the plasma boundary extends vertically relative to the minor radius. Unlike the full-boundary [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary), which represents the overall vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio of the cross-section, $\kappa_u$ isolates the upper-half geometry and is sensitive to up-down asymmetries induced by, for example, a single-null divertor configuration.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\kappa_u = \frac{Z_{\max} - Z_{\rm geo}}{a}
$$

where $Z_{\max}$ is the vertical coordinate of the topmost point of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z_{\rm geo}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis of the poloidal cross-section, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius.

This parameter is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by identifying the outermost closed flux surface or the specified plasma boundary contour and computing the ratio from the upper vertical extremum. The companion quantity [lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) measures the analogous shape of the lower half; differences between the two reflect up-down asymmetry in the plasma cross-section. In conventional single-null diverted H-mode plasmas, $\kappa_u$ falls in the range 1.2–1.9.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the topmost point of the plasma boundary lies above the geometric axis of the cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape parameter for the upper outboard corner of the plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system. It measures how the positive-Z, large-R boundary quadrant departs from the reference ellipse set by the boundary radius, upper elongation, and upper triangularity.
NAMES.long:
Upper outer squareness of the plasma boundary quantifies the non-elliptical shaping of the outboard, positive-$Z$ quadrant of the last-closed flux surface or separatrix. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the upper outer quadrant lies at larger $R$ than the radial center and above the vertical center. Positive values in the Luce convention make this quadrant fuller and squarer relative to the reference ellipse, while negative values make it more chamfered or indented.

A full Luce parameterization for the upper outer boundary quadrant is

$$
\begin{aligned}
R(\theta) &= R_0 + a\cos\left[\theta + \sin^{-1}(\delta_u)\sin\theta - \zeta_{UO}\sin(2\theta)\right],\\
Z(\theta) &= Z_0 + \kappa_u a\sin\left[\theta + \zeta_{UO}\sin(2\theta)\right],\qquad 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\zeta_{UO}$ is the upper outer squareness, $\theta=0$ is the outboard midplane point, and $\theta=\pi/2$ is the top point. $R_0=(R_{out}+R_{in})/2$ is the radial center, $a=(R_{out}-R_{in})/2$ is the boundary minor radius, $Z_0$ is the vertical center used for the boundary shape description, $\kappa_u=(Z_{top}-Z_0)/a$ is the upper elongation, and $\delta_u=(R_0-R_{top})/a$ is the upper triangularity. For small $|\zeta_{UO}|$, the effect is locally proportional to $\sin 2\theta$, but the parameter is defined by the full angular distortion rather than by a single midpoint displacement.

The quantity is obtained from an equilibrium boundary contour by identifying the radial and vertical extrema, fixing the associated radius, center, elongation, and triangularity, and fitting the upper-outboard segment to the Luce form. The analogous flux-surface quantity, [upper outer squareness of a flux surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), applies the same shape concept to an interior magnetic surface rather than to the plasma boundary.

Values near 0 correspond to an approximately elliptical upper outer quadrant. In shaped tokamak equilibria, typical absolute values are a few hundredths to a few tenths, commonly about 0.02-0.2, with strongly squared boundaries sometimes approaching 0.3.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless upper-half triangularity of a flux surface, defined by the inward major-radius displacement of the point at maximum vertical height from the surface horizontal mid-radius, normalized by the minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity of a flux surface quantifies the D-shape asymmetry of the upper half of a closed magnetic surface in a poloidal cross-section. It isolates the position of the topmost point relative to the same surface's horizontal mid-radius, so it distinguishes upper-half shaping from lower-half triangularity and from elongation.

In the right-handed IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the upper triangularity is defined by

$$
\delta_\mathrm{upper} = \frac{R_0 - R_\mathrm{top}}{a}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{top}$ is the major radius of the point with maximum $Z$ on the flux surface, $R_0=(R_\mathrm{out}+R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is the horizontal mid-radius of that surface, and $a=(R_\mathrm{out}-R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is its minor radius. The lengths $R_\mathrm{top}$, $R_0$, $R_\mathrm{out}$, $R_\mathrm{in}$, and $a$ are in meters, while $\delta_\mathrm{upper}$ is dimensionless; $R_\mathrm{out}$ and $R_\mathrm{in}$ are the maximum and minimum major radii of the same flux surface.

It is computed from an equilibrium flux contour or an analytic flux-surface shape by locating the horizontal radial extrema and the upper vertical extremum of the contour. Together with lower triangularity, elongation, and squareness parameters, it describes poloidal shaping and up-down asymmetry of nested flux surfaces.

Typical values in tokamak equilibrium descriptions are commonly between about -0.6 and 0.6. Values near zero indicate that the upper extremum lies close to the horizontal mid-radius, positive values indicate an inward-shifted upper point, and negative values indicate an outward-shifted upper point.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless parameter measuring how far the uppermost point of the plasma boundary is displaced radially inward relative to the plasma geometric center, normalized to the minor radius, capturing the triangular deviation of the upper half of the cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The upper triangularity $\delta_u$ characterizes the poloidal asymmetry of the upper portion of the plasma cross-section. It quantifies how far the uppermost point of the plasma boundary is displaced toward the high-field side relative to the plasma geometric center, and is a key shaping parameter governing MHD stability, pedestal formation, and divertor heat-load distribution in shaped tokamak discharges.

The upper triangularity is defined geometrically as:

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_0 - R_{top}}{a}
$$

where $R_0$ is the major radius of the plasma geometric center (midpoint between maximum and minimum major radius on the horizontal midplane), $R_{top}$ is the major radius of the uppermost point of the plasma boundary, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius.

Together with [lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:lower_triangularity_of_plasma_boundary), $\delta_u$ captures up-down asymmetry in plasma shape that is characteristic of single-null divertor configurations, where the half facing the divertor typically exhibits higher triangularity. Their mean approximates the overall [triangularity_of_plasma_boundary](name:triangularity_of_plasma_boundary). Typical H-mode values range from 0.2 to 0.7 in standard tokamak operation. For finer resolution of the upper boundary geometry, $\delta_u$ is complemented by the [upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) and [upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_plasma_boundary) parameters. Upper triangularity is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetics and boundary identification diagnostics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the uppermost point of the plasma boundary lies at smaller major radius than the plasma geometric center, displaced toward the high-field side.

NAMES.name: vacuum_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Vacuum poloidal current function is major radius multiplied by the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system. In a current-free vacuum subregion outside the plasma it is constant between current sources and represents the enclosed poloidal current that sets the vacuum toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum poloidal current function, $F_\mathrm{vac}$, is the vacuum contribution to the axisymmetric poloidal-current function that determines the toroidal magnetic field. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Within a connected vacuum subregion that contains no current density, $F_\mathrm{vac}$ is spatially constant; this constancy does not apply across external current sources.

The defining relation is

$$
F_\mathrm{vac} = R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}} = \frac{\mu_0 I_\mathrm{pol,enc}}{2\pi}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component, $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, and $I_\mathrm{pol,enc}$ is the net enclosed [poloidal current] linked by the toroidal Amperian loop. The equality to enclosed current follows from Ampere's law for an axisymmetric vacuum field.

In Grad-Shafranov equilibrium the total function $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$ is specified together with the pressure function $p(\psi)$, related to [pressure at flux surface](name:pressure_at_flux_surface), and couples to the [poloidal magnetic flux at flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) through the source term $-F\,dF/d\psi$. In a current-free vacuum subregion, the pressure gradient is absent and $dF/d\psi=0$, so the vacuum value is the constant limiting value of this function there.

In practice $F_\mathrm{vac}$ is obtained from calibrated toroidal-field coil currents, vacuum magnetic-field measurements, or equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic diagnostics. It is often numerically close to a reference product $R_\mathrm{ref} B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_\mathrm{ref})$, but $R_\mathrm{ref}$ is the radius associated with the vacuum-field specification and need not be the magnetic-axis major radius.

Typical magnitudes are device-dependent rather than a universal validity range because they scale with the specified reference major radius and vacuum toroidal field. In tokamak applications they are often of order 1-30 m.T, with sub-meter low-field devices below 1 m.T and large high-field devices reaching several tens of m.T.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vacuum toroidal magnetic field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the active limiter point, the location where a limited plasma boundary contacts the limiter, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the active limiter point is the $Z$ component of the point where a limited plasma boundary is in contact with the material limiter. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters.

If the active limiter contact point is denoted $P_\mathrm{AL}=(R_\mathrm{AL}, \phi_\mathrm{AL}, Z_\mathrm{AL})$, its vertical coordinate is

$$
z_\mathrm{AL}=Z_\mathrm{AL}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{AL}$ is the point's major radius in meters, $\phi_\mathrm{AL}$ is its toroidal angle in radians, and $Z_\mathrm{AL}$ is its vertical height in meters.

In equilibrium analysis, the active limiter point is identified from the contact between the reconstructed plasma boundary and the limiter geometry for a limited configuration. This coordinate is the vertical companion of major_radius_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point; related vertical coordinates include [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point), and [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

Typical values are device dependent and commonly lie between -2 m and 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks, with larger vertical excursions possible in elongated or vertically shifted plasmas. The value depends on the chosen vertical origin of the device coordinate definition and on which limiter element is contacted.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the active limiter point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the first-wall point geometrically nearest to the plasma boundary or separatrix, measured upward from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the closest wall point is the $Z$ value of the point on the first wall that minimizes the geometric distance to the plasma boundary or separatrix. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z$ is vertical height measured upward from the machine midplane, and this quantity identifies only the vertical component of that nearest wall location.

For a first-wall contour $\Gamma_w$ and a plasma boundary or separatrix contour $\Gamma_p$ in the same poloidal $(R, Z)$ cross-section, the closest wall point $q_*=(R_*,Z_*)$ is defined by the Euclidean poloidal-plane distance:

$$
q_* = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{q \in \Gamma_w}\; \min_{p \in \Gamma_p} \sqrt{(R_q - R_p)^2 + (Z_q - Z_p)^2}
$$

where $q=(R_q,Z_q)$ is a point on the first wall and $p=(R_p,Z_p)$ is a point on the plasma boundary or separatrix. The documented quantity is $Z_*$. If more than one wall point has exactly the same minimum distance, the geometric definition alone does not determine a unique point and an additional tie-breaking convention is required.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from a reconstructed plasma boundary or separatrix and a first-wall contour expressed in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, usually by interpolation and a nearest-distance search in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane. Together with the corresponding [major radius of the closest wall point], it specifies the poloidal location of the nearest wall point; by itself it gives only the vertical height.

Typical values are bounded by the vertical extent of the first wall. For a wall extending from $Z_{\min}$ to $Z_{\max}$, the coordinate lies between those limits in m; values near $0$ m indicate a closest point near the machine midplane, positive values indicate the upper side, and negative values indicate the lower side.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wall point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the machine midplane, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate Z, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of a position where a quantity constrains equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a constraint position is the height $Z$ of the spatial point at which a measured or prescribed quantity is applied as an equilibrium-reconstruction constraint. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The canonical unit is the meter (m).

In practice, this coordinate specifies the vertical location of constraint information used to infer an axisymmetric magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium, such as values associated with current density, pressure, or density. In a poloidal cross-section, it is the height read along the vertical $Z$ axis at the same point whose major radius is specified by the corresponding radial coordinate.

Typical values are set by the vertical size of the plasma and nearby diagnostic or modeling region. For medium-sized tokamaks, constraint-position values commonly lie in the range -3-3 m; larger devices can span wider ranges.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the position lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame relative to the defined vertical origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the control surface in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, identifying the height of the boundary surface used to evaluate the normal component of non-axisymmetric magnetic fields.
NAMES.long:
The control surface is a geometric boundary — typically a closed toroidal surface enclosing the plasma — at which the normal component of the non-axisymmetric magnetic field is evaluated. Its vertical coordinate identifies the height of each surface point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Together with the corresponding major-radius coordinate, the $Z$ coordinate fully specifies the poloidal cross-sectional location of any control-surface point.

Control surfaces are employed in non-axisymmetric magnetostatics, error-field analysis, and resonant magnetic perturbation studies. The surface geometry is prescribed, and the normal magnetic flux through each area element is then computed from the field values and the local surface-normal vector; the $Z$ coordinate of each surface point enters both the geometric specification of the surface and the projection of normal-field couplings between external coil perturbations and the plasma interior.

This coordinate belongs to the same geometric family as [vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point), all giving the $Z$ position of a specified geometric locus. For medium to large tokamaks, control-surface $Z$ values typically range from approximately $-3$ m to $+3$ m, spanning the full vertical extent of the plasma cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the control surface point lies above the device midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the plasma current center, defined as the toroidal current-density-weighted centroid of the plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the current center is the $Z$ position of the centroid of the toroidal plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the effective vertical location of the net plasma current in the poloidal cross-section.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the current center is defined by the signed toroidal current-density-weighted centroid:

$$
Z_\mathrm{cc} = \frac{\int_\Omega Z\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dA}{\int_\Omega j_\phi(R,Z)\, dA}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{cc}$ is the vertical coordinate of the current center in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is the poloidal area element in m$^2$, and $\Omega$ is the current-carrying plasma cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The denominator is the total signed toroidal plasma current.

In practice, this quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction or model that provides the toroidal current-density distribution. It is useful for describing vertical plasma position control because it tracks the centroid of the current channel rather than a purely geometric boundary center.

Typical values are near the magnetic or geometric midplane. In many medium-size tokamaks, vertical offsets are commonly within about $\pm 0.3$ m, while large or strongly shaped plasmas can have offsets approaching about $\pm 1$ m depending on the chosen $Z=0$ reference plane and operating scenario.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current-density-weighted centroid lies in the $+Z$ direction from the $Z=0$ reference plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_dr_dz_zero_point
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate, measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of a selected plasma-boundary or separatrix point where major radius has zero slope with respect to vertical height. The point marks an inner or outer radial extremum of the boundary shape.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a $dR/dZ=0$ point is the scalar $Z_0$ of a selected point on the plasma boundary or separatrix where the contour reaches a radial extremum in a poloidal cross-section. It is measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $R_b(Z)$ represent the local branch of the boundary contour near the selected radial extremum. The defining condition is:

$$
\left.\frac{dR_b}{dZ}\right|_{Z=Z_0} = 0
$$

where $Z_0$ is the documented vertical coordinate in meters, $R_b$ is the boundary major radius in meters expressed as a function of the vertical coordinate $Z$ in meters, and the derivative is evaluated on the selected branch. If both the high-field-side and low-field-side branches satisfy this condition, the relevant solution is the one associated with the intended radial extremum; it should be interpreted together with the companion major-radius coordinate or an explicit inner/outer branch specification.

In equilibrium analysis, $Z_0$ is obtained by tracing or interpolating the plasma boundary or separatrix in a fixed-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and solving for zeros of $dR_b/dZ$. The value is used with boundary-shape quantities such as the boundary major radius and minor radius to characterize radial extrema and vertical displacement of the plasma shape.

Typical values are machine-size dependent and lie within the vertical extent of the boundary. Midplane-centered, up-down symmetric equilibria commonly give $Z_0$ close to 0 m for radial extrema, while vertically shifted or asymmetric equilibria can give signed values from less than 0.01 m in magnitude to several m in large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected point lies in the $+Z$ direction from the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the plasma geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured upward from the machine midplane. It is the arithmetic midpoint between the maximum and minimum vertical positions of the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the geometric axis is the $Z$ location halfway between the uppermost and lowermost points of the last closed flux surface. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height measured upward from the machine midplane. This is an extrema-based midpoint, not a vertical centroid or area-weighted center of the boundary.

The quantity is defined from the vertical extrema of the plasma boundary:

$$
Z_\mathrm{geom} = \frac{Z_\mathrm{max} + Z_\mathrm{min}}{2}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{max}$ and $Z_\mathrm{min}$ are the maximum and minimum boundary vertical coordinates in meters, and $Z_\mathrm{geom}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis.

In practice, $Z_\mathrm{geom}$ is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction after identifying the last closed flux surface or separatrix and finding its upper and lower vertical extrema. It is complementary to the radial geometric-axis coordinate and can differ from the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis), especially in shaped or vertically displaced plasmas.

Typical values are near 0 m for plasmas centered on the machine midplane, often within -0.5 m to 0.5 m in medium-size tokamaks. Larger devices or deliberately vertically shifted equilibria can have values of order several meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric axis lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Vertical height coordinate of points on the plasma boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z is measured upward from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate gives the $Z$ component of each point tracing the plasma boundary contour — the outermost closed flux surface in limited configurations or the separatrix in diverted configurations — in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the vertical height from the machine midplane and $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis.

Together with the corresponding radial coordinate, these $Z$ values fully define the poloidal cross-sectional shape of the plasma boundary, which governs geometric descriptors such as [elongation_of_plasma_boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and the proximity of the plasma to the first wall, as characterized by [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point). In diverted plasmas the boundary follows the separatrix through the X-point region, whose vertical position is described by [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point).

The boundary outline is derived from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements and flux loop data. Typical $Z$ values span from approximately $-a\kappa$ to $+a\kappa$, where $a$ is the minor radius and $\kappa$ is the elongation; for medium and large tokamaks this corresponds to a range of roughly $\pm 1$ to $\pm 3$ m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point lies above the machine midplane, in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the secondary X-point, the poloidal magnetic null that anchors the secondary separatrix in double-null and snowflake divertor configurations.
NAMES.long:
The secondary X-point is a poloidal magnetic null at which both components of the poloidal magnetic field vanish and the secondary separatrix topology is established. It arises in advanced divertor configurations — double-null, snowflake, and related geometries — where a second separatrix surface exists, directly influencing power exhaust and particle control. The vertical coordinate $Z$ of this null locates it in the poloidal cross-section within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the height measured from the geometric midplane.

Null points of the poloidal field are saddle points of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi(R, Z)$, satisfying

$$
\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z} = 0
$$

where the secondary X-point is the solution located outside the primary separatrix. Equilibrium reconstruction determines $\psi(R, Z)$ and identifies all saddle points numerically to extract this coordinate.

In symmetric double-null configurations the secondary X-point lies near the negative of the primary X-point $Z$-value; in asymmetric or snow-flake geometries its height depends on plasma shape and coil currents. The [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) provides the companion coordinate for the dominant null, while [vertical_coordinate_of_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) documents the generic single-null case.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the secondary X-point lies above the geometric midplane, i.e., $Z > 0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the strike point, the location where the plasma separatrix intersects a divertor target plate or limiter surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long:
The strike point is the intersection of the plasma separatrix — the outermost closed magnetic flux surface boundary — with a plasma-facing component, typically a divertor target plate. In a diverted tokamak configuration, separatrix field lines originate at the poloidal magnetic null, the [X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), and terminate at the divertor surface. The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates this termination in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is directed vertically along the symmetry axis.

The strike-point position is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by intersecting the traced separatrix contour — derived from the reconstructed poloidal flux distribution — with the known device geometry. Both the primary and secondary separatrices can yield associated strike-point positions, corresponding to different divertor target plates in single-null and double-null configurations.

In standard single-null and double-null divertor configurations, strike points are positioned at $|Z|$ values of order $0.5$–$2.0$ m from the geometric midplane, reflecting the vertical depth of the divertor chamber and strongly depending on device size and plasma shaping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the tokamak geometric midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the X-point, the poloidal magnetic null point at which the separatrix forms, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X-point is a magnetic null in the poloidal cross-section where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes, causing adjoining flux surfaces to merge and form the separatrix that separates confined plasma from the scrape-off layer. Its vertical position $Z_X$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is a fundamental geometric parameter of divertor configurations.

The X-point location satisfies the simultaneous first-order null conditions on $\psi(R, Z)$:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}\right|_{(R_X,\,Z_X)} = \left.\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}\right|_{(R_X,\,Z_X)} = 0
$$

where $R_X$ is the major-radius position and $Z_X$ is the vertical position, both in meters.

The vertical coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by solving the Grad-Shafranov equation and locating saddle points of $\psi(R, Z)$, constrained by external magnetic measurements. Measured position estimates from real-time magnetics diagnostics may also serve as direct constraints in the reconstruction fit.

In lower single-null configurations $Z_X$ is negative (below the midplane), while upper single-null configurations yield positive $Z_X$; typical magnitudes lie in the range 0.5–2.0 m for medium-to-large tokamaks. When both X-points are present in double-null equilibria, their vertical coordinates are captured by [vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies above the geometric midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical component of an iron-core segment's magnetization in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, taken to be uniform within the segment. The quantity is mu0 times M_Z, so it is expressed in tesla rather than amperes per meter.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetization of an iron-core segment is the component along the $Z$ direction of the volume-averaged magnetization vector $\mathbf{M}$ within a discrete ferromagnetic iron-core segment, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Each segment is treated as having a single uniform magnetization, so this quantity is one scalar per segment. The physical magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume (units A m$^{-1}$); the value reported here is scaled by the permeability of free space so that it carries units of tesla.

The reported vertical component is the scaled quantity

$$
\mathcal{M}_Z = \mu_0 M_Z
$$

where $\mathcal{M}_Z$ is in T, $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space ($4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$), and $M_Z$ is the $Z$ component of $\mathbf{M}$ in A m$^{-1}$. In macroscopic magnetostatics the magnetization enters through the constitutive relation $\mathbf{B} = \mu_0(\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{M})$, where the magnetic flux density $\mathbf{B}$ is in T and the magnetic field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ and the magnetization $\mathbf{M}$ are both in A m$^{-1}$.

In equilibrium analysis this component is generally inferred from external magnetic measurements together with a magnetic model of the iron structure rather than measured directly within the material.
