Its magnitude and sign are governed by the local field, the segment geometry, and the nonlinear iron $B$-$H$ response including magnetic saturation and hysteresis. The companion radial component is given by [radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment](name:radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment), and the associated field response is described by [magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment](name:magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment).

For soft-iron cores the scaled magnetization saturates near the material's saturation flux density, so magnitudes of order a few tesla represent an effective upper bound, with smaller magnitudes typical in unsaturated operation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetization component points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is the signed Z-directed part of toroidally varying perturbation fields such as error fields and resonant magnetic perturbations.
NAMES.long:
Vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the $Z$ component of the toroidally varying part of a vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes the upward or downward component of perturbation fields that break toroidal symmetry, excluding the axisymmetric equilibrium contribution.

The component projection is defined by

$$
B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}(R,\phi,Z) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field in tesla, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ is the non-axisymmetric vacuum magnetic-field vector in tesla, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, $R$ is major radius in meters, $\phi$ is toroidal angle in radians, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. In current-free vacuum regions this perturbation field satisfies $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} = 0$ and, away from coil conductors, $\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}} = 0$.

Together with the [radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field) and [toroidal non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), this quantity completes the cylindrical component decomposition of $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{NA}}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The related [vertical magnetic field at wall](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall) is also a $Z$-component field, but refers to the total or relevant magnetic field at the wall rather than specifically to the toroidally varying vacuum perturbation.

It is commonly computed from Biot-Savart integration over non-axisymmetric coil currents or from vacuum magnetic-field calculations, and may be compared with magnetic-probe measurements after accounting for probe orientation and location. The quantity is evaluated at physical locations of interest to characterize error fields, resonant magnetic perturbations, and their coupling to the plasma boundary or surrounding structures.

Typical magnitudes are strongly device-, coil-current-, and location-dependent. The value is zero for a purely axisymmetric vacuum field and is usually interpreted in tesla or as a fraction of the local equilibrium magnetic field rather than by a universal numerical range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z^{\mathrm{NA}}$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_at_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical velocity of the plasma-current centroid, equal to the time derivative of its Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical velocity at the current center is the rate of change of the vertical coordinate of the plasma-current centroid. The current center is the centroid of the toroidal plasma current density in a poloidal cross-section, with coordinates defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the velocity associated with vertical_position_at_current_center and is complementary to radial_velocity_at_current_center.

The current-density-weighted definition can be written as:

$$
v_Z^{cc} = \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{\int_{\Omega_p} Z\, j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\, dZ}{\int_{\Omega_p} j_\phi(R,Z,t)\, dR\, dZ}\right]
$$

where $v_Z^{cc}$ is the vertical velocity of the current center, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal component of the plasma current density, $\Omega_p$ is the plasma region in the poloidal cross-section, and the denominator is the total toroidal [plasma_current](name:toroidal_plasma_current) through that cross-section.

In practice, the current-center position is obtained from an equilibrium solution or reconstruction of the toroidal current density distribution, and the velocity is computed from its time evolution, usually with smoothing or filtering because time differentiation amplifies noise. The quantity characterizes vertical motion of the current channel, which is especially important for position control and vertical-displacement dynamics in elongated plasmas. Unlike [toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), it describes the motion of the current-density centroid rather than mass-weighted bulk plasma flow.

Typical values are close to 0 m.s^-1 in a stationary or well-controlled equilibrium, because the current centroid is not translating vertically on average. During vertical transients the magnitude is device- and scenario-dependent and can become much larger than the controlled-state value, so universal numerical limits are not physically meaningful.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current centroid moves in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of the physical location of a toroidal magnetic field probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the height of a toroidal magnetic field probe above the geometric midplane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height. Toroidal magnetic field probes are inductive sensors deployed on or near the vacuum vessel to monitor the toroidal component $B_\phi$ of the magnetic field; precise knowledge of each probe's spatial position is essential for interpreting the local field measurement and for incorporating the data into MHD equilibrium reconstruction.

The $Z$ position is a fixed geometric attribute established by engineering survey during machine installation. Together with the corresponding major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates, it fully specifies the three-dimensional location of the probe. This coordinate role is shared across other magnetic diagnostic components, such as [poloidal field coil] elements and [general measurement positions](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position) used in equilibrium reconstruction, and analogously for [lower hybrid antenna](name:vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) reference points.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is located above the geometric midplane, in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Alpha angle of an iron core segment is the first signed inclination of an oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-section. It is measured in the poloidal R-Z cross-section of the IMAS cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame from the outward major-radius direction to the slanted alpha-side direction.
NAMES.long:
The alpha angle $\alpha$ is the first inclination angle used to parameterize an oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-section of an iron core segment. The cross-section is taken in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the IMAS cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It defines the orientation of the slanted side associated with [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment), complementary to the other inclined side length [length_of_iron_core_segment](name:length_of_iron_core_segment).

For an $\alpha$-inclined side, the unit tangent in the cross-section is

$$
\hat{t}_{\alpha} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{R} + \sin\alpha\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{t}_{\alpha}$ is the tangent along the alpha-side, $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the major-radius and vertical basis vectors of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, and $\alpha$ is in radians. A side of length $L_{\alpha}$ then gives in-plane displacements $\Delta R=L_{\alpha}\cos\alpha$ and $\Delta Z=L_{\alpha}\sin\alpha$, which fixes the vertices and face normals used in geometric, magnetic, and structural calculations.

In practice, $\alpha$ is obtained from engineering drawings, CAD geometry, or the coordinates of the endpoints of the slanted side in the local $R$-$Z$ cross-section. If the two endpoints are known, the same convention is recovered with $\alpha=\operatorname{atan2}(Z_2-Z_1,R_2-R_1)$, with $R$ and $Z$ in meters and the angular branch chosen consistently with the segment geometry.

There is no universal device-independent design range. The full angular branch is commonly interpreted over about $-3.14$-$3.14$ rad; reference orientations are $0$ rad for an outward radial side, $1.57$ rad for a vertical upward side, and about $3.14$ rad or $-3.14$ rad for an inward radial side. Nearly rectangular cross-sections have $\alpha$ close to one of these reference orientations, while tapered iron-core segments use design-specific offsets.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side tangent is rotated counter-clockwise from the outward $+\hat{R}$ direction toward $+\hat{Z}$ in an $R$-to-the-right, $Z$-up drawing of the IMAS cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate of the toroidal field coil conductor cross-section outline vertices along the binormal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame, measuring each polygon vertex's displacement in the binormal direction perpendicular to the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate locates each vertex of the polygonal cross-section outline of a toroidal field coil conductor along the binormal direction $\hat{b}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame. In this frame, the unit tangent $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor centerline, the principal normal $\hat{n}$ points toward the center of curvature of the conductor path, and the binormal vector is defined as

$$
\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}
$$

forming a right-handed orthonormal triad $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, with the cross-section lying in the $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$ plane.

Together with the [normal coordinate], the binormal coordinate fully specifies the 2D polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section perpendicular to the conductor path. The total span in the binormal direction for a rectangular conductor equals the [height of the toroidal field coil]. This framing is also used for non-axisymmetric coils; see [binormal coordinate of correction coil] for the analogous quantity.

These coordinates are derived from engineering design data and are used in electromagnetic and structural analyzes of TF coils, where the precise cross-section shape affects current density distribution, self-inductance, and mechanical stress. Typical TF conductor cross-section dimensions range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters in each local direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coordinate is in the direction of $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$, where $\hat{t}$ is the unit tangent along the conductor centerline and $\hat{n}$ is the principal normal directed toward the center of curvature.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Number of discrete toroidal field coil modules in the confinement device, excluding conductor turns within each module.
NAMES.long:
The count of toroidal field coils is the integer total of discrete coil modules arranged around the device to produce the dominant toroidal magnetic field. It counts coil modules, not individual conductor turns, pancakes, or strands within a module, and is a fixed engineering design parameter for the magnet system.

For an axisymmetric tokamak with uniformly spaced toroidal field coils, this count sets the rotational periodicity of the coil set. If the count is $N_\mathrm{TF}$, one geometric sector spans $2\pi/N_\mathrm{TF}$ in toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. The finite number and detailed shape of the coils determine the toroidal-field ripple spectrum and can affect fast-ion confinement and periodic heat-load patterns.

The count is obtained from the device magnet design by identifying the mechanically distinct toroidal field coil modules in the full torus. It is used together with geometric coil properties such as [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil), [conductor width](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil), and [major-radius position](name:major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil) when characterizing the toroidal field system. In stellarators and heliotrons, comparable coil counts usually refer to separate modular, helical, or planar coil families rather than to tokamak-style toroidal field coils.

Typical tokamak values are 12-20 toroidal field coils, with many medium and large devices using 16-18 coils. Smaller or specialized devices may use fewer coils, while increasing the count generally reduces the angular spacing between coils and changes the high-toroidal-mode content of the ripple field.

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a non-axisymmetric correction coil, used to assess radiation exposure and predict material degradation of coil components.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutrons produced predominantly by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions scatter through plasma-facing and structural components and irradiate the conductors of non-axisymmetric correction coils. The fast neutron flux quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing a unit area of the coil's inboard surface per unit time, with the inboard face experiencing the highest neutron loading due to its relative proximity to the plasma.

The threshold-integrated fast neutron flux is defined as:

$$
\Phi_{\rm fast} = \int_{E \geq E_{\rm th}} \phi(E) \, dE
$$

where $\phi(E)$ is the differential neutron flux spectrum (m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$), $E$ is neutron kinetic energy, and $E_{\rm th}$ is a threshold energy (commonly 0.1 MeV or 1 MeV) defining the fast-neutron energy range.

This quantity is computed from neutron transport calculations using the device three-dimensional geometry and the predicted fusion neutron source rate; results are validated against threshold-detector or activation-foil measurements placed near accessible coil positions. Time-integrating this flux over an operational pulse yields the neutron fluence, which governs displacement damage in conductor insulation and structural materials. The analogous quantity for the main toroidal field coil is [fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil); for direct detector measurements see [neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector).

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a toroidal field coil, providing a measure of radiation exposure relevant to material activation, radiation damage, and conductor insulation lifetime assessment.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutron flux at a toroidal field coil quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing unit area per unit time at the inboard-facing surface of the coil structure. In deuterium-tritium burning plasmas, 14.1 MeV fusion neutrons are the dominant source; these are attenuated and scattered by the blanket and shield, but a residual fast population reaches the coil and constitutes the primary radiation load on the superconducting windings and their organic insulation.

The quantity is the energy-integrated fluence rate above a fast-neutron threshold:

$$
\Phi_n = \int_{E_\mathrm{th}}^{\infty} \Phi(E)\, dE
$$

where $\Phi(E)$, in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$, is the differential neutron flux spectrum and $E_\mathrm{th}$ is the fast-neutron energy threshold adopted in the transport model.

This flux drives radiation damage processes including atomic displacement damage in conductor structural materials, helium bubble formation, and degradation of organic insulation resins — all of which set operational lifetime limits for the coil. It is assessed using Monte Carlo or deterministic neutron transport codes, validated against activation foil and threshold detector measurements. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Inner radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative distance from the center or central axis of an annular cross-section to its inner ferromagnetic boundary. It defines the hollow bore and must be smaller than the corresponding outer radius.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of an iron-core segment is the radius of the inner boundary of an annular ferromagnetic cross-section. It identifies the boundary between the hollow region and the iron material, and together with [outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment) fixes the annular geometry of the segment.

For a circular annulus, the defining distance is

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \left|\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{inner} - \mathbf{x}_0\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the center of the annular cross-section, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{inner}$ is any point on the circular inner ferromagnetic boundary, and the resulting radius is measured in meters. A physically valid annulus satisfies $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$, where $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the outer radius in meters; the corresponding iron cross-sectional area is $A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)$.

This radius is used when constructing geometric and electromagnetic representations of iron-core segments. Increasing the inner radius reduces the flux-conducting iron area for a fixed outer radius, thereby affecting magnetic reluctance, possible saturation, and mass distribution. Non-annular segment cross-sections are more naturally described by [width_of_iron_core_segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) and [height_of_iron_core_segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment).

Typical values are strongly device- and design-dependent. In tokamak iron-core models they are usually engineering-scale lengths, from about 0.1-5 m, with compact or local annular segments toward the lower end and large central-core or return-yoke elements toward the upper end.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element. It is the distance from the annulus center to the inner conducting boundary and, with the outer radius, sets the conductor thickness used in electromagnetic and resistive calculations.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of a passive loop is the radius of the hole or excluded central region in an annular conductor cross-section. Together with the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the conducting material thickness of the loop element and affects its resistance, inductance, and eddy-current response.

For an ideal annular cross-section, the conducting area is related to the inner and outer radii by:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the conducting cross-sectional area, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is the inner radius, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the corresponding outer radius.

The value is determined from the mechanical geometry of the passive conducting structure, such as a vacuum-vessel segment, stabilizing plate, shell, or other closed conducting loop. It is used in reduced electromagnetic models to compute the conductor area, resistance, mutual inductance, and induced eddy currents. The closely related [inner radius of a passive structure](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) describes the same geometric concept for passive conducting structures more generally.

Typical values range from 0.001-0.1 m for small annular conductor features and from 0.01-1 m for large vessel or support-structure elements, depending on the device scale and the level of geometric simplification.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame for a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section, measuring each outline vertex's displacement perpendicular to both the conductor centerline and the binormal direction.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate specifies the position of each vertex of the toroidal field coil conductor cross-section outline polygon along the principal normal axis $\hat{N}$ of the local Frenet-Serret frame. Together with the [binormal coordinate](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), it fully describes the 2D polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section in the plane perpendicular to the conductor centerline.

At any point along the conductor path, the Frenet-Serret frame is defined by the unit tangent $\hat{T}$ (along the centerline), the principal normal $\hat{N}$ (perpendicular to $\hat{T}$ in the plane of curvature), and the binormal $\hat{B} = \hat{T} \times \hat{N}$. The normal coordinate of an outline vertex is:

$$
s_N = \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \hat{N}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the displacement vector from the local centerline point to the vertex in meters, and $\hat{N}$ is the dimensionless unit normal vector.

The complete set of normal and binormal coordinate pairs for all outline vertices defines the conductor cross-section polygon, which determines conductor area, current density distribution, and electromagnetic force calculations on the coil. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil).

Typical TF coil conductor cross-sections in large tokamaks span a few centimeters to tens of centimeters, placing vertex coordinates in the range of roughly $-0.1$ to $0.1$ m relative to the conductor centerline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the Frenet-Serret normal vector $\hat{N}$.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, defining the outer radial boundary of the annulus geometry used in electromagnetic modeling.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the radial extent of the outer boundary of the annular (hollow circular) cross-section of a passive conducting loop element, such as a vacuum vessel segment or other passive toroidal conductor. Together with [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), it fully parameterizes the annular cross-section geometry used in electromagnetic circuit models to compute eddy-current responses, self-inductances, and resistances.

The cross-sectional area of the annulus is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_{\rm out}^2 - r_{\rm in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius and $r_{\rm in}$ is the correspondent [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), both in m. This area enters directly into resistance and inductance estimates of the passive loop element under the thin-shell approximation.

Geometry parameters are obtained from engineering drawings or CAD models of the passive conductor assembly. Typical values range from a few centimeters for small conducting ribs to approximately 0.5 m for large vacuum vessel sectors, depending on device scale. The [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) is the analogous quantity for active poloidal field coil conductors.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the geometric center of the annular cross-section outward to the conductor's outer boundary.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil conductor element, defining the radial outer boundary of the conductor geometry.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the outward radial extent of the annular cross-section used to model a poloidal field coil conductor element. Together with the [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the coil center position in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane, it fully specifies the annular geometry required for electromagnetic calculations such as mutual inductance and Biot-Savart field evaluation.

The annular cross-sectional area $A$ is:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil). This [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) enters directly into current density and inductance calculations.

For PF coil conductors in medium-to-large fusion devices, outer radii range from a few centimeters to approximately 0.3-0.5 m, depending on the conductor bundle size and design current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer boundary lies at a greater radial distance from the annulus center than the inner boundary, as required for a physically valid annular cross-section.

NAMES.name: radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: First inclination angle (alpha) of the oblique parallelogram or trapezoidal cross-section of a poloidal field coil element, measured in the poloidal plane from the outward major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal field coil conductors are frequently designed with non-rectangular cross-sections modeled as parallelograms or trapezoids in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The radial angle $\alpha$ defines the inclination of one pair of parallel sides (the alpha-sides) relative to the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$, characterizing how much the conductor winding departs from a purely radial orientation.

The oblique cross-section is fully parameterized by two inclination angles and two side lengths. The radial angle $\alpha$ pairs with the [vertical angle](name:vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) $\beta$ — measured from the vertical $+\hat{Z}$ direction — to define both side orientations, while [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil) give the corresponding alpha-side and beta-side lengths.

This angle is a fixed geometric design parameter derived from coil engineering drawings and used in computing cross-sectional area, mutual inductance, and electromagnetic force distributions in poloidal field coil systems. The analogous first inclination angle for iron core segments is described by [alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side of the cross-section is inclined counter-clockwise from $+\hat{R}$ (toward $+\hat{Z}$) in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

NAMES.name: radial_force
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic force on the poloidal-field coil system resolved along increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height. It equals the sum of the radial force components on the individual poloidal-field coils.
NAMES.long:
Radial force is the net electromagnetic force component acting on the poloidal-field coil system in the direction of major radius. It represents the aggregate radial Lorentz load over all active poloidal-field coils, complementary to the axial component described by [vertical_force](name:vertical_force).

The radial component can be written as the radial projection of the Lorentz force density integrated over the coil conductors, equivalently as a sum over individual coil contributions:

$$
F_R = \int_{V_{\mathrm{PF}}} (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\, dV = \sum_k F_{R,k}
$$

where $F_R$ and each $F_{R,k}$ are forces in N, $V_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is the conducting volume of the poloidal-field coil system, $\mathbf{j}$ is current density in A m^-2, $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic flux density in T, $dV$ is a volume element in m^3, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the outward radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The term $F_{R,k}$ is the [radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) for coil $k$.

This quantity is usually computed from electromagnetic models using the coil current distribution, conductor geometry, and magnetic field at the coil locations. It may also be obtained by summing the evaluated radial forces of the individual poloidal-field coils.

Typical absolute magnitudes are strongly device and scenario dependent: small experimental coil systems may have radial forces of order $10^3$-$10^5$ N, while medium and large tokamak poloidal-field systems commonly reach $10^6$-$10^8$ N. Values should be interpreted relative to the mechanical limits defined for the specific coil system.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force is directed toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Electrical resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction coil conductor, determining the ohmic power dissipation and static voltage drop across the coil terminals.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a correction coil characterizes the DC ohmic resistance of the conductor winding, governing resistive power dissipation and the steady-state voltage-current relationship in the coil circuit. Correction coils are non-axisymmetric coils that apply three-dimensional magnetic perturbations for ELM suppression, error field correction, or resonant magnetic perturbation experiments.

The ohmic power dissipated in the coil is:

$$
P_{\rm ohm} = I^2 R
$$

where $I$ is the [current through the coil](name:current_of_correction_coil) and $R$ is the resistance. The corresponding [terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_correction_coil) satisfies $V = IR$ under DC conditions; at finite frequency an inductive contribution adds to the impedance, but the resistive component captured here determines steady-state dissipation and thermal loading on the coil support structure.

Resistance is determined from conductor material resistivity (which varies with temperature), conductor cross-sectional area, and total winding path length, or measured directly by a DC voltage-current sweep at the coil terminals.

Values for correction coils in large tokamaks range from a few milliohms to several ohms, depending on conductor dimensions and winding geometry. The analogous quantity for toroidal field coils is [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a passive conducting loop, which together with its self-inductance sets the L/R time constant governing eddy-current decay during plasma transients.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a passive conducting loop quantifies the ohmic opposition to current flow in an axisymmetric conductor that is inductively coupled to the plasma but not connected to an external power supply. Passive loops carry eddy currents induced by changes in plasma current or equilibrium position, and their resistance governs how quickly those induced currents decay.

The resistance $R$ and self-inductance $L$ together determine the characteristic decay time constant:

$$
\tau = \frac{L}{R}
$$

where $\tau$ is the e-folding time for eddy-current decay, $L$ is the self-inductance, and $R$ is this resistance. A smaller resistance extends $\tau$, prolonging the stabilizing influence of the eddy currents during vertical displacement events or plasma disruptions.

For a loop of uniform cross-section, $R = \rho \ell / A$, where $\rho$ is the material resistivity (see [resistivity_of_passive_structure](name:resistivity_of_passive_structure)), $\ell$ is the mean conductor path length, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area determined by [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). Values range from sub-milliohm for low-resistivity conductors to tens of milliohms for higher-resistivity materials, depending on geometry. This quantity follows the established resistance-of-object pattern alongside [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a poloidal field coil winding. It relates coil current to resistive voltage drop and Joule heating at the specified operating state.
NAMES.long:
Resistance of a poloidal field coil is the effective series ohmic resistance of the coil winding at its operating state. It represents conversion of electrical energy into heat in the conductor, joints, and other series elements included in the coil definition, and it sets the resistive part of the terminal voltage demand.

In a lumped circuit model for coil $k$, the terminal-voltage balance is commonly written after choosing branch-current and terminal-voltage reference directions:

$$
V_k = R_k I_k + L_k \frac{dI_k}{dt} + \sum_{j \ne k} \epsilon_{kj} M_{kj} \frac{dI_j}{dt}
$$

where $V_k$ is the terminal voltage in V, $R_k$ is the coil resistance in ohm, $I_k$ and $I_j$ are currents in A, $L_k$ is self-inductance in H, $M_{kj}$ is mutual inductance in H, $dI/dt$ is in A/s, $j$ labels coupled circuits or conductors, and $\epsilon_{kj}$ is a dimensionless factor equal to $+1$ or $-1$ for the chosen mutual-reference orientation. The equation assumes the passive reference for the resistive drop, with $V_k$ positive as a voltage drop along the chosen positive $I_k$ direction; reversing a current reference or terminal-voltage polarity changes the algebraic signs of the inductive and mutual terms consistently, but does not change the non-negative value of $R_k$.

The value is computed from conductor material resistivity, winding length, cross-sectional area, cooling state, and the temperature distribution of the winding. It may be measured by four-terminal DC injection or inferred from slow current ramps after subtracting inductive and mutual voltage contributions. For normal-conducting coils the resistance increases with temperature; for superconducting coils the effective series resistance depends on whether joints, current-sharing regions, or quench behavior are included in the coil model.

Typical effective resistances are $10^{-4}$-$10^{-1}$ ohm for large normal-conducting poloidal field coils and $10^{-3}$-1 ohm for smaller shaping or laboratory coils. Superconducting poloidal field windings in steady superconducting operation are often represented as 0-$10^{-6}$ ohm effective series resistance when only persistent or joint losses are included; during current sharing or a quench, the apparent resistance can rise to $10^{-4}$-1 ohm and becomes strongly time dependent.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a toroidal field coil conductor, determining resistive power dissipation and voltage drop during coil operation.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a toroidal field coil is the ohmic impedance of its conductor winding at a given temperature and operational state, governing how the coil dissipates energy and sustains a voltage drop when carrying current.

The resistive power deposited in the coil is defined by:

$$
P_\mathrm{ohm} = I^2 R_\mathrm{TF}
$$

where $I$ is the coil current and $R_\mathrm{TF}$ is the coil resistance. The resistance depends on conductor geometry and material electrical resistivity $\rho_e$ through $R_\mathrm{TF} = \rho_e L / A_c$, where $L$ is the total conductor length and $A_c$ is the conductor cross-sectional area.

Coil resistance is determined by direct four-wire (Kelvin) electrical measurements or from conductor material properties and geometry as a function of temperature. For superconducting TF coils operated below the critical temperature, the effective resistance is negligible; for normal-conducting (resistive) TF coils, values range from a few milliohms to tens of milliohms depending on device scale and conductor material.

The resistive voltage drop $V_R = I \cdot R_\mathrm{TF}$ contributes to the total terminal voltage captured by [voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil). Analogous quantities for other coil systems include [resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [resistance_of_correction_coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section contour point, expressed relative to the cross-section reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It is used with major radius and vertical height to locate the contour point.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross section is the angular coordinate of a conductor-contour point measured relative to a designated reference point on that cross section. It is the toroidal component of the point location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For contour point $i$, the relative toroidal angle is defined as the difference between the point and reference toroidal coordinates:

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i} = \phi_i - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $\phi_i$ is the toroidal coordinate of the contour point, $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal coordinate of the reference point, and $\phi_{\mathrm{rel},i}$ is expressed in radians. Because toroidal angle is periodic, values that differ by $2\pi n$, with integer $n$, represent the same toroidal direction; the physical definition does not impose a device-independent wrapping interval.

In practice, this coordinate is computed from the engineered conductor geometry by evaluating the toroidal coordinate of each contour point and subtracting the reference-point toroidal coordinate. Together with the radial coordinate [major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil) and vertical height [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil), it locates the contour point in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The corresponding generic conductor quantity is [toroidal_angle_of_conductor_cross_section](name:toroidal_angle_of_conductor_cross_section).

Typical numerical values are design-specific and depend on the chosen reference point and conductor cross-section geometry. The relevant universal scale is the angular periodicity $2\pi$ rad, so the values should be interpreted as relative toroidal coordinates rather than as absolute toroidal positions of the coil.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point is displaced from the reference point in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inclination angle beta of the second oblique side of a poloidal field coil parallelogram cross-section, measured counter-clockwise from the vertically upward direction in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical angle $\beta$ parameterizes the tilt of the second inclined side of the oblique parallelogram cross-section of a poloidal field coil conductor element, specified in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with the [radial angle $\alpha$](name:radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) (measured counter-clockwise from the outward $\hat{R}$ direction), $\beta$ fully defines the oblique orientation of the non-rectangular conductor winding-pack geometry.

The angle is defined by the dot-product relation:

$$
\hat{e}_{\beta} \cdot \hat{Z} = \cos\beta
$$

where $\hat{e}_{\beta}$ is the unit vector along the beta-side inclined edge and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertically upward unit vector; the signed direction is determined by measuring $\beta$ counter-clockwise from $+\hat{Z}$ in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane.

This geometric parameter is derived from engineering design data for the coil winding pack and is used in electromagnetic analysis to compute conductor self- and mutual inductances and Lorentz forces on the cross-section. The extent of the beta-side edge is given by [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil), while [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) gives the alpha-side edge extent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beta-side edge direction $\hat{e}_{\beta}$ is rotated counter-clockwise from $+\hat{Z}$ in the poloidal $R$-$Z$ plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Vertical Z-coordinate of a geometric reference point on the cross-section of a passive conducting structure, measured in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates a geometric point defining the cross-sectional shape of a passive conducting structure element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the height above the machine midplane. Passive structures are unpowered conducting elements — such as stabilizing loops, conducting shells, or vacuum vessel segments — that respond to time-varying magnetic fields through induced eddy currents, influencing plasma vertical stability and equilibrium evolution.

Cross-sections of passive elements are described by parametric shapes: polygon outlines (sequences of vertices), arcs of circles, oblique trapezoids, or thick-line segments defined by two endpoint coordinates. This $Z$ coordinate specifies one such geometric vertex or endpoint, and must be paired with the corresponding major-radius coordinate to fully define a point in the poloidal plane. Geometry is typically specified from engineering drawings or as-built surveys of the device. Analogous coordinates for active coil elements are given by [vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor) and [vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section](name:vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section).

Typical values span the vertical extent of the machine, ranging from approximately $-2$ to $+2$ m in medium-sized tokamaks and up to $\pm 4$ m in larger devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: width_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Width of a poloidal field coil is the non-negative scalar full radial extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section. It is a length measured along the major-radius direction, not a directed displacement.
NAMES.long:
Width of a poloidal field coil is the full radial extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section. It is a non-negative scalar length in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section with radial bounds $R_\mathrm{in}$ and $R_\mathrm{out}$, the width is

$$
w = R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in} = \max(R) - \min(R)
$$

where $w$ is the coil width, $R_\mathrm{out}$ and $R_\mathrm{in}$ are the larger and smaller radial bounds of the conductor cross-section, and all lengths are measured in meters.

The width is determined from the conductor geometry, for example from the radial bounds represented by the [radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil). Together with the [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), it defines the rectangular cross-section used in electromagnetic and structural calculations; for a rectangle, the [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) satisfies the inline relation $A = w h$, where $h$ is in meters and $A$ is in square meters.

Valid values satisfy $w \ge 0$. A strictly positive value represents a finite conductor cross-section, while $w = 0$ is a degenerate geometric limit rather than a physical coil width.

NAMES.name: width_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative transverse width of a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section, measured in the local normal direction of the conductor frame and perpendicular to the conductor path. It is the full normal-direction extent for rectangular or square sections and the outer diameter for circular or annular sections.
NAMES.long:
The width of a toroidal field coil conductor is the non-negative length describing the normal-direction size of the conductor cross-section. At each point on the conductor centerline, use the local right-handed conductor frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, where $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor path, $\hat{n}$ is the cross-section normal direction, and $\hat{b}=\hat{t}\times\hat{n}$ is the binormal; the width is measured along $\hat{n}$, while [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil) is measured along $\hat{b}$. For rectangular or square conductors it is the full extent along $\hat{n}$; for circular sections it is the diameter, and for annular sections it is the outer diameter.

For a rectangular conductor cross-section, the width and height determine the geometric cross-sectional area:

$$
A = w h
$$

where $A$ is the [area_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil) in m^2, $w$ is the width in m, and $h$ is the [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil) in m.

In practice, the width is taken from the coil conductor design definition, manufacturing survey, or a reconstructed conductor outline in the local cross-section plane $(\hat{n}, \hat{b})$. For an outline-based description, it corresponds to the full projected extent of the conductor boundary along $\hat{n}$, with the geometric model determining whether the same parameter represents a rectangular width, a circular diameter, or an annular outer diameter.

Typical toroidal field coil conductor widths in medium-to-large tokamaks are about 0.01-0.10 m, with larger values possible for heavily reinforced cases or winding packs in high-field devices.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the complex first-order plasma temperature perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability analysis, plasma perturbations for a given toroidal mode number are expressed as complex spatial eigenfunctions. This quantity gives $\text{Re}[\tilde{T}]$, the real part of the complex temperature perturbation eigenfunction $\tilde{T}(\mathbf{r})$, encoding the in-phase spatial structure of the temperature mode relative to the chosen eigenmode normalization.

The time-evolving perturbation field is reconstructed from the eigenfunction components as:

$$
\delta T(\mathbf{r}, t) = \text{Re}\!\left[\tilde{T}(\mathbf{r})\, e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}\right]
$$

where $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency whose imaginary part gives the linear growth or damping rate.

This component is computed by linear MHD stability solvers as one element of a complete set of perturbed field eigenfunctions; together with the [imaginary part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part), it fully specifies the complex eigenfunction $\tilde{T}$. Analogous decompositions apply to [perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure_real_part) and [perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part). The absolute magnitude of $\text{Re}[\tilde{T}]$ is set by the eigenmode normalization convention and must be scaled by the physical mode amplitude to represent an actual temperature perturbation.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex radial component of the linearized magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma, for a specified toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex radial vacuum magnetic-field perturbation, $\delta B_R^{\rm im}$, is the quadrature component of the first-order linearized magnetic-field perturbation projected along $+\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma. In linear MHD stability analysis, perturbed fields are cast as complex Fourier harmonics in the toroidal angle $\phi$; the imaginary part encodes the phase of the eigenmode relative to the normalization reference, together with the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part).

In the vacuum region, $\delta\mathbf{B}$ satisfies $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. The complex radial component decomposes as:

$$
\delta\tilde{B}_R^{\rm vac} = \delta B_R^{\rm re} + i\,\delta B_R^{\rm im}
$$

where $\delta B_R^{\rm re}$ is the [real part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and $\delta B_R^{\rm im}$ is this imaginary part. The perturbation amplitude is $|\delta\tilde{B}_R^{\rm vac}| = \sqrt{(\delta B_R^{\rm re})^2 + (\delta B_R^{\rm im})^2}$ and the phase is $\theta = \mathrm{atan2}(\delta B_R^{\rm im},\,\delta B_R^{\rm re})$.

This quantity is computed by linear MHD stability codes for a specified toroidal mode number $n$. Matching conditions at the plasma-vacuum interface link it to its plasma-region counterpart, [the radial plasma imaginary part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part). Alongside [the toroidal vacuum imaginary component](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), it characterizes the helical spatial structure of the perturbed vacuum field. As with all linear eigenfunctions, the partition between real and imaginary parts depends on the phase normalization convention applied to the eigenmode.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight average of the total oxygen impurity number density, encompassing all charge states from neutral to fully stripped, divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged oxygen density is the chord-mean of the local oxygen number density—summed over all charge states from neutral O$^0$ through fully stripped O$^{8+}$—along a measurement path through the plasma. It characterizes the mean impurity concentration of oxygen along a given line of sight and is directly related to the local [oxygen_density](name:oxygen_density) integrated along the chord.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_O \rangle_\ell = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_O(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_O(\ell)$ is the local oxygen number density at position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the chord length in m.

Line-averaged impurity densities are extracted from chord-integrated spectroscopic measurements of oxygen emission lines combined with ionization balance models. Passive spectroscopy of ultraviolet oxygen transitions or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of helium-like and hydrogen-like oxygen lines provides the chord-integrated signal from which the line-averaged density is inferred. As a chord-averaged observable, spatial resolution is inherently limited, and tomographic inversion or profile modeling is required to recover local distributions.

Oxygen is a low-concentration impurity in fusion plasmas under normal operating conditions; line-averaged values fall several orders of magnitude below the electron density, with representative ranges of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on wall conditioning and impurity seeding. The [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) provides the plasma-volume–weighted counterpart, while analogous chord-averaged densities for other impurity species include [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen impurity particles are present along the measurement chord at nonzero concentration.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_pellet_path_point
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of a point along the pellet injection path, giving the radial distance from the machine toroidal symmetry axis in the cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of a pellet path point is the radial distance $R$ from the toroidal symmetry axis to a discrete location along the trajectory of an injected pellet or shattered pellet injector (SPI) fragment, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ increases outward from the machine axis.

Together with [vertical_coordinate_of_pellet_path_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_pellet_path_point) (the $Z$ component) and [toroidal_angle_of_along_pellet_path](name:toroidal_angle_of_along_pellet_path) (the $\phi$ component), this coordinate fully specifies the three-dimensional position of a point on the pellet or SPI fragment trajectory. The radial coordinate determines how far from the plasma center the injected material deposits fuel or impurity species, directly governing the radial deposition profile.

Pellet path geometry is defined by discrete anchor points — such as the injector exit and, for SPI systems, the shattering position — with the trajectory reconstructed from optical pellet diagnostics or injection geometry specifications. For SPI applications, the shattering-position $R$ value locates where the intact pellet transitions into a dispersing fragment cloud.

Typical values range from about 1.5 m in compact tokamaks to beyond 6 m in large devices, bounded below by the first-wall major radius and above by the outer vessel radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured radially outward from the machine toroidal symmetry axis, as defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; $R \geq 0$ for all physically realizable positions.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius of a detector pixel is the cylindrical $R$ coordinate of the pixel center. It is the perpendicular distance from the machine toroidal symmetry axis to the point representing the center of the pixel's active area in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

When the same point is represented in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with origin on the toroidal symmetry axis and $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the major radius is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the pixel center in m, and $R$ is the major radius in m.

In practice this coordinate is obtained from the diagnostic geometry, survey information, optical design, or alignment model that maps each detector pixel into machine coordinates. Together with the corresponding toroidal angle and vertical position, it fixes the spatial location used to determine viewing geometry, lines of sight, and spatial calibration for pixel-resolved radiation measurements.

Typical values are set by the diagnostic location and device size: detector pixels in compact tokamaks may have major radii of about 0.3-2 m, while pixels associated with cameras or spectrometers on larger devices may lie at about 2-10 m from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_density
NAMES.short: Local non-negative volumetric rate at which plasma emits electromagnetic radiation, representing radiated power per unit volume.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power density is the local, non-negative volumetric rate at which plasma thermal energy is converted to electromagnetic radiation. It includes continuum, line, recombination, and other photon emission processes that contribute to bolometric radiated power.

The total radiated power associated with a plasma volume is the volume integral of the local emission density:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad} = \int_V p_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{rad}$ is total radiated power in W, $p_\mathrm{rad}$ is radiated power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes spatial position, and $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$. For an axisymmetric reconstruction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height, the poloidal-plane volume element is $dV = 2\pi R\,dR\,dZ$; this reduction assumes toroidal symmetry of $p_\mathrm{rad}$.

Bolometer measurements infer this quantity from calibrated line-of-sight signals through an optically thin plasma. For channel $i$, the measured signal is commonly modeled as a path integral, $b_i \approx \int_{\ell_i} G_i(\mathbf{x})\,p_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{x})\,dl$, where $b_i$ is the calibrated channel response, $G_i$ is the geometric and instrumental response kernel, $\ell_i$ is the viewing chord, and $dl$ is path length in meters. Tomographic inversion combines many such chords, with regularization and uncertainty estimates, to recover the spatial emission distribution.

Typical local values are about $10^3$-$10^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in relatively low-radiation core plasmas, $10^6$-$10^8$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly radiating edge, divertor, or impurity-accumulation regions, and near zero outside the emitting plasma within measurement uncertainty.

NAMES.name: radius_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Radius of a circular diagnostic aperture, defined as the distance from the aperture center to its circular edge. It characterizes the opening size used to compute the corresponding aperture area.
NAMES.long:
The radius of a circular diagnostic aperture is the distance from the center of an idealized circular opening to its edge. It is the appropriate size parameter when the entrance aperture, collimating aperture, or sensitive circular region is modeled as a circle; non-circular apertures are characterized by quantities such as [width_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:width_of_diagnostic_aperture).

For an ideal circular aperture, the associated aperture area is

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius in meters and $A$ is the [area_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture) in square meters. The corresponding [diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture) is $d = 2r$, where $d$ is the full edge-to-edge distance through the aperture center.

The radius is obtained from mechanical drawings, dimensional metrology, optical inspection, or calibration of the fabricated diagnostic component. For a non-ideal or partially obscured circular opening, an effective radius may be chosen so that the ideal circular area matches the usable open area. The radius contributes to geometric throughput and solid-angle calculations together with the aperture position, orientation, and viewing geometry, but it does not by itself determine the full acceptance.

Representative engineering scales are device- and diagnostic-dependent. Small pinholes or tightly collimated openings may have radii of about 0.0001-0.001 m, while many optical, fiber, or detector apertures use millimeter- to centimeter-scale radii of about 0.001-0.01 m; larger values can occur in wide-aperture systems.

NAMES.name: spectral_absorptivity_of_filter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless wavelength-dependent probability that an incident photon is absorbed in a diagnostic filter material rather than transmitted or redirected by other loss channels. It ranges from 0 for no absorption to 1 for complete absorption at the specified wavelength.
NAMES.long:
Spectral absorptivity of a filter is the fraction of incident photons at wavelength $\lambda$ that are absorbed within the filter material. It is dimensionless, bounded by $0 \le A_\lambda \le 1$, and describes the wavelength dependence of filter attenuation rather than a wavelength-integrated response.

For a monochromatic photon population, the absorptivity can be written as a photon balance:

$$
A_\lambda = \frac{N_\mathrm{abs}(\lambda)}{N_\mathrm{inc}(\lambda)} = 1 - T_\lambda - R_\lambda - S_\lambda
$$

where $\lambda$ is wavelength in meters, $N_\mathrm{inc}$ and $N_\mathrm{abs}$ are the incident and absorbed photon counts, $T_\lambda$ is the transmitted photon fraction, $R_\lambda$ is the reflected fraction, and $S_\lambda$ represents other nonabsorbed losses such as scattering out of the accepted beam or escaping fluorescence. For a homogeneous slab of thickness $d$ in meters with linear attenuation coefficient $\mu(\lambda)$ in m$^{-1}$, the unscattered transmitted fraction is often approximated by $T_\lambda \simeq \exp[-\mu(\lambda)d]$; then $A_\lambda \simeq 1-\exp[-\mu(\lambda)d]$ only when reflection, scattering, and escaping secondary radiation are negligible or are intentionally included in the lost-photon category.

Spectral absorptivity is obtained from tabulated or measured optical constants, mass attenuation coefficients, material composition, layer thicknesses, and surface coatings, and may be verified by calibration with known photon spectra. It is defined only over the wavelength interval for which those material properties and calibration data are valid; outside that interval, extrapolated values should be treated as model assumptions rather than measured filter behavior. The corresponding transmission relation is $T_\lambda = 1 - A_\lambda - R_\lambda - S_\lambda$, reducing to $T_\lambda \simeq 1-A_\lambda$ only when the additional nonabsorbed loss channels are negligible.

Typical values span nearly the full range 0-1: thin filters may have absorptivity below 0.01 in their pass band, intermediate attenuation often gives 0.1-0.9, and wavelengths near strong absorption edges or below the filter cutoff can approach 1. Sharp spectral structure can occur near material absorption edges, so neighboring wavelengths may have substantially different absorptivity.

NAMES.name: spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength-resolved ratio of the vacuum speed of light to the phase velocity in a diagnostic optical element material, capturing the spectral dispersion required for chromatic transmission and reflection modeling.
NAMES.long:
The spectral refractive index $n(\lambda)$ of an optical element quantifies how the phase velocity of light is reduced relative to vacuum as a function of wavelength $\lambda$. Its wavelength dependence, known as dispersion, governs chromatic aberration, wavelength-dependent Fresnel reflection coefficients, and the focusing and transmission characteristics of lenses, windows, and filters across a diagnostic spectral range.

The defining relation is:

$$
n(\lambda) = \frac{c}{v_\phi(\lambda)}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum and $v_\phi(\lambda)$ is the phase velocity at wavelength $\lambda$. In practice, $n(\lambda)$ is well described by a Sellmeier dispersion relation, $n^2(\lambda) = 1 + \sum_i B_i \lambda^2 / (\lambda^2 - C_i)$, with empirically determined material coefficients $B_i$ and $C_i$ specific to the optical glass or crystal.

The spectral refractive index is evaluated on the same wavelength axis defined by [spectral_wavelength](name:spectral_wavelength) and is typically sourced from manufacturer material specifications or measured by prism minimum-deviation refractometry or spectroscopic ellipsometry. For infrared optical elements, $n(\lambda)$ is paired with the extinction coefficient to fully characterize the complex optical response governing transmission and reflection. The full dispersion curve constitutes the spectral resolution of the broadband [refractive_index_of_optical_element](name:refractive_index_of_optical_element).

Typical values span $n \approx 1.45$–$1.47$ for fused silica in the UV-visible range, $n \approx 1.5$ for BK7 optical glass, and $n \approx 2.4$ for ZnSe at mid-infrared wavelengths. Compare with [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), which describes the refractive index projected along a wave beam directional axis in plasma wave-propagation contexts.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the phase velocity of light in the material is less than the speed of light in vacuum, as holds for all conventional dielectric and metallic optical elements used in fusion plasma diagnostics.

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Upper wavelength limit of the passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window. It is the long-wavelength, low-photon-energy cutoff of the filter-window transmission band.
NAMES.long:
The upper wavelength of a filter is the long-wavelength boundary of the passband transmitted by a filter window. It is the largest wavelength included by the filter-window transmission criterion and therefore corresponds to the lowest photon energy admitted by that filter passband. Together with [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter), it defines the wavelength interval of the transmitted band, normally with $\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}} \le \lambda_{\max}$.

The corresponding minimum photon energy is related to the cutoff wavelength by

$$
E_{\min} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_{\max}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\max}$ is the upper wavelength cutoff in meters, $E_{\min}$ is the corresponding photon energy in joules, $h$ is Planck's constant in joule seconds, and $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second.

For a real filter window the spectral transmission edge is gradual rather than perfectly sharp, so the upper wavelength should be interpreted using the stated passband criterion, such as a specified transmission threshold or calibrated edge definition. It is obtained from the filter-window transmission curve, computed from material optical properties and thickness or measured by spectral transmission calibration.

Representative X-ray and soft-X-ray filter-window upper cutoffs are commonly in the range $10^{-11}$-$10^{-8}$ m, depending on filter material, thickness, and the selected transmission criterion. The wavelength-dependent attenuation within and outside the passband is described by [spectral_absorptivity_of_filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_bolometer
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the center of a bolometer detector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius, phi is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a bolometer is the $Z$ position of the detector center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The coordinate value is measured in meters relative to the device coordinate origin and locates the detector center above or below the reference midplane.

This coordinate is determined from the diagnostic geometry, typically using mechanical design data, metrology surveys, or alignment calibration. Together with the detector radial coordinate, toroidal angle, aperture position, and viewing direction, it contributes to the geometric definition of a bolometer line of sight or viewing cone, but does not by itself define the full chord geometry.

Typical values are device dependent. Detector centers are commonly near diagnostic ports or the vessel periphery, with $Z$ values of about -2 to 2 m in medium-sized tokamaks and up to roughly -10 to 10 m in large devices.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector center lies in the $+Z$ direction, vertically above the coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Vertical height Z of the center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is an absolute machine-geometry coordinate of the pixel center, not a detector-local row index or the active-height span across pixels.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a detector pixel is the $Z$ coordinate of the geometric center of an individual pixel of a radiation-imaging detector (such as an X-ray camera or crystal spectrometer) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is an absolute machine-geometry coordinate measured from the $Z=0$ reference plane, distinct from any detector-local active-height coordinate, row index, or the full vertical extent of the pixel.

Together with the corresponding radial and toroidal coordinates of the same pixel center, this quantity fixes the spatial location of each sensing element, which in turn defines the viewing geometry used to relate detected radiation to its plasma source region.

Typical absolute values are set by the diagnostic installation height and commonly lie within $-2$ to $2$ m for medium-sized tokamaks, extending to several meters in larger devices. Differences in $Z$ between neighboring pixel centers are much smaller, of order $0.001$ to $0.1$ m, set by pixel pitch and detector orientation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pixel center lies above the $Z=0$ reference plane, displaced in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: x2_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a hard X-ray detector outline vertex along the X2 axis in the detector-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
The X2 coordinate of a hard X-ray detector is the signed position of a detector-outline vertex along the second axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame. Together with the companion x1_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector, it defines the detector outline in the local plane; the value is relative to the detector-local origin and axis orientation, not to an absolute machine position.

For a vertex displacement from the detector-local origin, the coordinate is the scalar projection onto the local X2 direction:

$$
x_2 = \Delta \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the X2 coordinate in meters, $\Delta \mathbf{r}_v$ is the vector from the detector-local origin to the vertex in meters, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the positive X2 axis of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

In practice, X2 vertex coordinates are obtained from the detector mechanical design, survey information, or geometry model. Paired with X1 coordinates, they specify the polygonal detector outline used in geometric area, etendue, and sight-line acceptance calculations. The same local-outline concept is used for related diagnostic aperture and detector coordinates such as [x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:x2_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture) and [x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:x2_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).

Typical magnitudes are set by the physical detector face and the chosen local origin. Compact hard-X-ray detector outlines are often millimeter-to-centimeter scale, with representative coordinate magnitudes around 0.001-0.1 m; exact values are device-specific and may be positive or negative within the local outline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the detector-local origin has a component in the positive X2 direction of the detector-local Cartesian $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_particle_density
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Number density of suprathermal particles in the co-passing orbit class, from the fast-particle distribution function restricted to the co-passing region of velocity space.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast particle density is the number of non-thermal particles per unit physical volume whose guiding-center orbits are passing and belong to the co-passing branch. It is a partial zeroth moment of the fast-particle distribution function, complementary to the counter-passing and trapped fast-particle contributions.

The density at position $\mathbf{x}$ is defined by integrating the fast-particle distribution over the co-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
n_{\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})} f_{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal distribution function with units $\mathrm{s^3\,m^{-6}}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the subset of velocity space corresponding to co-passing orbits. The trapped-passing boundary is set by magnetic geometry and particle invariants such as energy and magnetic moment; in pitch coordinates it should be treated as the local trapped-passing separatrix rather than a universal pitch cutoff.

In practice, this quantity is computed by applying an orbit-classification operator to a kinetic fast-particle distribution and taking the partial zeroth moment over the co-passing domain. The same definition applies whether the distribution is expressed in Cartesian velocity, energy-pitch, or guiding-center variables, provided the appropriate velocity-space Jacobian is included. When the orbit classes form a complete disjoint partition, the total fast-particle density is the sum of the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped contributions.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent because fast-particle populations are set by sources, slowing-down, redistribution, and loss processes. Representative values can range from below $10^{14}$ m$^{-3}$ in weak suprathermal populations to $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in strongly heated or fusion-product-rich plasmas, usually remaining below the bulk thermal particle density.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_particle_source_rate
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric source rate of thermal particle density for the co-passing orbit population. It represents the net rate at which particles are added to or removed from that orbit class.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing thermal particle source rate is the rate per unit volume at which thermal particles enter or leave the co-passing passing-orbit population after averaging over a magnetic flux surface. Co-passing denotes the passing orbit class whose guiding-center motion is aligned with the reference plasma-current direction, complementary to counter-passing and trapped orbit classes.

It is the source term in the flux-surface-averaged particle balance for the co-passing population:

$$
\frac{\partial \langle n_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho}{\partial t}
+ \frac{1}{V'}\frac{\partial}{\partial \rho}\left(V'\left\langle \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{cp}}\cdot\nabla\rho\right\rangle_\rho\right)
= \langle S_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle_\rho$ denotes an average over the magnetic flux surface labeled by the dimensionless radial flux coordinate $\rho$, $V'=dV/d\rho$ is the differential volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, $n_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the co-passing thermal-particle density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the particle flux density in $\mathrm{m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the volumetric source rate in $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$.

In practice this quantity is obtained from kinetic or transport modeling by integrating the modeled collisional, wave-particle, and orbit-class transition terms over the co-passing part of velocity space and over the flux surface. It may also be inferred as the residual source required by a particle balance when the co-passing density evolution and radial particle flux are known.

No device-independent typical magnitude follows from the definition alone, because the value depends on species, radial location, distribution function, wave fields, collision rates, and the chosen separation between passing and trapped orbit classes. A useful scale is the particle replacement time $\tau_{\mathrm{cp}}=\langle n_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho/|\langle S_{\mathrm{cp}}\rangle_\rho|$; for example, $10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ changes a $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ co-passing population on a 0.1 s time scale.
NAMES.sign: Positive when local processes add thermal particles to the co-passing orbit population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Local collisional power density for the counter-passing part of a fast-particle distribution. It is the rate at which Coulomb collisions with the included charged collision partners change the kinetic-energy density of counter-passing fast particles.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-particle collisional power density is the local rate at which Coulomb collisions change the kinetic-energy density of fast particles in the counter-passing orbit class. The counter-passing class contains passing guiding-center trajectories whose parallel transit is opposite to the reference co-passing direction, and this quantity is a collisional source or sink for that class rather than its stored energy.

For fast species $a$, it is commonly evaluated as the second velocity moment of the Coulomb collision operator restricted to counter-passing phase space:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{fast}} \sum_b \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2 C_{ab}[f_a,f_b](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units $W m^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in meters, $m_a$ is the fast-particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in $m s^{-1}$, $f_a$ has units $m^{-3}(m s^{-1})^{-3}$, and $C_{ab}$ has units $m^{-3}(m s^{-1})^{-3}s^{-1}$ and gives the time derivative of $f_a$ due to Coulomb collisions with partner species $b$. The index $b$ denotes the charged collision partners included in the kinetic model, typically thermal electrons, main ions, impurity ions, and other fast species only when fast-fast collisions are explicitly retained; for a partner-resolved quantity the corresponding single $b$ term is used instead of the full sum. The use of $C_{ab}$, not $f_a$, makes this an energy-transfer rate and not the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing particles.
