This quantity is not measured directly. It is inferred by applying a Fokker-Planck or guiding-center collision operator to a fast-particle distribution constrained by diagnostics and by the local background plasma density, temperature, composition, and magnetic equilibrium.

Typical magnitudes range from 10^2-10^5 W m^-3 for weak fast-particle tails or outer-plasma regions to 10^5-10^7 W m^-3 in core regions with strong neutral-beam, radio-frequency, or alpha-particle populations. Values can be close to zero where the counter-passing population is small or nearly collisionally equilibrated.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic-energy density of the counter-passing fast-particle population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_power_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged volumetric energy source rate for the counter-passing orbit population. It is the local power density transferred to or from that population by wave-particle interactions, collisions, or particle sources.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing power density is the flux-surface-averaged rate at which kinetic energy is added to the counter-passing orbit population per unit physical volume. Counter-passing refers to the passing part of velocity space whose guiding-center motion is opposite to the co-passing direction; it excludes trapped orbits.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the net source operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain, followed by a flux-surface average:

$$
S_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\varepsilon}(\rho,t) = \left\langle \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v^2\, \mathcal{S}_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v \right\rangle_{\rho}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{cp}}^{\varepsilon}$ has units W m$^{-3}$, $\rho$ is a radial flux-surface label in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing velocity-space domain, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $d^3v$ has units m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The operator $\mathcal{S}_s$ is the net time rate of change of the distribution function from sources, collisions, and wave interactions; if $\int f_s d^3v$ is a number density in m$^{-3}$, then $\mathcal{S}_s$ has units s$^2$ m$^{-6}$. The notation $\langle A\rangle_{\rho}$ denotes the flux-surface average at fixed $\rho$, equivalently the surface integral of $A$ weighted by $1/|\nabla\rho|$ divided by the corresponding weighted surface area.

In practice this quantity is computed from kinetic or Fokker-Planck models by taking the velocity-space energy moment of the relevant collision, external source, and wave-particle operators over the counter-passing domain. It is constrained indirectly by deposited heating, fast-particle measurements, loss measurements, and power-balance analysis. Together with [co_passing_power_density](name:co_passing_power_density) and [trapped_power_density](name:trapped_power_density), it partitions the orbit-integrated [power_density](name:power_density).

Typical magnitudes are 10$^3$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with localized radio-frequency or neutral-beam deposition reaching about 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$. Weakly driven regions can be near zero, and collisional drag or loss terms can give negative values with comparable magnitudes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counter-passing orbit population gains kinetic energy from the net source operator.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: On-axis electron number density at the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
The electron density at the magnetic axis is the local free-electron number density per unit volume evaluated at the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame — where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height — at which $\nabla\psi = 0$, identifying the center of the nested flux-surface family. As the on-axis value of the electron density radial profile, it represents the profile peak in centrally-heated plasmas and serves as the normalization reference for the density peaking factor.

The on-axis electron density $n_{e,0}$ is linked to companion on-axis ion densities through the quasineutrality condition:

$$
n_{e,0} = \sum_i Z_i \, n_{i,0}
$$

where $Z_i$ is the charge number and $n_{i,0}$ is the on-axis number density of ion species $i$. This connects $n_{e,0}$ to quantities such as [total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), [hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:hydrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis), and impurity species like [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis).

The on-axis value is measured by Thomson scattering, which provides spatially localized electron density and temperature simultaneously, or inferred from line-integrated interferometry combined with profile inversion. Typical on-axis values in current medium-sized tokamaks range from $2 \times 10^{19}$ to $1 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, approaching the Greenwald limit at high plasma current. It also enters collisionality estimates as $\nu_* \propto n_{e,0} / T_{e,0}^2$, where $T_{e,0}$ is the on-axis electron temperature. See [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) for the species-agnostic parent definition.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Coulomb-collisional power density received by the fast electron population. It is the volumetric rate of kinetic-energy exchange between suprathermal electrons and other plasma species.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron collisional power density is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the suprathermal electron population. It represents the fast-electron channel of electron collisional energy exchange; together with the thermal-electron channel it forms the total electron collisional power density.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Fokker-Planck collision operator for the fast-electron distribution:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{fast}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_s \int \frac{1}{2} m_e v^2\, C_{es}[f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}, f_s](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where the sum is over collision partners $s$, $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}\,d^3v$ gives the fast-electron density, $f_s$ is the distribution of species $s$, $m_e$ is the electron mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is speed in m/s, and $C_{es}$ has units of $f_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ per second. With these definitions the integral has units of W m^-3. For relativistic fast electrons, the kinetic-energy weight is replaced by the appropriate relativistic kinetic energy.

In practice this quantity is computed by applying a Coulomb collision operator to a modeled or reconstructed fast-electron distribution and integrating over velocity space. If the fast population is partitioned by orbit class, the co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped components sum to this quantity when the same collision model and phase-space partition are used.

Typical local absolute magnitudes are scenario dependent: about 10^2-10^5 W m^-3 for weak suprathermal tails, 10^5-10^7 W m^-3 in strongly driven electron-heating or current-drive cases, and up to 10^8 W m^-3 or more in localized runaway-electron regimes. During ordinary slowing down, the value is often negative because fast electrons transfer energy to the thermal plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast electron population.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Density source rate of fast electrons due to the Dreicer generation mechanism, in which a parallel electric field accelerates high-energy tail electrons faster than Coulomb collisions slow them. It refers to the fast-electron population; the analogous runaway-electron term uses runaway-electron nomenclature.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation is the local volumetric production rate of fast electrons created when the parallel electric field accelerates suprathermal tail electrons through collisional drag. It is a contribution to the total [fast_electron_source_rate](name:fast_electron_source_rate) and describes the same primary electric-field generation channel as [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer), with the population labeled as fast electrons rather than specifically runaway electrons. It is distinct from avalanche multiplication and from hot-tail generation.

The model-independent definition is the Dreicer contribution to the fast-electron density balance:

$$
S_\mathrm{D} = \left.\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t}\right|_\mathrm{Dreicer}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{D}$ is the fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation in $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$, $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron number density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $t$ is time in $\mathrm{s}$, and the subscript denotes the part of the density time derivative caused by the Dreicer mechanism alone.

The rate is usually inferred from analytic runaway-source formulas or kinetic Fokker-Planck modeling rather than measured as an isolated observable. Inputs typically include electron density $n_e$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, electron temperature $T_e$ in eV or J, effective charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ with unit 1, Coulomb logarithm $\ln\Lambda$ with unit 1, and the parallel electric field $E_\parallel$ in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The dependence is very sensitive to $E_\parallel/E_D$, where $E_D$ is the [electric_field_due_to_dreicer](name:electric_field_due_to_dreicer), while [critical_electric_field](name:critical_electric_field) sets the lower electric-field scale for sustained runaway acceleration.

The quantity denotes a local scalar rate density. If used in a radial transport reduction with the flux coordinate $\rho_\mathrm{tor,norm}$, the corresponding value is the flux-surface average of the local $S_\mathrm{D}$ over that magnetic surface and retains the unit $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$. No component of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system is selected by the scalar rate itself; only $E_\parallel$ in the generation model refers to the local magnetic-field direction.

Typical modeled values range from effectively 0 in weak-electric-field conditions to $10^{17}$-$10^{22}$ $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ in strong-electric-field transients, with intermediate seed-production values spanning many orders of magnitude. Because Dreicer generation depends steeply on plasma temperature, density, collisionality, and electric field, quoted ranges are scenario and model dependent.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Dreicer generation increases the fast-electron number density.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from background ions to the total fast ion population. It is summed over all fast ion species and charge states represented in that population.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion power due to collisions is the net rate at which Coulomb collisions with background ions change the kinetic energy of the total fast-ion population. The total includes all represented fast-ion species and charge states, so state-resolved contributions add to this population-integrated quantity.

A kinetic definition is the energy moment of the fast-ion collision operator associated with background ions:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fi}\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_{a\in\mathrm{FI}} \int_V \int \frac{1}{2} m_a v^2\, C_{a\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_a,\{f_i\}]\, d^3v\, dV
$$

where $a$ labels fast-ion species or charge states, $m_a$ is the particle mass, $v$ is particle speed, $f_a$ is the fast-ion distribution, $\{f_i\}$ denotes the background-ion distributions, $C_{a\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the part of the collision operator that changes $f_a$ through collisions with background ions, and $V$ is the plasma volume.

In practice this quantity is computed by taking the collisional energy moment of a kinetic fast-ion distribution and integrating over velocity space and plasma volume. Equivalently, it is the volume integral of the corresponding fast-ion collisional power density. For the same interacting populations and volume, energy conservation gives the reciprocal balance $P_{\mathrm{fi}\leftarrow i}^{\mathrm{coll}} + P_{i\leftarrow\mathrm{fi}}^{\mathrm{coll}} \simeq 0$, where the second term is the matching contribution to thermal-ion power due to collisions, apart from numerical error or additional species partitions.

Typical magnitudes range from 10^3-10^7 W in present-day auxiliary-heated experiments and can reach 10^7-10^8 W in reactor-scale plasmas. The signed value is often negative when energetic ions slow down on cooler background ions, because energy is then transferred from fast ions to the thermal-ion population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the background ion population to the fast-ion population.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Coulomb collisional power density for fast ions in a specified charge state, giving the local energy exchange rate per volume between that fast-ion population and the background plasma. It is positive when collisions add kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion state and negative when they remove it.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state collisional power density is the local kinetic-energy exchange rate per unit volume between fast ions in a specified charge state and the surrounding plasma due to Coulomb collisions. It is a signed scalar source term in the fast-ion energy balance, resolved by charge state rather than summed over all charge states.

The quantity is defined as the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator acting on the fast-ion distribution for charge state $q$:

$$
p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \frac{1}{2} m_q v^2\, C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}[f_{\mathrm{fast},q}, f_{\mathrm{bg}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{fast},q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ has units of W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ in m s$^{-1}$, $m_q$ is the ion mass in kg, $f_{\mathrm{fast},q}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution for charge state $q$, $f_{\mathrm{bg}}$ represents the background electron and ion distributions, and $C_q^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the Coulomb Fokker-Planck collision operator with units of distribution function per second. For fast-ion slowing-down calculations this operator is commonly treated as a linearized test-particle operator with drag and diffusion coefficients expressible through Rosenbluth potentials.

In practice this term is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by measurements of the fast-ion population and by background density, temperature, and composition, which determine the Coulomb collision frequencies. Volume integration gives [fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_due_to_collisions), summing over charge states gives [fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions), and orbit-topology partitions give [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), [counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and [trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:trapped_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10$^{3}$-10$^{7}$ W m$^{-3}$ in beam-heated, radio-frequency-heated, or fusion-alpha-heated tokamak plasmas. Values can be much smaller in weak-source or edge regions and larger locally in compact, high-power deposition regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the selected fast-ion charge-state population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional kinetic-energy transfer rate for a specified fast-ion charge state, restricted to counter-passing particles. Positive values mean that charge state gains kinetic energy from collisions; negative values mean it loses kinetic energy.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast ion state power density due to collisions is the local collisional source term in the kinetic-energy balance of a specified fast-ion charge state, evaluated only over the counter-passing part of velocity space. Counter-passing fast ions have guiding-center parallel motion whose toroidal circulation is opposite to the plasma-current direction. The charge-state label denotes one resolved ionization state of the fast-ion species.

The quantity is the kinetic-energy moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the counter-passing velocity-space domain:

$$
P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}} \mathcal{E}_z(\mathbf{v})\, C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}](\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing collisional power density for charge state $z$, $\Omega_{\mathrm{counter}}$ is the counter-passing region of velocity space, $\mathcal{E}_z$ is the particle kinetic energy in joules, and $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ is the collisional part of the time derivative of the local fast-ion distribution function for that charge state. If $f_{\mathrm{fast},z}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{\mathrm{fast},z}\,d^3v$ is the number density, then $C_z[f_{\mathrm{fast},z}]$ has units of number density per time per velocity-space volume, and $d^3v$ has units $(\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^3$, giving $P_{\mathrm{fast},z}^{\mathrm{counter}}$ in W m$^{-3}$.

In practice this quantity is computed from a kinetic fast-ion distribution and a Coulomb collision operator, often constrained by measurements such as neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, fast-ion loss signals, charge-exchange spectroscopy, or gamma-ray diagnostics. Orbit classification partitions the distribution into trapped, co-passing, and counter-passing domains; summing the orbit components gives [fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), while summing over charge states gives [counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). The complementary counter-current decomposition is [co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:co_passing_fast_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), and a thermal-ion analog is [counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:counter_passing_thermal_ion_state_power_density_due_to_collisions).

Typical magnitudes are highly regime dependent: orbit- and charge-state-resolved values can be below 1 W m$^{-3}$ in weakly populated regions, 10$^2$-10$^6$ W m$^{-3}$ in auxiliary-heated core plasmas, and locally approach 10$^7$ W m$^{-3}$ in strongly driven fast-ion populations. Negative values occur where collisions remove kinetic energy from the specified fast-ion charge state and transfer it to other species or charge states.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions increase the kinetic energy density of the specified fast-ion charge state.

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_density
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Suprathermal (non-Maxwellian) neutral particle number density at a point in the plasma, summed over all internal quantum states of the neutral species. It represents the neutral population not described by the local thermal neutral distribution.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral density is the number of neutral atoms or molecules per unit volume belonging to a suprathermal, non-Maxwellian population of a specified neutral species. It excludes the locally thermalized neutral component and is summed over internal quantum states such as excitation levels when those states are not resolved.

At a spatial point $\mathbf{x}$, it is the zeroth velocity moment of the fast component of the neutral distribution function:

$$
n_\mathrm{fast}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_\alpha \int f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\alpha$ labels internal quantum states, $f_{\alpha,\mathrm{fast}}$ has units of m$^{-6}$ s$^{3}$ when velocity is in m s$^{-1}$, and the integral is over the velocity distribution assigned to the suprathermal component. The fast component is not defined by a universal sharp cutoff at the local thermal speed; it is the non-Maxwellian part separated from the locally thermal neutral distribution by the physics model or diagnostic interpretation.

In practice, fast neutral density is inferred or computed from neutral transport, beam attenuation, recycling, and charge-exchange source models, often constrained by spectroscopic emission or charge-exchange measurements. The operational separation from [thermal_neutral_density](name:thermal_neutral_density) is based on whether the neutral population is locally equilibrated with the background gas or plasma-neutral environment; beam neutrals, halo neutrals, and energetic charge-exchange neutrals are typical contributors to the fast component.

Typical values vary strongly with fueling, beam power, wall recycling, and plasma opacity. Hot confined plasmas may have local fast neutral densities around $10^{12}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, while intense neutral-beam paths, edge, or scrape-off-layer charge-exchange regions can reach about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$; the value is generally less than or comparable to the [total_neutral_density](name:total_neutral_density).

NAMES.name: fast_neutral_state_density
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Number density of fast (non-thermal) neutral particles occupying a specified internal quantum state of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutral state density is the number of neutral particles per unit volume in a specified internal quantum state that belong to the fast, non-thermal part of the neutral population. It distinguishes energetic neutrals, such as charge-exchange atoms, beam neutrals, or wall-reflected neutrals, from the bulk thermal neutral gas while retaining the state identity needed for excitation, ionization, and radiation modeling.

A common kinetic definition is the velocity-space integral of the state-resolved neutral distribution above a chosen fast-particle energy threshold:

$$
n_i^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{E(\mathbf{v}) \ge E_{\mathrm{th}}} f_i(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3 v
$$

where $n_i^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast density of internal state $i$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $f_i$ is the state-resolved neutral velocity distribution in units s$^3$ m$^{-6}$ when integrated over velocity, $E(\mathbf{v})$ is kinetic energy in J, and $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the fast-particle threshold energy in J. In applications that use eV for neutral kinetic energy, $E$ and $E_{\mathrm{th}}$ must be converted consistently.

In practice this quantity is computed with kinetic neutral transport or collisional-radiative models, often constrained by diagnostics sensitive to energetic neutrals such as neutral particle analyzers, charge-exchange measurements, or line emission from state-selective transitions. The separation between thermal and fast neutrals depends on the modeled distribution and on the selected energy threshold or non-thermal component definition.

Typical values span a wide range: about $10^{10}$-$10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$ in hot confined plasma regions, and about $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in edge, scrape-off-layer, divertor, or source-adjacent regions where recycling, neutral beams, or wall reflection can create stronger fast-neutral populations.

NAMES.name: fast_particle_energy
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Total kinetic energy of the fast (suprathermal) particle population integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Fast particle energy quantifies the global energetic inventory stored in particles with velocities substantially exceeding the bulk thermal speed. These suprathermal particles arise from external heating systems including neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, and electron cyclotron heating, as well as from fusion-born alpha particles.

The quantity is defined as the volume integral of the kinetic energy density over the non-thermal distribution:

$$
W_\text{fast} = \int \int \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \, f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v \, d^3r
$$

where $f_\text{fast}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v})$ is the fast-particle distribution function in phase space, $m$ is the particle mass, and $v$ is the particle speed. This total decomposes additively into [parallel_fast_particle_energy](name:parallel_fast_particle_energy) and [perpendicular_fast_particle_energy](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_energy) relative to the local magnetic field direction.

Estimated through integrated fast-ion diagnostics such as fast-ion loss detectors, neutron emission spectroscopy, or neutral particle analyzers, often combined with global energy balance comparisons. Orbit-following Monte Carlo transport codes evaluate this integral numerically from the modeled fast-particle distribution function.

Typical values range from 0.1–5 MJ in medium-scale tokamaks during high-power NBI or ICRH operation, reaching 10–50 MJ in larger devices. The accumulated fast particle energy constitutes a significant fraction of [total_particle_energy](name:total_particle_energy) in high-power heating scenarios, and is bounded by slowing-down and thermalization rates, with the corresponding particle count tracked by [fast_count](name:fast_count).

NAMES.name: fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb collisional power transferred from the fast (non-Maxwellian) particle population to the bulk electron population.
NAMES.long:
Fast particles — such as neutral-beam-injected ions, minority ions accelerated by RF heating, or fusion-born alpha particles — carry a non-Maxwellian velocity distribution well above the thermal speed of the bulk plasma. As they slow down via Coulomb collisions, energy is deposited into both bulk electrons and ions; this quantity captures the total power delivered to the electron channel alone, integrated over the plasma volume.

The governing relation connects this quantity to its local density analog [fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions):

$$
P_{f \to e} = \int_V S_{f \to e}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $S_{f \to e}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electron-channel collisional power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, and $V$ is the plasma volume. The fraction of fast-particle energy deposited into electrons versus ions is governed by the ratio of the fast particle speed to the critical slowing-down velocity $v_c$; above $v_c$, electron drag dominates.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic calculations — Monte Carlo orbit-following or Fokker-Planck solvers — that evolve the fast particle distribution function and compute the Coulomb collision operator. In large tokamaks with multi-megawatt injection, the electron channel receives several to tens of megawatts; for fusion-born alpha particles in burning plasmas the contribution scales with the fusion power.

The power received by the thermal electron population from this exchange equals [thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions), and the corresponding ion-channel quantity is [thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions](name:thermal_ion_power_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy flows from the fast particle population to the electron population via Coulomb collisions.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Source density of total-ion toroidal angular momentum produced by diamagnetic-drift transport, summed over all ion species and charge states. It is the signed contribution of ion pressure-gradient drift fluxes to the ion momentum balance.
NAMES.long:
Total-ion diamagnetic-drift momentum source density is the local rate per unit volume at which pressure-gradient-driven ion drift transport changes [toroidal_ion_momentum](name:toroidal_ion_momentum). It is an internal transport contribution, not an externally applied torque, and the sum includes all ion species and charge states. The toroidal component is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Written as a conservative transport contribution, the source density is the negative divergence of the diamagnetic flux of ion toroidal angular momentum:

$$
S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \sum_{a\in\mathrm{ions}} \left(m_a n_a R v_{\phi,a}\right)\mathbf{v}_{D,a}
$$

where $S_{\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is in kg.m^-1.s^-2, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{L_\phi,\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the [ion diamagnetic momentum flux](name:ion_momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) in kg.s^-2, $\nabla\cdot$ is the spatial divergence operator with components in m^-1, and $a$ indexes ion species and charge states. Here $m_a$ is ion mass in kg, $n_a$ is ion number density in m^-3, $R$ is major radius in meters in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $v_{\phi,a}$ is toroidal fluid velocity in m.s^-1, and $\mathbf{v}_{D,a}$ is diamagnetic drift velocity in m.s^-1 generated by the perpendicular ion pressure gradient.

In practice the term is computed by combining equilibrium geometry, ion pressure-gradient estimates, species composition, and toroidal-flow information to construct the charge-state-resolved diamagnetic momentum fluxes and then taking their divergence. It is usually inferred from momentum-balance and transport analyzes rather than measured directly; charge-state-resolved contributions correspond to [ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and the total plasma contribution is [momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). The related neutral contribution, when included in the same source decomposition, is [neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:neutral_momentum_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

Typical absolute magnitudes are order $10^{-4}$-$10^1$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 in weak-gradient core regions and $10^1$-$10^4$ kg.m^-1.s^-2 locally in pedestal, edge, or scrape-off-layer regions with short pressure-gradient scale lengths. The value can change sign with the direction of toroidal flow, pressure-gradient orientation, magnetic geometry, and spatial convergence or divergence of the diamagnetic momentum flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when convergence of the ion diamagnetic-drift momentum flux increases total-ion toroidal angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: ion_state_diamagnetic_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic velocity of a specified ion charge state, arising from the perpendicular gradient of that state's partial pressure. It is the signed scalar component of the diamagnetic drift along the local diamagnetic direction defined by the cross product of the magnetic field unit vector with the partial-pressure gradient, resolving individual charge states rather than the aggregate ion fluid.
NAMES.long:
The ion-state diamagnetic velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the charge-state-resolved drift speed produced when the partial pressure of a single ionization stage varies across the magnetic field. It is local to the plasma position and isolates one charge state of an impurity or main-ion species from the combined ion fluid.

The scalar reported here is the signed component of the diamagnetic drift velocity along the local diamagnetic direction $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}} = (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \nabla_\perp p_s)/|\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \nabla_\perp p_s|$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/B$:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia},s} = \frac{|\nabla_\perp p_s|}{Z_s e\, n_s\, B}
$$

where $p_s$ is the partial pressure of ion charge state $s$ (Pa), $n_s$ is its number density (m^-3), $Z_s$ is its charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge (C), $\nabla_\perp p_s$ is the component of the partial-pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude (T). Only the perpendicular pressure-gradient component contributes; pressure variation along the field produces no diamagnetic drift.

This quantity is obtained from charge-state-resolved density and temperature gradients together with the local magnetic field from an equilibrium or field model. If $p_s = n_s T_s$ is used, $T_s$ must be expressed as energy per particle. Coordinate components such as the radial, toroidal, or parallel diamagnetic velocities are obtained by projecting the same drift vector onto explicitly defined directions.

Representative speeds for low-charge ions in tokamak fields of a few tesla are $10^2$-$10^4$ m.s^-1 in the core and rise to $10^4$-$10^5$ m.s^-1 across steep pedestal or scrape-off-layer pressure gradients. The magnitude scales approximately as $T_s/(Z_s B L_p)$, where $L_p = p_s/|\nabla_\perp p_s|$ is the perpendicular pressure-gradient length.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift is directed along $\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \nabla_\perp p_s$ for the positive ion charge $q_s = Z_s e$.

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity at which a specific ion charge state convects its thermal energy radially across flux surfaces in the charge-state-resolved energy transport equation.
NAMES.long:
In flux-surface-averaged radial transport models, the total radial energy flux of an ion charge state is decomposed into diffusive and convective contributions. The ion state energy convection velocity $v_E$ is the effective velocity parameterizing the convective part for a given charge state, providing finer charge-state resolution than the species-averaged ion_energy_convection_velocity.

The convective energy flux contribution $q_{\mathrm{conv}}$ for the charge state is:

$$
q_{\mathrm{conv}} = \frac{3}{2} n_s T_s v_E
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of the charge state in m$^{-3}$ and $T_s$ is its temperature in J.

This quantity is computed by transport codes that resolve the charge state distribution and is not directly measurable; it is inferred from energy balance analysis or prescribed within transport models. The particle-convection analog for the same charge state is ion_state_convection_velocity, and the analogous quantity for neutral states is [neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity](name:neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity). The charge-state-summed counterpart is [total_ion_energy_convection_velocity](name:total_ion_energy_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convective energy flux is directed outward, away from the magnetic axis in the direction of increasing normalized poloidal flux.

NAMES.name: ion_state_upper_bound_charge
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Maximum ionization charge number (Z_max) of an ion charge-state bundle; equals the lower-bound charge when the bundle contains only a single resolved charge state.
NAMES.long:
The upper-bound charge number specifies the highest ionization state included in an ion charge-state bundle, where the ionization charge $Z$ counts the number of electrons removed from the neutral atom. In multi-fluid plasma models, consecutive ionization states of the same ion species are often grouped into bundles to reduce computational expense; this quantity gives the ceiling $Z_\mathrm{max}$ of the charge range $[Z_\mathrm{min}, Z_\mathrm{max}]$ spanned by the bundle.

When a bundle encloses only a single charge state, $Z_\mathrm{max}$ equals the corresponding [lower-bound charge]. For multi-state bundles the interval width $Z_\mathrm{max} - Z_\mathrm{min} \geq 1$, and the [concentration-weighted average charge] or [mean charge] provides a representative effective charge for transport and source-term calculations.

Charge-state values are non-negative integers bounded above by the nuclear charge number $Z_n$ of the species: for hydrogen $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 1$, for carbon $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 6$, and for heavy impurities such as tungsten $Z_\mathrm{max} \leq 74$. The bundle definition is set at model initialization and does not vary with plasma conditions at a given time step.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion carries net positive charge, corresponding to the removal of one or more electrons from the neutral atom.

NAMES.name: loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Toroidal electromotive force integrated around the last closed flux surface, measuring the net inductive and resistive voltage driving ohmic plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The loop voltage at the plasma boundary is the line integral of the total electric field around a toroidal contour lying on the last closed flux surface (LCFS), equal to the time rate of change of the total poloidal magnetic flux threading that boundary.

The defining relation is:

$$
V_{loop} = -\frac{d\Psi_b}{dt}
$$

where $\Psi_b$ is the total poloidal magnetic flux enclosed by the LCFS. In a resistive plasma at quasi-steady state this balances as $V_{loop} \approx R_p I_p$, where $R_p$ is the total parallel plasma resistance and $I_p$ is the plasma current; during ramp phases the inductive term $L_p dI_p/dt$ adds significantly. This quantity therefore characterizes both ohmic flux consumption and the resistive state of the plasma column.

It is inferred from voltage loops or flux loops positioned outside the plasma, after subtracting time derivatives of external coil fluxes. The externally driven component alone is captured by [external_loop_voltage](name:current_weighted_average_external_loop_voltage), and the [toroidal_electric_field](name:toroidal_electric_field) profile provides the radially resolved field from which boundary values are extracted.

Typical magnitudes are 0.1–5 V during the current flat-top in medium-to-large tokamaks, rising to 10–20 V during rapid current ramp-up.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electromotive force drives plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius, evaluated at the internal transport barrier location.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic shear at the internal transport barrier is the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor $q$ with respect to the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{tor}$, evaluated at the radial position of the internal transport barrier. The sign and magnitude of this quantity govern the stability of microinstabilities at the barrier, with reversed (negative) shear strongly associated with ITB formation in advanced tokamak scenarios.

The defining relation is:

$$
s = \frac{\rho_{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_{tor}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor — the number of toroidal field-line transits per single poloidal circuit — and $\rho_{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius, equal to zero at the magnetic axis and unity at the last closed flux surface.

The safety-factor profile needed to evaluate this quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction, often constrained by motional Stark effect polarimetry or Faraday rotation measurements resolving the internal $q$-profile. The full radial context is provided by the [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal) profile; analogous point evaluations are defined at [the magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) and [the pedestal top](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal).

In reversed-shear configurations the value is negative near the $q$-minimum, commonly ranging from $-2$ to $0$; in conventional positive-shear ITB scenarios values are small and positive, in the range $0$ to $1$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the safety factor $q$ increases with the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{tor}$, i.e., when $dq/d\rho_{tor} > 0$.

NAMES.name: neutral_source_rate
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Net volumetric production rate of neutral particles, equal to creation minus loss processes per unit volume. It enters the neutral particle density balance as a source term, with positive values representing a net gain of neutral particles.
NAMES.long:
Neutral source rate is the local net rate at which neutral particles of a given species are produced or removed by atomic, molecular, and plasma interaction processes. It represents creation minus loss per unit physical volume and directly changes the neutral number density.

A common local neutral continuity equation is

$$
\frac{\partial n_n}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left(n_n \mathbf{u}_n\right) = S_n
$$

where $n_n$ is the neutral number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\mathbf{u}_n$ is the neutral flow velocity in $\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $S_n$ is the neutral source rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The equation is coordinate independent; when expressed in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $S_n$ is the net rate per physical volume at position $(R, \phi, Z)$.

In practice, $S_n$ is computed from neutral transport and collisional-radiative models using rates for ionization, recombination, charge exchange, molecular dissociation, recycling, gas fueling, pellet ablation, and neutral beam deposition when relevant. It can also be constrained indirectly by particle balance, spectroscopy, pressure gages, and neutral particle diagnostics, with volume or flux-surface averaging applied only after the local volumetric rate has been defined.

Typical magnitudes vary strongly with plasma region and fueling conditions: core values with weak neutral penetration may be $10^{16}$-$10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, edge and scrape-off-layer recycling regions are commonly $10^{20}$-$10^{23}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and highly localized pellet, gas-puff, or beam-related sources can locally exceed $10^{24}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net processes add neutral particles to the neutral population, increasing the neutral number density.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial coordinate derived from the square root of the normalized poloidal magnetic flux, mapping the magnetic axis to 0 and the last closed flux surface to 1.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is a dimensionless radial label for nested flux surfaces derived from the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, providing a monotonic coordinate that equals zero at the magnetic axis and one at the last closed flux surface.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux on the flux surface of interest, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its value at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is its value at the last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction, which solves for the poloidal flux distribution $\psi(R, Z)$ over the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame using magnetic diagnostic measurements. For point measurements, $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ is assigned the local value at the measurement position; for line-integrated diagnostics, it is taken as the minimum value reached along the line of sight within the closed flux surface region.

Typical pedestal locations in H-mode plasmas fall near $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = 0.90$–$0.98$. In nearly circular, low-$\beta$ plasmas, $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ closely approximates the normalized minor radius $r/a$ (where $r$ is the local minor radius and $a$ is the separatrix minor radius); in strongly shaped or high-$\beta$ configurations, significant deviations arise. The closely related [normalized toroidal flux coordinate] uses the enclosed toroidal flux and is often preferred for transport calculations requiring a well-behaved Jacobian.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the evaluation point lies on a flux surface between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface; the coordinate is non-negative by construction and equals zero only at the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Field-aligned component of the electric current density driven by frictional momentum exchange between plasma ions and background neutral particles in partially ionized edge and divertor plasmas.
NAMES.long:
In partially ionized plasmas — found in the edge, scrape-off layer, and divertor regions of a tokamak — collisions between plasma ions and coexisting neutral atoms transfer momentum between the two fluids, producing an ion-neutral friction force $\mathbf{R}_{in} = m_i n_i \nu_{in}(\mathbf{v}_n - \mathbf{v}_i)$, where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, $\nu_{in}$ is the ion-neutral collision frequency, and $\mathbf{v}_i$, $\mathbf{v}_n$ are the ion and neutral fluid velocities respectively. This friction force drives an electric current whose full vector form is given by [current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction); the present quantity is the projection of that vector onto the local magnetic field direction.

The parallel component is defined as:

$$
j_{\parallel,\text{in}} = \mathbf{j}_{\text{in}} \cdot \hat{b}
$$

where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field and $\mathbf{j}_{\text{in}}$ is the full ion-neutral friction current density vector.

This component enters the parallel momentum balance and the generalized Ohm's law for partially ionized plasmas, and is most significant in regions of high neutral density such as the divertor target and scrape-off layer. It is computed from fluid or kinetic simulations of edge plasmas that resolve neutral transport. The complete set of geometric projections includes [radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), [poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), and [vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion-neutral friction current flows in the direction of the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_particle_energy
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Total parallel kinetic energy of fast (suprathermal) particles, integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Parallel fast-particle energy is the part of the kinetic energy of the suprathermal particle population associated with motion along the local magnetic field. It is the field-aligned counterpart of perpendicular fast-particle energy and excludes the perpendicular gyromotion contribution.

For a distribution-function definition, the parallel contribution is obtained from the field-aligned velocity moment of the fast-particle distribution:

$$
W_{\parallel,f} = \sum_s \int_V \int \frac{1}{2} m_s v_\parallel^2 f_{f,s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\, d^3v\, dV
$$

where $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass, $v_\parallel$ is the velocity component along the local magnetic field, $f_{f,s}$ is the fast-particle distribution function, and $dV$ is a physical volume element in m^3. If the same moment is represented by a parallel pressure $p_{\parallel,f}$, then $p_{\parallel,f}$ has units Pa = J m^-3 and the one-degree-of-freedom contribution is $W_{\parallel,f}=\frac{1}{2}\int_V p_{\parallel,f}\,dV$.

In practice this quantity is computed from fast-particle distribution functions, kinetic transport calculations, or pressure-moment reconstructions constrained by heating, slowing-down, and loss physics. It is sensitive to pitch-angle anisotropy: particles born or accelerated mainly along the magnetic field increase the parallel share, while strongly trapped or perpendicular populations shift energy toward the perpendicular contribution.

Representative values are highly device and scenario dependent, spanning roughly 10^3-10^7 J in many auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas and reaching 10^7-10^8 J in large high-power or burning-plasma scenarios. The fraction of total fast-particle energy in the parallel degree of freedom depends on source geometry, collisional pitch-angle scattering, and confinement losses.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Particle flux density of ions in a specified charge state projected onto the local magnetic-field direction. It is the signed rate at which that charge-state population streams along the field per unit area.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion charge-state particle flux is the signed particle flux density of ions in one ionization stage resolved along the local magnetic field direction. It describes field-aligned streaming of that charge-state population and is a charge-state-resolved contribution to [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux).

For charge state $z$, the common fluid definition is:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,z} = n_z v_{\parallel,z}
$$

where $n_z$ is the number density of ions in charge state $z$ in $m^{-3}$, and $v_{\parallel,z}$ is their mean velocity component along $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ in $m\,s^{-1}$. The product has units of particle flux density, $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$.

In charge-state particle balance, this quantity enters through the field-aligned divergence term, commonly written inline as $\nabla \cdot (\Gamma_{\parallel,z}\hat{b})$, together with perpendicular transport and sources or sinks from ionization, recombination, charge exchange, and external fueling. It is usually computed from kinetic distribution moments or fluid density and flow variables, and may be constrained indirectly using spectroscopy, charge-exchange measurements, and transport reconstruction.

Typical magnitudes vary widely with species, charge state, confinement region, and collisionality. Trace impurity charge states in the confined plasma may be below $10^{18}$ m^-2.s^-1, while edge, scrape-off-layer, and divertor charge states with strong field-aligned flows commonly reach $10^{20}-10^{24}$ m^-2.s^-1.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions in the specified charge state flow in the direction of the local magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$, equivalently along $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Effective local diffusivity for ion thermal-energy transport along the magnetic field. It applies to a specified ion species when the transported energy is species resolved, and to a total-ion effective channel when ion energies are summed.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion energy diffusivity is the local effective diffusion coefficient that relates field-aligned gradients of ion thermal energy to the conductive part of the ion heat flux. It characterizes how rapidly ion thermal energy is smoothed along magnetic field lines; for a species-resolved energy variable it is species-specific, while for a summed ion energy variable it is an aggregate total-ion coefficient. It is a local transport coefficient, not a line, flux-surface, or volume average unless an averaging operation is explicitly part of the physical model.

A common Fick's-law closure for the conductive field-aligned energy flux is:

$$
q_{E_i,\parallel} = -\chi_{E_i,\parallel}\,\nabla_\parallel w_i
$$

where $q_{E_i,\parallel}$ is the scalar parallel ion heat-flux density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ and is positive for energy transport along $\hat{b}$, $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector in the direction of the local magnetic field, $\chi_{E_i,\parallel}$ is the parallel ion energy diffusivity in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $w_i$ is the local ion thermal energy density in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $\nabla_\parallel=\hat{b}\cdot\nabla$ is the derivative along the magnetic field in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The minus sign means that the conductive heat flux is down the field-aligned energy-density gradient. For a single ion species $s$, $w_s$ may be written as $(3/2)n_s\mathcal{T}_s$, with $n_s$ in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_s$ the ion temperature expressed as energy per particle in joules; if $T_s$ is given in eV, then $\mathcal{T}_s=eT_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge. For total-ion energy, $w_i$ represents the summed thermal energy density over the ion species included in the model.

This coefficient is usually inferred or prescribed rather than measured directly. It may be obtained from transport analysis, from collisional or fluid closure estimates, or by fitting field-aligned heat transport in a reduced model; the interpretation depends on the thermal-energy variable to which the coefficient is applied.

Typical magnitudes are strongly regime and model dependent. Collisional estimates scale roughly with ion thermal speed squared times the ion-ion collision time; representative effective values can range from $10^2-10^6\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ in cold, collisional edge or scrape-off-layer plasmas to $10^8-10^{11}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ in hot, weakly collisional core plasmas.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the total ion particle flux density along the local magnetic field direction, aggregated over all charge states of the ion species.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion particle flux $\Gamma_{\parallel,i}$ quantifies the net flow of ions per unit area per unit time along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, summed over all charge states of the ion species. It enters the ion density continuity equation as the divergence term governing parallel transport, and is the dominant particle transport channel along open magnetic field lines in the scrape-off layer and divertor regions.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Gamma_{\parallel,i} = n_i \, v_{\parallel,i}
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density and $v_{\parallel,i}$ is the component of the ion fluid velocity parallel to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity is computed in edge and plasma transport models from the fluid momentum balance or by integrating the ion distribution function over the parallel velocity dimension. For charge-state-resolved transport, the counterpart [parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_charge_state_particle_flux) provides per-charge-state resolution. The analogous quantities for other plasma components are [parallel_electron_particle_flux](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux) and [parallel_neutral_particle_flux](name:parallel_neutral_particle_flux).

Typical magnitudes in the scrape-off layer range from $10^{20}$ to $10^{22}$ m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, with values increasing toward divertor target plates as parallel flow accelerates toward the Bohm condition at the magnetic presheath entrance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion particle flow is co-directed with the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Inverse relaxation time for dissipation of the field-aligned flow momentum of a specific ion charge state, driven by Coulomb collisions and neoclassical viscous stresses.
NAMES.long:
The parallel ion state momentum damping rate $\nu_\parallel$ is the inverse time scale at which the magnetic-field-aligned flow momentum of an ion species in a specified charge state is removed by collisional friction, pitch-angle scattering, and neoclassical viscous stresses. It provides charge-state resolution of the parallel momentum sink, distinguishing contributions from individual ionization levels and enabling accurate tracking of impurity momentum balance across species.

The rate enters the parallel component of the ion momentum transport equation as a linear sink:

$$
\frac{\partial u_\parallel}{\partial t} = \cdots - \nu_\parallel \, u_\parallel
$$

where $u_\parallel = \mathbf{u} \cdot \hat{b}$ is the parallel flow velocity of the charge state, $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, and $\nu_\parallel$ is this damping rate. The parallel component is distinguished from the poloidal and radial projections: see [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate) and [radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate). The charge-state-summed counterpart is [parallel_ion_momentum_damping_rate](name:parallel_ion_momentum_damping_rate), and this quantity is a directional component of [ion_state_momentum_damping_rate](name:ion_state_momentum_damping_rate). The rate is computed from neoclassical transport theory or Fokker–Planck kinetic models as a function of plasma density, temperature, ion charge, and collisionality regime.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel momentum of the ion charge state is being dissipated, corresponding to a damping sink acting to reduce the parallel flow velocity toward zero.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged parallel total current density, defined by the total current density projected on the magnetic field and normalized by the signed reference toroidal magnetic field. It is the net field-aligned current density used in transport current-balance physics.
NAMES.long:
Parallel total current density is a signed scalar measure of the net total current flowing along the magnetic field, expressed with the flux-surface-averaged, reference-field-normalized convention used in transport physics. It combines all physical mechanisms contributing to the total current before evaluating the field-aligned component.

The defining convention is the flux-surface average of the magnetic-field projection of the total current density divided by the signed reference toroidal magnetic field:

$$
j_{\parallel,\mathrm{tot}} = \frac{\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $B_0$ is the signed reference toroidal magnetic field in T, and $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes an average over a magnetic flux surface.

In practice, the quantity is computed by forming the total current density, taking its scalar product with the magnetic field, applying the flux-surface average, and dividing by $B_0$. Magnetic-equilibrium constraints determine the current distribution, while kinetic and current-drive physics may determine how individual contributions add to the total; this quantity is the summed total after applying the same convention.

Representative magnitudes in tokamak transport analyzes are commonly $10^4$-$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, depending on plasma current, cross-sectional area, magnetic geometry, and non-inductive current drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\left\langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{tot}}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right\rangle$ has the same sign as the signed reference toroidal magnetic field $B_0$; $B_0$ is positive when the reference toroidal field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: parallel_trapped_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged field-aligned component of the pressure tensor for trapped fast particles. It is evaluated from the trapped-orbit part of the non-thermal distribution function and represents the parallel kinetic stress of that population.
NAMES.long:
Parallel trapped fast particle pressure is the component of the fast-particle pressure tensor along the magnetic field, restricted to particles whose guiding-center orbits are trapped between mirror points. It is a flux-surface-averaged second velocity moment of the trapped-orbit part of the non-thermal distribution and quantifies the field-aligned kinetic stress carried by that population.

The flux-surface-averaged parallel pressure is defined by the trapped fast-particle velocity moment:

$$
p_{\parallel,\mathrm{fast,tr}}(\psi) = \left\langle \sum_s m_s \int \left(v_\parallel - U_{\parallel s}\right)^2 f_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_\psi
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes an average over a closed magnetic flux surface labeled by $\psi$, $s$ indexes fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $v_\parallel$ and $U_{\parallel s}$ are velocities along the magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, and $f_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}$ is normalized so that $\int f_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}\,d^3v = n_{\mathrm{fast,tr},s}$ with density in m$^{-3}$. If the retained fast-particle distribution has negligible mean parallel flow, $U_{\parallel s}$ is set to zero; for multiple fast species, the result is the mass-weighted sum of their separate moment contributions.

This quantity is usually computed from a kinetic fast-particle distribution after classifying phase-space elements by trapped-orbit topology in the reconstructed magnetic equilibrium. It is not a direct diagnostic observable, but it can be constrained by energetic-particle measurements and by consistency with equilibrium and transport analysis. Because trapped particles reverse $v_\parallel$ along their bounce motion, the first parallel moment may be small while this second moment remains finite.

Typical flux-surface-averaged values range from 10$^2$-10$^5$ Pa in heated tokamak core plasmas, with lower values toward the edge or in weak fast-particle populations. High-fast-pressure regimes can approach 10$^6$ Pa locally or on central flux surfaces, while the trapped parallel component may be much smaller than the total fast-particle pressure when the distribution is strongly perpendicular-anisotropic.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.subject: particle
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the species-summed fast-particle pressure tensor for co-passing orbits, produced by velocity components transverse to the local magnetic field. Co-passing denotes passing guiding-center motion with the same toroidal sense as the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure is the perpendicular component of the fast-particle pressure tensor after restricting the distribution to co-passing passing orbits and summing over the included fast species. It represents kinetic stress from velocity components orthogonal to the local magnetic field. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, co-passing denotes passing guiding-center orbits whose toroidal motion is in the same sense as the plasma current.

The species-summed kinetic moment is

$$
P_{\perp,\mathrm{co}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}} \frac{1}{2} m_s v_\perp^2 f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $s$ labels the included fast-particle species, $m_s$ is the species mass in kg, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $t$ is time in s, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field in m s$^{-1}$, $f_s$ is the fast-particle distribution function in s$^3$ m$^{-6}$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element in m$^3$ s$^{-3}$. The domain $\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}$ is the passing part of velocity space whose guiding-center orbit has bounce-averaged toroidal velocity $R\dot{\phi}$, in the same $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, in the same sense as the plasma current; trapped and counter-passing orbits are excluded. For common heating and fusion-product applications the fast species are usually energetic ions, but the definition applies to any suprathermal species included in the sum.

This quantity is computed as a second velocity moment of an orbit-class-resolved fast-particle distribution, typically after classifying particles by pitch, constants of motion, or guiding-center trajectories. It is not usually measured directly as a local tensor component; instead it is inferred through kinetic modeling constrained by diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal particles. Together with [parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure), it describes pressure anisotropy of the co-passing fast population, while [perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure) includes the corresponding perpendicular contributions from all fast-particle orbit classes.

Typical values are strongly scenario dependent. As an order-of-magnitude guide, auxiliary-heated tokamak cores can have perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressures of about $10^2$-$5\times10^4$ Pa, with much smaller values in weakly heated regions or where the co-passing fast-particle population is depleted.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Scalar component of runaway-electron particle flux across magnetic flux surfaces, projected onto the outward flux-surface normal.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular runaway-electron particle flux is the scalar flux of runaway electrons crossing magnetic flux surfaces. It is the normal component of the runaway-electron particle-flux vector and describes cross-field transport, distinct from particle motion along the local magnetic-field direction as represented by parallel particle-flux components such as [parallel_electron_particle_flux](name:parallel_electron_particle_flux) and [parallel_ion_particle_flux](name:parallel_ion_particle_flux).

The projection defining the scalar perpendicular flux is

$$
\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron particle-flux vector in m^-2.s^-1 and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the dimensionless unit normal to the magnetic flux surface, oriented from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary. The scalar $\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}}$ has units m^-2.s^-1.

In transport modeling this quantity may be computed from the continuity balance for [runaway_electron_density](name:runaway_electron_density) or represented with an effective convection-diffusion closure along a local flux-surface-normal coordinate $r_\perp$ in meters. A common form is $\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}} = -D_\perp\,\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial r_\perp + V_\perp n_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $D_\perp$ is [perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity) in m^2.s^-1, $V_\perp$ is [perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) in m.s^-1, $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is runaway-electron density in m^-3, and $\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial r_\perp$ has units m^-4. This closure is a modeling representation; the physical quantity itself is the normal projection of the particle flux.

The flux is generally inferred rather than measured directly, using reconstructed or modeled runaway-electron density evolution together with transport assumptions. No device-independent numerical range is implied by the standard name; representative magnitudes should be assessed from the scale $|\Gamma_{\perp,\mathrm{RE}}| \sim D_\perp n_{\mathrm{RE}}/L_\perp + |V_\perp| n_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $L_\perp$ is the characteristic density-gradient length in meters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flux is directed along the outward flux-surface normal from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the plasma center-of-mass velocity, computed as the mass-weighted mean of all contributing species fluid velocities projected onto the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long:
The center-of-mass velocity describes the bulk fluid motion of the plasma as a whole, accounting for all ionic, electronic, and neutral particle species weighted by their mass density. The poloidal component $v_{\theta,\mathrm{cm}}$ characterizes the net poloidal circulation of this composite fluid, which governs neoclassical poloidal rotation and enters the radial force balance that determines the radial electric field.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_{\theta,\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s v_{\theta,s}}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $n_s$ its number density, and $v_{\theta,s}$ its individual poloidal fluid velocity, with the sum running over all plasma species.

The poloidal component complements [toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity) to describe the bulk plasma flow in the poloidal plane; [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity) and [poloidal_neutral_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity) give the individual species contributions. This quantity is inferred from multi-species charge exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with momentum-balance constraints in fluid transport modeling.

Poloidal rotation speeds in tokamak plasmas are typically small relative to toroidal rotation, with values in the range 0.1-5 km/s in the plasma core and potentially higher magnitudes near internal transport barriers and the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bulk plasma flow is directed in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Poloidal particle diffusivity, also called a diffusion coefficient, for a specified ion charge state in edge plasma. It relates the diffusive particle flux along poloidal arclength to the charge-state density gradient.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state diffusion coefficient is the scalar transport coefficient for density-gradient-driven particle diffusion of a specified ion species in a specified charge state along the poloidal direction. It represents the diffusive part of particle mixing around magnetic flux surfaces and is distinct from convective, source, sink, or radial transport terms.

The Fickian contribution to the poloidal particle flux is commonly written:

$$
\Gamma_{\theta,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\theta,i,q}\,\frac{\partial n_{i,q}}{\partial l_\theta}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\theta,i,q}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal diffusive particle flux of ion species $i$ in charge state $q$ in $m^{-2}\,s^{-1}$, $D_{\theta,i,q}$ is the poloidal diffusion coefficient in $m^2\,s^{-1}$, $n_{i,q}$ is the charge-state density in $m^{-3}$, and $l_\theta$ is poloidal arclength in meters. The leading minus sign means that a positive diffusivity drives particles from higher density toward lower density along the poloidal path.

In practice this coefficient is inferred or prescribed in edge transport modeling from particle balance, impurity or main-ion density evolution, comparison with spectroscopic and probe measurements, or reduced descriptions of turbulent and collisional cross-field mixing. It is often an effective coefficient that may combine unresolved turbulent transport with collisional contributions for the selected charge state.

Typical effective edge and scrape-off-layer values are about 0.1-10 m^2.s^-1, with smaller values possible for nearly neoclassical transport and larger values in strongly turbulent or transient boundary-plasma conditions. As a scalar diffusivity it is normally non-negative; fitted negative values usually indicate limitations of a reduced transport model or missing off-diagonal transport terms rather than physical diffusion.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_state_momentum_damping_rate
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Reciprocal of the relaxation time for collisional or neoclassical damping of the poloidal momentum of a specified ion species and charge state. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the meridional plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) system and points along increasing theta in explicit flux coordinates such as (rho, theta, phi).
NAMES.long:
Poloidal ion-state momentum damping rate is the reciprocal of the relaxation time over which the poloidal momentum of a specified ion species and charge state is dissipated. The poloidal component is tangent to a magnetic flux surface in the meridional $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; equivalently it is the component along increasing $\theta$ in an explicitly specified flux coordinate system such as $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$.

In a local momentum-density balance, the damping contribution is represented as a linear relaxation term:

$$
\left(\frac{\partial p_{\theta,a}}{\partial t}\right)_\mathrm{damp} = -\nu_{\theta,a}\, p_{\theta,a}
$$

where $a$ labels the ion charge state, $\nu_{\theta,a}$ is the damping rate, and $p_{\theta,a} = m_a n_a V_{\theta,a}$ is the poloidal momentum density with $m_a$ in kg, $n_a$ in m$^{-3}$, and $V_{\theta,a}$ in m s$^{-1}$. The minus sign makes the term dissipative: a non-negative $\nu_{\theta,a}$ relaxes the existing poloidal momentum toward zero regardless of its sign.

This rate is typically obtained from collisional and neoclassical momentum-balance models, or inferred by fitting observed poloidal-flow relaxation to such a balance. It depends on charge state, ion mass and charge, density, temperature, magnetic geometry, collisionality, and coupling to other species through Coulomb friction and poloidal viscous stresses. Charge-state resolution matters for impurity species occupying several ionization stages simultaneously, each carrying a distinct damping coefficient; the species-summed counterpart is the poloidal ion momentum damping rate.

As an order-of-magnitude guide, hot, weakly collisional core conditions tend to give values near $10^2$-$10^5$ s$^{-1}$, while cooler, denser, more collisional edge conditions and high-charge states can reach $10^5$-$10^7$ s$^{-1}$; these ranges are contextual rather than canonical.

NAMES.name: poloidal_momentum_effective_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective radial convection velocity for transport of aggregate ion poloidal momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is the velocity-like coefficient of the convective, or pinch, term rather than the poloidal flow speed itself.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal momentum effective convection velocity is the velocity-like coefficient that represents radial advection of aggregate ion poloidal momentum across magnetic flux surfaces. It is a transport coefficient in the momentum balance, not the poloidal flow speed itself, and no additional moment-arm or angular-momentum normalization is implied.

The coefficient is defined by the convective term in a diffusion-convection decomposition of the radial flux of poloidal ion momentum:

$$
\Pi_{\theta,r} = -D_\theta \frac{\partial (m_i n_i v_\theta)}{\partial r} + V_\theta^{\mathrm{eff}} m_i n_i v_\theta
$$

where $V_\theta^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is this quantity in $m.s^{-1}$, $\Pi_{\theta,r}$ is the radial flux of poloidal momentum in $kg.m^{-1}.s^{-2}$, $D_\theta$ is the poloidal momentum diffusivity in $m^2.s^{-1}$, $m_i$ is ion mass in $kg$, $n_i$ is ion number density in $m^{-3}$, $v_\theta$ is poloidal flow speed in $m.s^{-1}$, and $r$ is a minor-radius-like radial label in meters increasing outward across the flux surfaces. The component $\theta$ is the poloidal direction in flux coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$, where $\theta$ is poloidal angle and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. For multiple ion species or charge states, $m_i n_i v_\theta$ denotes the aggregate ion poloidal momentum density used in the balance.

In practice, this coefficient is specified by a transport closure or inferred by fitting an evaluated radial poloidal-momentum flux to a chosen diffusive-convective form. The split between diffusion and convection is meaningful only after the transported momentum density, radial label, and diffusivity convention have been fixed. This aggregate-ion quantity has the same physical role as poloidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity, while [poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_momentum_convection_velocity) denotes the corresponding charge-state-resolved coefficient; related component analogs include toroidal_ion_momentum_convection_velocity and [parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity](name:parallel_momentum_effective_convection_velocity).

Representative magnitudes are strongly model- and regime-dependent. In core momentum-transport studies the magnitude is often of order 0-10 m.s^-1, while fitted edge, pedestal, or transient coefficients can reach several tens of m.s^-1; either sign is possible depending on whether the effective convective transport is outward or inward.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective convective transport of poloidal momentum is radially outward, from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: neutral_state
NAMES.short: Effective poloidal diffusivity for energy transport of neutral particles in a specified state.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal neutral-state energy diffusion coefficient is the effective diffusivity multiplying the poloidal gradient of neutral energy density for particles in a specified neutral state. In this context, diffusion coefficient and diffusivity denote the same physical transport coefficient, with dimensions of area per time.

For a Fickian closure in a flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, the poloidal neutral-energy flux density may be written as

$$
q_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)} = -D_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}\,\frac{1}{h_\theta}\frac{\partial U_E^{(n,s)}}{\partial \theta}
$$

where $q_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$ is the poloidal neutral-energy flux density in W m$^{-2}$, $D_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$ is this diffusion coefficient in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, $U_E^{(n,s)}$ is the neutral energy density in J m$^{-3}$, $h_\theta$ is the poloidal metric scale factor in meters, and $(n,s)$ identifies the neutral species and state. The flux component $q_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$ is positive in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$; the minus sign means that, for positive $D_{E,\theta}^{(n,s)}$, energy diffuses down the poloidal energy-density gradient.

This coefficient is usually not measured directly. It is inferred or prescribed in neutral transport modeling from collisional mean-free-path estimates, kinetic or fluid neutral calculations, and calibration against measurements sensitive to neutral energy transport, such as neutral pressure, emission, and edge power-balance constraints.

Typical effective values are broad because neutral mean free paths vary strongly with ionization, charge exchange, and wall recycling conditions.
