This quantity is computed from kinetic transport, Fokker-Planck, Monte Carlo, or reduced fast-particle models by applying Coulomb collision operators to the trapped part of the distribution and taking the kinetic-energy moment. Experimentally constrained estimates use reconstructed fast-particle distributions, magnetic-equilibrium information for orbit classification, and background density and temperature profiles that determine the collisional coefficients.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 10^3-10^7 W m^-3 in neutral-beam, radio-frequency, or fusion-alpha fast-particle populations, with values below 10^3 W m^-3 in weak tails or near depleted regions and localized peaks approaching 10^8 W m^-3 in compact high-power scenarios. The sign can be either positive or negative depending on whether collisions heat or slow the trapped fast-particle population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy to the fast-particle population associated with trapped orbits.

NAMES.name: vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion_state
NAMES.short: Z component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, of the pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift velocity of a specified ion charge state. It is perpendicular to the local magnetic field and that charge state's pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
The vertical ion-state velocity due to diamagnetic drift is the $Z$ component of the ion charge-state diamagnetic drift velocity in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The corresponding vector quantity is [ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift); together with [radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), this component describes the projection of that drift onto the cylindrical basis.

For an ion species and charge state $(i,k)$ with isotropic pressure, the vertical component is defined by the pressure-gradient drift formula:

$$
v_{\mathrm{dia},Z}^{i,k} =
\frac{\left(\nabla p_{i,k} \times \mathbf{B}\right)\cdot \hat{Z}}
{\mathcal{Z}_{i,k} e\, n_{i,k}\, |\mathbf{B}|^2}
$$

where $p_{i,k}$ is the charge-state pressure in $\mathrm{Pa}$, $\nabla p_{i,k}$ is its spatial gradient in $\mathrm{Pa\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in $\mathrm{T}$, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude in $\mathrm{T}$, $n_{i,k}$ is the charge-state density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $\mathcal{Z}_{i,k}$ is the dimensionless positive ion charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge in $\mathrm{C}$, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is generally evaluated from measured, reconstructed, or calculated pressure and magnetic-field information rather than measured as an independent flow component. The pressure may be obtained from charge-state density and temperature, using $p_{i,k}=n_{i,k}T_{i,k}$ when $T_{i,k}$ is expressed as energy per particle with consistent conversion to $\mathrm{Pa}$. It represents the pressure-gradient part of the perpendicular fluid drift and is physically distinct from the electric-field-driven [vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:vertical_ion_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift) and from parallel flow.

Typical absolute values in magnetized edge plasmas are 100-10000 m.s^-1, depending on pressure-gradient scale length, magnetic-field strength, density, and charge state. The vertical component can be smaller in regions where the projection of $\nabla p_{i,k} \times \mathbf{B}$ onto $\hat{Z}$ is weak, and it can change sign across pressure extrema or where the local magnetic geometry changes the projected drift direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic drift velocity component points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_carbon_density
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the total carbon number density, summed over all charge states from neutral to fully stripped carbon.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged carbon density is the spatial mean of the total carbon particle number density over the confined plasma volume, aggregating contributions from all ionization states. It serves as a single global scalar monitor of the total carbon impurity inventory in the confined plasma, applied in impurity transport analysis and energy-balance accounting.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_C \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \sum_{z=0}^{6} n_{C,z}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_{C,z}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local number density of carbon in ionization state $z$ (from neutral $z=0$ through fully stripped $z=6$), and $V$ is the plasma volume bounded by the last-closed flux surface. This quantity is the volume-averaging transformation applied to [carbon_density](name:carbon_density).

In practice it is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of carbon emission lines, ultraviolet spectroscopy, or impurity transport modeling integrated over the full plasma cross-section.

Typical values range from $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in low-impurity plasmas with conditioned walls, rising toward $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in carbon-wall machines with significant recycling. The companion [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density) provides a chord-weighted rather than volume-weighted mean; the two quantities differ in the presence of radial density gradients. Analogous volume-averaged impurity densities for other light species are [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) and [volume_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which follow the same transformation-subject-base grammar pattern.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_neon_density
NAMES.subject: neon
NAMES.short: Mean elemental number density of neon averaged over the plasma volume, where the local neon density is the sum over all ionization states from neutral neon to fully stripped neon.
NAMES.long:
Volume-averaged neon density is the plasma-volume mean of the total elemental neon number density. The local elemental neon density includes all charge states of neon, from neutral atoms to fully stripped ions, so it measures neon content rather than any single neon ionization state.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{Ne}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V \left(\sum_{q=0}^{10} n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}(\mathbf{x})\right)\,dV
$$

where $V$ is the plasma volume in m$^3$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, $n_{\mathrm{Ne}^{q+}}$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$ of neon with charge state $q$, and $q=0$ denotes neutral neon while $q=10$ denotes fully stripped neon.

In practice, this quantity is inferred by combining impurity diagnostics and plasma modeling that relate neon line radiation, charge-state balance, transport, and ionization-recombination physics to an elemental neon density distribution. The volume average provides a single bulk measure of neon impurity inventory, useful for comparing seeding level, dilution, and radiative impurity content across plasma scenarios.

Representative values are highly scenario dependent. Trace neon concentrations may give volume-averaged densities around $10^{15}$-$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$, while deliberate neon seeding for radiation control can produce values of order $10^{17}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on plasma density, confinement, and impurity source strength.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the total nitrogen number density, summed over all ionization states from neutral to fully stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged nitrogen density $\langle n_N \rangle$ is the spatial mean of the local nitrogen number density over the entire plasma volume, with contributions from all charge states between neutral $N^0$ and fully stripped $N^{7+}$. It condenses the spatially varying impurity field into a single scalar that represents the total nitrogen inventory of the discharge, complementing the local [nitrogen_density](name:nitrogen_density) profiles resolved in space.

The defining spatial average is:

$$
\langle n_N \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_N(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume and $n_N(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nitrogen number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, aggregated across all ionization states.

Nitrogen is deliberately seeded in fusion devices to radiate power in the divertor and scrape-off layer, reducing heat loads on plasma-facing components. The volume-averaged density is inferred from spectroscopic measurements of nitrogen line emission or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with global particle-balance analysis.

In nitrogen-seeded H-mode discharges, values range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, a small fraction of the total electron density yet radiatively significant. For a chord-integrated counterpart, see [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density); [nitrogen_fraction](name:nitrogen_fraction) normalizes this density to the local electron density. The analogous quantity for neon impurity seeding is [volume_averaged_neon_density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density).

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of the bulk thermal (Maxwellian) electron population, excluding fast and suprathermal electron contributions.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron density $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the number of thermal (Maxwellian) electrons per unit volume, representing the bulk electron component whose velocity distribution is described by a Maxwellian at the local electron temperature. It is the dominant electron population in most quiescent plasma conditions and is the relevant density for transport equations, pressure balance, and quasineutrality constraints.

The total [electron_density](name:electron_density) partitions into thermal and fast contributions:

$$
n_e = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [fast electron density]. In the absence of significant suprathermal populations this fast term is negligible and $n_{e,\mathrm{th}} \approx n_e$.

Thomson scattering and microwave reflectometry measure the electron density profile; where the fast electron population is negligible, the inferred $n_e$ directly approximates $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$. During electron cyclotron current drive or lower hybrid heating scenarios the fast electron contribution becomes appreciable and the two populations must be tracked separately.

Typical core values range from $1 \times 10^{19}$ to $2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in tokamak plasmas, falling to $10^{17}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer. The thermal electron density enters the electron thermal pressure $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} T_e$ and the charge-neutrality relation, and is the electron-species analog of [thermal_ion_density](name:thermal_ion_density).

NAMES.name: total_neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure of neutral particles, summing both thermal and non-thermal (fast) contributions across all internal states of the neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Total neutral pressure is the combined kinetic pressure of the neutral particle population, comprising isotropic thermal pressure from neutrals near local thermodynamic equilibrium and non-thermal pressure from suprathermal (fast) neutrals, aggregated across all internal quantum states of the species.

The total pressure decomposes as:

$$
p_\mathrm{neutral} = p_\mathrm{th} + p_\mathrm{fast}
$$

where $p_\mathrm{th} = n_\mathrm{th}\,k_B\,T_\mathrm{neutral}$ is the thermal contribution, $n_\mathrm{th}$ is the thermal neutral number density, $T_\mathrm{neutral}$ is the neutral temperature, and $p_\mathrm{fast}$ is the non-thermal pressure from suprathermal neutrals, computed as one-third of the second velocity moment of the fast neutral distribution function.

In plasma transport modeling, the neutral pressure profile is computed from coupled fluid or kinetic neutral models in which charge exchange and ionization redistribute momentum between the neutral and plasma populations. This quantity enters plasma momentum and energy balance equations as a source term and governs neutral penetration depth into the confined plasma.

In core plasma regions, strong ionization screens neutral penetration and total neutral pressures remain well below 1 Pa. In the edge plasma and scrape-off layer, values range from 0.01–10 Pa under standard recycling conditions; near divertor strike points during high-recycling operation, values can approach tens of Pa. The state-resolved counterpart is [total_neutral_state_pressure](name:total_neutral_state_pressure); the thermal-only contribution is described by [thermal_neutral_pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure); and the analogous ion quantity is [total_ion_state_pressure](name:total_ion_state_pressure). The parent quantity [neutral_pressure](name:neutral_pressure) describes gage measurements of bulk neutral gas pressure in the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles exert an outward kinetic pressure on an enclosing surface element, consistent with pressure as a non-negative second-order moment of the neutral velocity distribution.

NAMES.name: vertical_vorticity
NAMES.short: Vertical vorticity is the projection of the plasma vorticity vector onto the vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the Z-component of the curl of the plasma fluid velocity and measures signed local rotation in the R-φ plane.
NAMES.long:
Vertical vorticity is the component of the plasma-fluid [vorticity](name:vorticity) vector along the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$. It measures the signed local angular shear of the velocity field associated with circulation about the vertical direction. The complementary cylindrical components are [radial_vorticity](name:radial_vorticity) and [toroidal_vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity); related magnetic-geometry projections include [poloidal_vorticity](name:poloidal_vorticity) and [parallel_vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity).

For a plasma fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}$ with cylindrical components $v_R$ and $v_\phi$, the vertical component of the curl is

$$
\omega_Z = (\nabla \times \mathbf{v})\cdot\hat{Z} = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial (R v_\phi)}{\partial R} - \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial v_R}{\partial \phi}
$$

where derivatives are taken in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and $\omega_Z$ has unit s^-1. In axisymmetric conditions the toroidal-derivative term is absent, so vertical vorticity is mainly the radial shear of $R v_\phi$; in non-axisymmetric or turbulent flows, toroidal variation of the radial velocity can also contribute.

Vertical vorticity is computed by differentiating measured or modeled velocity fields. In experiments the required velocity components can be inferred from flow diagnostics and from reconstructed $E\times B$, diamagnetic, or parallel-flow contributions; in transport and turbulence modeling it is obtained directly from the simulated plasma velocity field or from drift-reduced stream-function formulations.

Typical magnitudes are 10^3-10^5 s^-1 for slowly varying core rotation shear, 10^4-10^6 s^-1 in edge transport barriers and scrape-off-layer turbulence, and up to 10^6-10^7 s^-1 during rapid transient or small-scale shear events. The signed value may change across shear layers, vortices, and turbulent eddies.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $(\nabla \times \mathbf{v})$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron number density averaged over the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface, providing the primary global scalar for discharge density characterization and density feedback control.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged electron density $\langle n_e \rangle$ is the mean of the local electron number density integrated over the plasma volume $V$ bounded by the last closed flux surface (LCFS). It compresses the full radial electron density profile into a single global scalar that quantifies the total electron content of the discharge, serving as a primary parameter in confinement characterization and fueling control.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_e \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_e(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $n_e(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [electron density] and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the LCFS.

Multi-channel interferometry estimates $\langle n_e \rangle$ directly by combining line-integrated electron density measurements from multiple viewing chords spanning different minor-radius positions. Profile diagnostics such as Thomson scattering and reflectometry constrain the spatial distribution, while equilibrium reconstruction provides the LCFS boundary geometry that defines $V$.

Representative values in H-mode tokamak discharges span $0.3$–$1.5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with the volume average lying below the on-axis peak for centrally-peaked profiles. Together with [volume_averaged_electron_temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) and [volume_averaged_ion_density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), it forms the set of global scalar parameters entering energy confinement scaling laws and Greenwald density-limit assessments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electrons are present within the plasma volume.
